en: *Fǔyào Jì* (Supplementary Notes on the *Shí bīní yì cāo*), Volume One (including preface),
from the beginning of the text up to the end of the section on "Transforming Karma and Changing Faculties.
Recorded by the Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.
This transcription was composed by our ancestor, who extracted the essential principles from the Great Vinaya Piṭaka to form this text.
Having finally completed it with his lead pencil, a scholar from Silla secretly stole it and returned to his country; thus, for two hundred years, the original manuscript was lost to this land.
In the fifth year of the Huichang era, it was recovered through Li Yuanzo, an Attendant-in-Ordinary, who sent it from the kingdom of Haidong (Silla) via the Golden Secretary (Kim Sa-jin).
I sought it at Huiming Monastery in the royal capital and at Dongquan Monastery in Shizixiang;
the monk Xuanling then collated and transcribed it, sending it here on the eighth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Dazhong era. Alas!
Some may blame me for having stolen it, but I say this is not so. Why? It is because the Way of the Great Master was destined to be spread throughout the world; thus, the spirit...
Borrowing his hand to further the benefits of the Dharma, it is by this means that the texts of this land will circulate before they have gone far and then return.

During the Jingyou era, while I was composing the *Jieben Shuji* (Commentary on the Sūtra of Precepts) at Fulong, the Vinaya Master Chongyu of Zhehe personally brought this manuscript to knock at my door to bestow its kindness upon me.
Thus, whenever I took up the pen to draft the abridgment, I was able to consult it; yet even so, there were still points requiring further examination.
To enter a sandalwood grove and yet still smell the fragrance of *campaka* flowers—how could the subtle benefits of the Dharma’s principles be mere empty words?
Yet, from the Great Tang dynasty until today, more than two hundred years have passed; during this interval, scribal errors and distorted interpretations have remained prevalent.

Although I have previously attempted to provide a rough classification of the text at Chongfasi, I was hindered by exhaustion and my efforts did not reach the point of committing them to brush and ink.
After completing my record, I moved to Jingzhu Temple. One day, after finishing my lecture, I opened my case and reviewed it once more;

I examined every citation against the original texts, thereby correcting the error of "Emperor Hu. Consequently, I produced six fascicles of this record, titled *Fuyao* (Aiding the Essentials), hoping it might assist in upholding the ultimate essentials of the former sages.
I trust that those of superior talent will not reproach me for my rash and inelegant composition.
Preface written on the third day of the first month of summer in the second year of the Great Song’s Qīnglì era, the *rénwǔ* year of the sexagenary cycle.
The ten characters in the title of the *Shí bīní yìchāo* (Excerpts on the Meaning of the Vinaya): the first three characters indicate the master’s own school-affiliated name;
the following seven characters show the specific title of the present commentary. Furthermore, the five characters “Sifen lü” (Four-Part Vinaya) and “bīní” (vinaya) pertain to the source text.
The single character "Explaining" (*xuán*) signifies that which is explained; the two characters "Gathering and Extracting" (*shí cǎo*) indicate the title of this compendium.

"Scrollable" means it can be rolled up or spread out. "Upper" distinguishes it from the middle and lower [volumes]. In Sanskrit, it is called *catur-varga*; in the Chinese language, it is translated as "Four Parts.

The *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen jieshu*) states: "The 'Four Parts' is the designation for the revealed doctrine. It is traditionally transmitted that this name and teaching arose one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
From the Theravāda school, the essential and comprehensive points were extracted and compiled into a single work in four sections (*caturvarga*).

Because the transmitted texts exhaustively explain all the characteristics of the subject matter, it is called "Four Parts" (*Caturvarga*); this refers to the extent of the discourse and is not a classification based on meaning.
For instance, the *Viṃśati-khandaka* could be divided into three parts if categorized by meaning. Regarding the term *yǔlè* (律), it is the Western [Sanskrit] sound for *vinaya*, etc.
This term "lü" (律) refers to the penal system of this region; thus, the *Fengsu tong* states that Gao Yao advised Emperor Shun of Yu in establishing the laws.

Therefore, we know that while the Chinese and Sanskrit names differ, their substance is one—just as in our own school, the two terms *vinaya* and *lü* do not exist simultaneously as distinct entities.
Mount Zhongnan is the numinous peak where [the Master] resides. According to the *Hanshu*, Mount Taiyi—referred to as Zhongnan in ancient texts—is the southern mountain of Chang’an.
A poem says: "Lofty is that Southern Mountain, its crags and rocks towering.
This mountain is also known as Dizui (Earth-Lung), for it can provide refuge from floods; thus, the *Gaoshi zhuan* states that Qi Li Ji and others collectively entered Shang [Mount].

Mount Lipu (Earth-Lung) in Luoyin is this very place. "Śramaṇa" is fully transliterated as *shā mén nà*; here it means "diligent cessation," referring to the diligent practice of various virtues and the cessation and extinction of all evils.
The "Treatise on Sacrifices at the Suburban Altars" in the *Book of the Later Han* states: "Śramaṇa, in the language of Han, means 'one who has ceased the mind' (*xī xīn*).
They shave their hair and leave the household life, severing passions and washing away desires to return to non-action (*wú wèi*). The term "Śākya" is a surname.

The original intent of this undertaking was to summon their true essence; therefore, names and forms were assigned according to their respective categories. For instance, regarding the origins of surnames in the Eastern Continent (China), there were originally only nine;
for those of the Great Summer Continent (India), there are four. However, when clarifying the lineages of the Buddhas, they are divided into five distinct categories:

first is Gautama (the name of a star; some say it means "mud," but this is not so); second is Ikṣvāku (because the Bodhisattva once stayed and practiced the Way in a sugarcane grove, he was named after that grove).

1) Śākya (this means "Capable Benevolence," so named due to his father’s lament); 2) Gautama; 3) Śākyamuni (in the Vinaya it is said that Buddha was of the Śākya clan, which is also the name of the country); 4) Sūryavaṃśa (in the Vinaya it is said his father’s personal name was Sūrya); 5) Ādityagotra. These five clarify the differences while unifying them under one lineage.

Because they evolved according to specific circumstances, such divisions arose. However, as for the single surname Śākya, many scriptures clarify it; as for the others, their appearance or disappearance is left to conditions, and thus I have cited them accordingly. Therefore, [Daoshi] says: [Note:

The provided text fragment ends with "Therefore, Yuo" (祐), likely referring to Daoshi, the author of the *Fayuan Zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), from which this passage is excerpted.]
The Vinaya Master said: "I look up with reverence to the prophecy of Dīpaṃkara, which designated the title Śākyamuni.
A profound mandate and a hidden resonance thus caused him to entrust himself to the Śākya clan; his name emerged before form had yet taken shape, and his traces manifested after birth.

His brilliance illuminated gods and humans, continuing through vast kalpas. How deep indeed is his source! Now, when one speaks of 'Śākya,' it is to distinguish him from the heterodox paths of India."
The term "Śramaṇa" refers to the Śākya clan from which he descended; thus, these are combined for designation. The name of Master Daoxuan is [Daoxuan]; his courtesy name is Fabian.
Regarding his surname, year of birth, spiritual responses, conduct, religious practices, and his passing, all are detailed in his separate biography.

"Zhuàn" (Compilation) refers to the compilation of ancient surviving texts; "Shù" (Exposition) refers to expounding without creating anew. Zheng Kangcheng stated that "shù" means to explain its meaning.
Furthermore, this commentary was composed in the ninth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, whereas the *Śīla-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Precepts) was produced in the eighth year;

had it been written later, it would have appeared after that. Thus, the colophon states: "On the nineteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Yonghui era, the commentary was finally completed."
Regarding the term "jiāng" (將) in "jiāng jiǎng zhě" (將講者): it means "about to. As the *Shijing* says, "Fāng jiāng wàn wǔ" (方將萬舞), it also carries the sense of "assistance.
This means that because the textual meanings within the Vinaya-piṭaka are vast and extensive, I have now merely gathered and selected portions to serve as an auxiliary aid.

Since this is not a comprehensive work, it is called the "Lüe" (略, Brief Summary), which preserves six sections. Let me attempt to discuss this: the former masters have stated that this commentary contains three errors, the first of which concerns the text.
Yi Lu Zhi said: "First, his interpretations are mostly superficial; second, his writings are incomplete, his name buried and his era passed, with no preface before and no commentary after;
third, to preserve what was forgotten, he briefly presented the *Yizhang* (Exposition of Meanings), stating, 'I shall now lecture on the four *pārājikas*.
How can such a formulation of words be so utterly blasphemous toward the former sages? When one examines the logic and phrasing, it is still [merely] superficial."

"It is pure and upright on the outside without artificial ornamentation, yet direct and sparse while harboring profound depths; it possesses the pen of Dong Hu—how could it be as coarse as the wood of He Lu?
Furthermore, regarding the initial commentaries, they were transmitted from teacher to disciple and followed one another in succession, just as in the *Ritual* (Li) where Zichun said:
'I heard this from Zengzi; Zengzi heard it from the Master. This is also the case here. What cause for concern could there be?"

As for the fact that the latter three parts are incomplete, it is likely because the copyist (the *caoshu*) was immediately plagiarized by others as soon as he finished composing the text, leaving him no leisure to write a preface.

Alternatively, it may be because the wording is still concise and essential, and thus the preceding and following sections were omitted; this is just like the Heart Sūtra (*Hṛdaya-sūtra*), which lacks both a preface and a dissemination section (*pariṇāmanā*).
Since this work summarizes the essentials of the extensive *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is truly comparable to it. Furthermore, it begins with the *Vipaśyanā*...
From the general outline of the Bhikṣuṇīs to the rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), each section opens its own gateway of meaning to explore and extract the profound essentials.

Whenever a question is posed, one fears that the key to a heavy lock may be difficult to open; yet when a single answer is extended, it is seen that the ice upon the great river is suddenly melted away.

Were it not for exquisite refinement and deep reflection, how could the subject be fully exhausted? How could it merely serve to prevent forgetfulness? It is simply because the ancients did not examine [the matter].
The textual meanings have been handed down in succession; since these explanations are addressed to later students, should they not be careful?

"Di" (第) means "to dwell," and "yi" (一) is the beginning of numbers. As for "Tathāgata," Nāgārjuna said that because he came by way of the path of reality (*tathatā*) to achieve perfect enlightenment, he is called "Tathāgata.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that non-arising and non-ceasing is itself liberation. Thus it is said:
This liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Regarding the term "world" (*loka*): in common parlance, thirty years constitute a world; furthermore, the succession of father and son constitutes a world.
What is now called "the world" refers to the single vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), consisting of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;

and the second is the sentient-being world (*sattva-loka*), consisting of the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings. Thus, the Sublime Great Awakened One, vast and far-reaching in his transformative influence, brings forth the vessel-world.

The "world" refers to the world of sentient beings who benefit from it; the "five names" refer to the names of the five divisions. Since the five names had already begun to emerge while the Tathāgata was still in the world, the reason they were not divided immediately was as follows:
The Deer Park and the Crane Forest refer to the places where the Tathāgata, having attained enlightenment, necessarily resided while preaching the Dharma;
thus, by briefly citing the beginning and the end, the intervening period is subsumed within the span of no more than forty-nine years.

If one considers his entire life in the world to have lasted eighty years—namely, nineteen years until he left the city, five years of traveling abroad, six years of ascetic practice, and thirty-five years from the attainment of the Way until his passing—then [the teaching period] is likewise accounted for.
The total duration of his preaching the Dharma over ten [reigns] amounts to eighty years.

The reason why it is commonly said that he preached for forty-nine years is that he was born in the fourth month of the tenth year of King Zhuang of the Zhou dynasty under the Ji clan, and entered *parinirvāṇa* in the second month of the nineteenth year of King Hui;

although the number of years is full, when calculated by months, it is actually seventy-nine. This is because, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he entered *parinirvāṇa* during that very year.

Regarding the explanation of the Deer Park: Formerly, when the King of Vārāṇasī entered the mountains for a hunt, he encountered two herds of deer, each numbering five hundred and each with its own leader.
One leader was the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, his body the color of the seven treasures;
the other leader was the Bodhisattva Devadatta. When this leader saw the king slaughtering his herd, he gave rise to great compassion.
The deer king went straight before the king and said, "If you require provisions, we shall send them in rotation, one deer per day. The king approved of his words.
Thereupon, the two leaders each assigned a rotation for sending the deer. When it was the turn of the herd led by Devadatta, a mother deer among them said to her leader, "It is my turn to die;
however, I am pregnant, and my offspring has not yet reached its turn to die. This continued until the time of the Bodhisattva.
The Śarabha King said, "I alone shall take his place," and he went immediately to the king's presence to recount the matter in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the king spoke this verse: "I am indeed a beast, called a 'deer-headed man'; Though you are a beast, you are called a 'man-headed deer.
Speaking according to principle, it is not by form that one is human; If one can possess compassion, even though—"
These beasts were actually humans; from this day forward, I shall not eat any meat at all. By bestowing this gift of fearlessness, I may also bring peace to your minds.
Because it was the dwelling place of a herd of deer, it is called the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*);

it is also called the Forest Given to the Deer (*Mṛgamada-vana*), because King Brahmadatta gave the grove to the deer. It is also known as the Place of the Wheel of Sages (*Ṛṣicakra-sthāna*), because of [the presence of] Rāṣṭrapāla.
Because the Rishi first turned the Wheel of Dharma there, the Tathāgata likewise turned the Wheel of the Four Truths at this very place, first delivering the five Bhadravargīyas.
As for the Śāla Grove, it is located by the Ajiravatī River near the city of Kuśinagara;
the trees are in pairs, and are also called "double trees" because there are two pairs in each of the four directions. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, latter section, states: "To the east..."
The two pairs on the west joined together to form one tree, and the two pairs on the north and south joined together to form another tree;

these hung down and covered the precious couch, sheltering the Tathāgata. At that moment, the trees suddenly turned a somber white, like white cranes; therefore, it was called the Crane Forest (*Haelin*).
It was at this very spot that he was about to enter parinirvāṇa; thus, during the middle watch of the night, he again issued this final command to bestow his bequeathed teachings.

There is none who does not respond to the capacities of others—whether sharp or dull—by establishing prohibitions and precepts according to their nature; since these numbers are unequal, they are said to differ in ten thousand ways.

What follows below infers and explains the meaning of this difference: it is precisely because the two subsequent lines demonstrate that differences in faculties do not exceed the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.

Because it is the root, the following section demonstrates the distinctions among dharmas—namely, the clusters of the seven and five categories of light and heavy offenses, and the characteristics of the laxity or urgency regarding prohibitions and natures.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-uttaragrantha* states: "In the Vinaya, it is said that there are five classes of offenses. The commentary explains: "These are the chapters [of this text];
for example, the *Pārājika* class contains sixteen offenses, and so forth. Although there are differences, they are reconciled below to demonstrate their beneficial function.

This is because there are differences due to the distinctions among these lower causes. If this is so, then the names of the five schools are fully contained within them, and all calculations are included therein.
Furthermore, the citations from the sutras below are all based on what was spoken by the Tathāgata while he was in the world, stating that after my parinirvāṇa there will be five schools.

If that were so, then the names of the five schools would have been clearly manifest even during the Buddha’s lifetime. As for the citation from the *Dharmatrāta-dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (or *Dharmakośa*), it contains no such text;

in fact, it serves as a counter-proof, meaning that if the Tathāgata had truly intended for the Dharma and Vinaya to consist of five distinct meanings, then the transmission records should have stated that they were divided into these five meanings while the Buddha was still in the world. Since this is not the case, [the claim is refuted].

The *Śāstra* states: "The Great Sage Lord, the Muni, has completely severed all views. If one were to add the character "should" (*yīng*) beneath the character "transmit" (*chuán*) in the text, the meaning would become clear.
Furthermore, the *Vaipulya Sūtras* also speak of the differences between the five schools;

since they do not refute the errors regarding persons or dharmas therein, the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "This merely speaks of existence [of the schools] without refuting persons or dharmas. Moreover...
Within the *Mahāvaipulya* [sūtras] as well, it is attested that there are five divisions; since this is a clear and explicit text, how could one possibly require further citation?

Nevertheless, it does not explicitly clarify the division made after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is only in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* that it says, "After his parinirvāṇa, he will be divided into five.

This is a prophetic prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), yet it is not the primary intent [of the teaching]. It is like a father predicting that his son must inevitably divide into different branches later on. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī...
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, in the section on the Analysis of the Schools (*Vibhaṅga-varga*), states:

At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, how will the future disciples differentiate the various schools? What will be the root schools and what the branch schools?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "In the future, my disciples shall have twenty schools, which will enable all dharmas to abide for two [aeons]."
The ten schools all attain the four fruits; the Tripitaka is equal, without inferior, middling, or superior grades. It is like the water of the ocean, whose taste is without difference.
Just as a man may have twenty sons, this serves as proof that the five schools and twenty [sects] were all prophesied by the Tathāgata during his lifetime.
These are the words of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) itself. Those who achieve the realization of the One Vehicle are originally...

Desire is merely for the sake of benefiting others; the subtle Dharma-bliss of the One Vehicle realized therein appears as three distinct streams from the single pool of awakening solely because there are differences in the faculties and practices through which beings enter it. This is indeed a skillful and expedient means;
thus the Sūtra says: "There is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle, neither two nor three; except for the Buddha’s teaching of expedient means."
Now, this [passage] below also reverses the previous point to clarify the intended meaning:
"If there were originally five intentions, then one should likewise establish five names for the Three Vehicles and divide them into five sections.

It is precisely because there are no five intentions that, at the time of the compilation, it remained as a single section consisting of eighty recitations. Therefore, a verse in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* says: "The eighteen... and so forth.
Both [the first] and the second arise entirely from the Mahāyāna; there is neither "is" nor "is not.

I say that in the future, those who recognize this will know that at the very end, when drawing water back to its source, there is still no difference—how much less so when one is actually present, where the five distinctions are truly manifest?

Regarding the gravity [of offenses], the Tathāgata established regulations according to the faculties [of his disciples], such that they vary in weight. Furthermore, what the five schools calculate also varies in weight, as in the case of the four [parājikas].

If one divides [the offenses] and commits a *pārājika* repeatedly, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that it is merely a *duṣkṛta*. However, if the five mental factors (*pañca-cetanā*) are absent, one should not arbitrarily maintain that there is a distinction between light and heavy [offenses].

Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, [the Dharma] will be divided into five. Since this prophesies the division into five, it clearly indicates that the five mental factors exist;
how then can you say they do not? In the response, since it says "after my parinirvāṇa," we know by contrast that [these factors] do not exist in Japan.
The principle of the five intentions is not erroneous; this follows the analogy of the *Daśama-svapna-sūtra*, which does not restrict the five intentions to a single day.

As for the "five persons," they are the five sages beginning with Kāśyapa. The *Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because the Buddha possesses five virtues by which he sustains beings, he is not divided [into separate entities].
First, he can transform all who are capable of being transformed (as people have no divergent attachments). Second, he can sever the net of doubts (all who have doubts are resolved)."

(1) The Dharma is free from divergent attachments; (2) it is revered by the three classes of beings—humans, devas, and asuras—and followed by all who possess virtue; (3) its teaching is invariably beneficial, such that anyone who hears it shall emerge from and exhaust all afflictions (*kleśa*); (4) it can subdue heterodox arguments, for it is capable of overcoming both celestial Māras and non-Buddhist paths; (5) by virtue of these five meanings, [the Dharma] was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime. If this is so, why was it not divided after his passing? The answer is: although the Teacher is no longer present, the Dharma remains. Furthermore, there were no disputes among the disciples regarding the Dharma, nor was there any need for the Sangha to be divided. Moreover, the Buddha’s disciples were all endowed with great supernatural powers and possessed the capacity to maintain the True Dharma. For these reasons, the Dharma was not divided. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples gradually declined, and because they lacked the power to preserve the True Dharma, it was subsequently divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all of noble character and possessed great wisdom. Because they were able to uphold the True Dharma through their own power, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples’ faculties became dull and their wisdom diminished. Because they could no longer maintain the True Dharma through their own power, it was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence. Because they did not fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, some disciples fell into the view of eternalism, while others fell into the view of nihilism. Because they held such divergent views, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all united in their purpose and shared a single mind. Because they were in harmony and free from contention, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples became contentious and their minds were discordant. Because they were divided and at odds, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to practice the path with diligence and vigor. Because they applied themselves to cultivation without slackening, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples became lax and indolent. Because they failed to apply themselves to cultivation, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to protect the True Dharma and repel heterodoxies. Because they could defend the Dharma against external challenges, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples were unable to protect the True Dharma and repel heterodoxies. Because they could not defend the Dharma, it was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to propagate the True Dharma throughout the world. Because they could spread the teachings far and wide, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples were unable to propagate the True Dharma throughout the world. Because they could not spread the teachings, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to manifest various miraculous powers to convert sentient beings. Because they could transform beings through their spiritual power, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples lacked such miraculous power. Because they could not convert beings, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to maintain the precepts purely and without violation. Because they were pure in conduct, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples violated the precepts and their conduct became impure. Because their conduct was defiled, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to dwell in the forest and practice meditation in solitude. Because they were secluded from worldly distractions, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples lived amidst the clamor of the world and abandoned their solitary practice. Because they were distracted by worldly affairs, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to attain the fruits of the path and realize liberation. Because they had realized the ultimate goal, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples were unable to attain the fruits of the path or realize liberation. Because they had not reached the ultimate goal, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to understand the Buddha’s profound intent and grasp the subtle meaning of the Dharma. Because they understood the Buddha’s mind, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples were unable to understand the Buddha’s profound intent or grasp the subtle meaning of the Dharma. Because they did not understand the Buddha’s mind, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to harmonize the various teachings and unify the different schools. Because they maintained doctrinal unity, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples could not harmonize the various teachings or unify the different schools. Because they allowed doctrinal fragmentation, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to respect the elders and honor the virtuous. Because they observed proper etiquette and showed reverence, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples disregarded the elders and failed to honor the virtuous. Because they lacked respect and decorum, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to remain humble and free from pride. Because they were modest and without arrogance, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples became conceited and full of pride. Because they were arrogant and haughty, the Dharma was divided. This is why the Dharma was not divided during the Buddha’s lifetime, yet was divided after his passing. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples were all able to practice the four bases of sympathetic response (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to gather and sustain sentient beings. Because they gathered beings through skillful means, the Dharma was not divided. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples failed to practice the four bases of sympathetic response. The method by which her hair fell away and the dharma-robes appeared upon her body, whereby she became a bhikṣuṇī and through diligent cultivation attained the fruit of arhatship—possessing the three knowledges (trividyā), the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa)—as well as the nuns Bhadrikā, Śuklā, and Sumanā, who were all ordained by the "Come, O Bhikṣuṇī" (ehibhikṣuṇī) formula: for these reasons, it is said that there were not merely one or two. If this is so, why does the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* not mention them? The answer is given in the *Jieshu*: The *Jieshu* states: [The *Vibhāṣā*] does not mention them because they were not included within the scope of the discussion. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* was compiled based on the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. Since the *Hṛdaya* did not include those cases, the *Vibhāṣā* likewise did not discuss them. Moreover, the *Vibhāṣā* was established primarily to refute the views of other schools; since those instances were not points of contention for other schools, they were not discussed. Finally, the *Vibhāṣā* was composed to clarify the specific characteristics of the Sarvāstivāda school; since those instances did not pertain to the unique tenets of that school, they were not mentioned. Thus, it is not a fault that they are not recorded therein. It is simply that their accounts are found in other sūtras and śāstras. For example, the account of the nun Śuklā is found in the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*, and the account of the nun Sumanā is found in the *Ekottarika-āgama*. Therefore, one should not rely solely on the *Vibhāṣā* to determine whether or not such cases exist. One must consult various sūtras and śāstras to understand the full extent of the Buddha’s teachings. This is the meaning. Thus, it is known that the Buddha’s Dharma is vast and profound, and its manifestations are inexhaustible. One must not harbor narrow-mindedness or biased views when studying the scriptures. One should always maintain an open mind and seek out the truth across all texts. Only then can one truly grasp the essence of the Buddha’s intent. This is what is meant by the statement: "If one studies only a single treatise, one will never exhaust the ocean of the Buddha's wisdom. One must study widely and synthesize the various teachings to achieve a comprehensive understanding. This is the path of a true seeker of the Dharma. This concludes the explanation. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the purpose of ceasing slander lies with ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); it must be a noble one (*ārya*) who can dispel false attachments, and thus this is not limited by the teachings.
Therefore, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* says that those who are noble are those to whom the Buddha proclaims, "Come, [O monk]," whereas those who are not noble are not saved.
The *Fǎxiǎn zhuàn* (Biography of Faxian) concerning the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā says: "In her causal stage, she was an ugly courtesan; because of a lotus..."
By offering flowers to a pratyekabuddha, one subsequently attained a handsome appearance in this life; by begging for five hundred portions of food, one likewise received the fruit of beauty.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* relates that when the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā went forth from home, the Buddha said, "Welcome," and her hair fell away of its own accord—all such instances are cases where [the results] manifest across lifetimes.

Question: Regarding the meaning of "inferior intention," if one considers both those who are reached and those who are not reached, since the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣuṇī) ordination was indeed reached [by Mahāprajāpatī], it would logically follow that she should have been permitted to receive ordination.

Why, then, is there a teaching stating she was not ordained? Answer: There are three points to consider. First, the prohibition against women entering the order was established eight years after the Three Refuges were instituted.

Second, it was only fourteen years later that Mahāprajāpatī herself shaved her hair and sought to receive the Eight Heavy Rules (gurudharma). Because she did not meet the [initial] timing requirement, it is said she was not ordained. However, this is the intended meaning of the answer.
In the question, this point is clarified by itself: "This statement does not apply to those who have received the full ordination through the three refuges," and so forth.

One might fear that because the statement does not apply to the three-refuge full ordination, it would follow that the five, eight, and ten precepts also do not apply to nuns; therefore, it is said that "in principle, they do indeed apply.

Furthermore, observing the text of the answer here, both [the five and ten precepts] are explained as being superior to the nun's [eight precepts] because the latter is limited by time and thus inferior.

Although the procedures for receiving the three refuges and full ordination are common [to both genders], they omit the occasion of answering the call "Come" (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*) and the text regarding those not being ordained;

however, since these were already made explicit in the preceding text, they are shown here in an abbreviated form. Thus, the previous passage states that the Tathāgata did not ordain women with the words "Come," solely to prevent slander—not because the timing was unsuitable.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya) cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, which says: "The Buddha did not ordain bhikṣuṇīs in order to stop slander."

Therefore, if one who was converted by the "Welcome" (Ehi-bhikṣuṇī) ordination were to be a follower of an external path, they would say: "Originally she lived in the royal palace, amusing herself with court ladies;
having left home, she has now returned to convert others for her own pleasure. If, however, she is a noble person, the Buddha also converts her—the principle is the same as cited above.

It is not said here that a monk may not travel alone, but rather that he must observe the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) when ordaining a nun, because the specific circumstances require two persons.
Regarding the "five five-hundred-year periods," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* clarifies five such periods: first, the five hundred years of firmness in liberation;
second, the five hundred years of firmness in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); third, the five hundred years of firmness in maintaining the precepts (*śīla*);

fourth, the five hundred years of firmness in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*); and fifth, the five hundred years of firmness in strife and contention. The present commentary points to the very first of these. *Ka-ja*.
The following passage refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Jambudvīpa is also called Śāmbu or Jambū; extending laterally to the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), there are only four continents within the seas.

These are distinguished by their orientation according to Mount Sumeru, and this present location is the southern continent (Jambudvīpa). According to geographical records, it lies east-west along the course of the waters and lands.
It is twenty-four thousand *li* from north to south and twenty-eight thousand *li* from east to west.

Furthermore, according to the treatises, its three sides are equal at two thousand *yojanas*, while the southern side is three and a half *yojanas*. Thus, it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like the face of an elephant.
If one calculates that the Buddha attained enlightenment here in the center of this continent, it is precisely the Vajrāsana; therefore, the Sūtra says:
It is said that [this place] is the center of three thousand suns and moons and twelve thousand heavens and earths;

it refers to the three continents of the east, west, and north, as well as the three continents of the east, south, and west. This is as stated in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"O Bhikṣus, when you travel through the human world, do not travel together in pairs," and so forth. As for the "one hundred and ten people":
Having delivered one hundred and ten arhats, he dispatched them in various directions to propagate the teachings extensively; however, Piṇḍola was not included among their number.
Thus it is said that [the Vinaya] is "nameless. The *Śīlaskandha-vinaya* states: "In this world, there are one hundred and ten arhat disciples.
Piṇḍola is his personal name (*nāma*), and Pārupa is his clan name (*gotra*). It was because the elder Jyotiṣka offered him a *cīvara* (robe) that he received this name.

When the Venerable Cunda took the alms bowl by manifesting supernatural powers, the Buddha rebuked him, saying, "You have manifested superhuman states before one who has not yet received the precepts.

Having rebuked him, the Buddha expelled him; thus he went to the two continents. From this we know that at the time of his expulsion, the "three-fold formula" (tri-vācika) had already fallen into disuse;

therefore, it is said that [the Dharma] does not reach Aparagoyānī (the Western Continent, also known as Go-varta). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that humans there are sixteen cubits tall, and their faces...
Their lifespan is five hundred years, and the diameter of that land is two thousand five hundred *yojanas*.

This is consistent with the *Vinaya-sūtra*, chapter thirty-seven, regarding the supreme *vinaya*, which states only that when many disciples are ordained, one should construct monasteries and dwellings.
As for the *Airāvata* [continent], namely Pūrvavideha, the inhabitants are eight cubits tall and their faces are shaped like a half-moon.
The lifespan there is two hundred and fifty years; its three sides are each two thousand *yojanas* in width, while the eastern side is three hundred and fifty *yojanas* wide.
To the north lies Uttarakuru; the *Abhidharmakośa* states that the people there are thirty-two cubits tall, their faces are square, and their lifespan is one thousand years.
Its four sides are each two thousand *yojanas* wide, situated within the [Great] Ocean.
Because such difficulties are frequent, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Only in Uttarakuru is there no Buddha-dharma, nor is there the attainment of precepts;
because of the obstruction of their karmic rewards and because of their ignorance, they do not receive the noble Dharma."
Regarding the "fruit," this refers to the time of attaining the Way; it concerns the final momentary mind among the thirty-four moments of mind.
At the time of the Path of Liberation, which corresponds to the Knowledge of Destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood;

at that time, the perfect virtues are fully possessed. If one follows the interpretation of the Great Master [Vasubandhu] below, however, it means that the Bodhisattva conceals the signs of his supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Riding the auspicious white elephant, he entrusted himself to the womb of Queen Māyā to manifest the form of a Prince; this was a descent of provisional response and not a literal birth.
When he reached the Śāla Grove to announce his tranquility, the golden coffin concealed its radiance within the state of non-extinction to manifest extinction;
thus, it was not a literal death. Therefore, one knows that although the Great Sage manifests a body subject to birth and death, his essence is fundamentally devoid of coming and going.
How could the traces of these events be determined by the status of cause and effect to define the limits of receiving the precepts?

The *Changhan* (Long Containment) states that a deva of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven knew the Tathāgata’s mind; like a strong man bending or extending his arm, he vanished from that heaven and suddenly arrived here.
Others say that a deva of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven presented a razor for shaving the hair and bestowed the Dharma robes.
The *Gan-chuan* (Record of Miraculous Responses) states that the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly, saying:

"When I first left the city to renounce the world and entered the mountains to study the Way, I traded my priceless precious robe for a deer-skin garment. At that time, a tree spirit appeared before me, holding a *saṃghāṭī* in her hands, and said to me:
'In the past, when the Buddha Kāśyapa entered nirvāṇa, he entrusted this cotton *saṃghāṭī* to me.'"
"In my [teaching], I have them well-guarded until the appearance of a worthy one (*satpuruṣa*) in the world"—the various scriptural passages such as this differ accordingly.
Question: Since the precepts for ordinary beings below are for the purpose of preventing wrongdoing, and since the Buddha is already without fault, what use has he for precepts? Answer:
Below, all the merits of the myriad virtues arise because of the precepts, and all evil karma is extinguished by means of the precepts; how could it be otherwise? How could evil... [be tolerated]?
If there were no precepts, there would be no merit; since merit would not be fulfilled, how could the Tathāgata—who is adorned with the ten thousand virtues—possibly lack them?
As for the "fruit-head," it refers to the thirty-four moments of mind through which one suddenly severs the fetters and delusions to realize the fruit, as this is the very pinnacle [of realization].

The "three protections" refer to the protection of body, speech, and mind. This means that because ordinary beings fall into transgressions, they must diligently apply these three protections so that non-virtue does not arise at the stage of the fruit.
When the transgressions are exhausted, the three protections (*trisaṃvara*) are no longer required; however, because they do not arise [as faults], they do not obstruct the precepts.
These are wholesome dharmas that must not be absent. This is analogous to what is called in the "Four Statements": first, the mind withdraws from objects but does not withdraw from the Noble Ones;

there are no afflictions because objects are not yet exhausted, and thus the precepts remain without being lost. (The remaining statements are as found in the *Dacāo*). "Pratyekabuddha" distinguishes them from *Niyuta-buddhas* (緣覺); another name for them is "Rhinoceros" (*Khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).

The second analogy concerns those who travel in groups (*vargacārin*). Because these noble ones appear in worlds where no Buddha is present, they observe the flourishing and decay of external objects as analogous to the arising and ceasing within their own bodies.
Through this, they awaken and realize the Truth, thereby attaining the Precepts; thus it is said that they "rely upon distinct matters. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Having left the secular world to become a renunciant, dwelling alone in a quiet and secluded place, he himself spoke a verse: 'By remaining far removed from unwholesome dharmas, one shall surely attain the wholesome.'"

When both good and evil dharmas have been extinguished, one then attains the Way; at that time, both the body and the verbal teachings are accomplished, and subsequently, one attains the precepts of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

According to this, the two instances of the term "liberation" (*vimukti*) in the *Shu-yao* (Commentary) belong respectively to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) prātimokṣa and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) liberation;
since both are attained, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Within the uncontaminated mind, what..."
Question: How can one possess both impure (sāsrava) and pure (anāsrava) precepts? Answer: Such is the nature of these dharmas.
By the power of karma, both impure and pure precepts can exist within a pure mind.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Prātimokṣa precepts exist only while the Buddha is in the world, whereas the dhyāna and pure precepts exist at all times.
If [the Buddha] exists at all times, how can one obtain the liberation precepts? As that treatise states:
"If the Buddha were not included within the Saṃgha, he would not exist as the Buddha Jewel; if there is no Buddha Jewel, the Three Refuges cannot be established.

Since the Three Refuges are thus lacking, how can one speak of obtaining the precepts? Regarding the first explanation, this refers to the three refuges for laypeople and so forth. That treatise asks:
If one recites the Buddha and the Dharma but not the Sangha, or even recites the Dharma and the Sangha but not the Buddha Jewel, does this constitute the Three Refuges?

Furthermore, can one receive the five precepts, the eight fast-day precepts, or the ten precepts without having received the Three Refuges? The answer is: none of these can be fully obtained [in such cases].

However, it is not so; therefore, the treatise states: "To receive the full ordination (upasampadā), one must obtain it through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations); it is not accomplished by the Three Refuges alone. This is the standard.

Since this possession of the precepts is not restricted solely to those who have attained enlightenment through the three refuges, there is no doubt that it can be obtained even though the Buddha is no longer present.
Regarding the attainment of the *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation) precepts, it is said that both types are obtained. "Form-concomitant" (*xingju*) means lasting as long as one's physical form;

even if, in past lives, one’s physical form has ended and the precepts have lapsed so as not to extend to the present life, it is further stated that the three refuges, the five precepts, and so forth cannot be obtained [in such cases].

This is likely based on the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. For that text states that because these exist only when a Buddha has appeared in the world, if a Buddha has not yet appeared, there can certainly be no self-administered reception of the precepts.
However, according to the *Samantapāsādikā*, this does not apply exclusively to the complete sets [of precepts], as they are available at all times.
Thus, its seventh fascicle says: "The five precepts and the ten precepts are trainings; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, they exist in the world."

Because this precept is ever-present within them, those who possess the "spontaneous precept" (svayambhū-śīla) receive it without a teacher; as stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas receive it without a teacher.

Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the spontaneous, teacherless precept refers to the Buddha, who—without relying on a teacher’s instruction—comprehends the principles to their full extent and thereby experiences the arising of the precept.
Now, by analogy, since the Pratyekabuddha is identical to the Buddha in attaining the spontaneous precept, it follows that even in the absence of a Buddha...

The phrase "the world attains it fully without doubt" (世得具不疑) follows the Buddha’s statement; its underlying intent is to pose a counter-question: "Since the Buddha attained [enlightenment] beneath the tree, was he not also a householder?

Furthermore, since the Buddha himself was a king, did he need to receive [the precepts] from another Buddha? This proves that one naturally attains the precepts; thus, we know that *prātimokṣa* is not restricted solely to the era of a Buddha.
The following lines provide dual proof for both the attainment of the full set [of precepts] and the nature of their inherent perfection (*prakṛti-siddha*).

This is the very essence [of the path]. It is the first of the sixteen moments of mind in the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), known as the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time, one first attains the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, the precept co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) arises. As for "Knowledge of Exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*): it is so named because it arises together with the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-prāpti*) following the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-mārga*).
Alternatively, it is said that Knowledge of Exhaustion is liberation (*vimukti*), because within the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), all afflictions and defilements are exhausted.
Because all [defilements] have already been exhausted, it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "inferior to the [Buddha]," this refers to the disciples (*śrāvaka*). They require five conditions: as the *Yeyu* (Explanatory Notes on Karma) states: first, relying on the Buddha’s instructions; second, making a vow;

third, practicing asceticism according to those teachings; fourth, the total exhaustion of the three poisons; and fifth, perceiving emptiness and thereby giving rise to the precepts. Therefore, they differ from the Buddha.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata had attained the precepts, there were separately the Buddhas of the ten directions who presided over the rite and conferred upon him the rank of Dharma King. Thus, the *Linggan Zhuan* (Account of Spiritual Resonance) states:
"Vairocana Buddha extended his golden hand, rubbed the crown of Śākyamuni’s head, and preached the Sublime Dharma. It further says:
"Now, the Buddhas of the ten directions desire to perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) to confer upon Śākyamuni Buddha the status of Unsurpassed Dharma King. All the Buddhas [act thus].
As the Buddhas presided over this *karmavācanā* at the celestial altar, the immeasurable multitudes of devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,

heard the Buddha’s *karmavācanā* and became simultaneously silent, like bhikṣus entering the third dhyāna. Once the Buddhas had presided over the *karmavācanā* and received the position of Dharma King,
the earth shook in six ways, and the Buddhas emitted light that universally illumined the ten directions, extensively performing the work of a Buddha.
The benefits for both ordinary beings and sages cannot be fully recounted; thus, one should know that although disciples have attained the higher Dharma, they remain far from the precepts.
To expand on the words below: even Pratyekabuddhas themselves possess the two teachings of body and speech.

As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, dwelling alone in seclusion is their teaching of the body, while reciting verses to distance oneself from dust and leave evil behind is their teaching of speech. [This applies to] good and evil.
Only after both [the defiled and undefiled] have been extinguished does one attain the Path;

this is the possession of both the *sāsrava* (tainted) and *anāsrava* (untainted) precepts. Regarding the bhikṣu, he is one who attains ordination through the "Come, O Bhikṣu" formula while practicing as a bhikṣu.

As for the upāsaka discipline, it is said that Yaśoda’s father went to the Buddha's dwelling, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; immediately upon sitting, all his defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having personally examined his realization of the fruit, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the status of an upāsaka. This was the first instance of an upāsaka receiving the three refuges, with Yaśoda’s father as the foremost.
As for the upāsikās receiving the three refuges, Yaśodā’s mother and her former husband were the foremost; all of these were likewise [the first].

Because he personally received the Buddha’s transformation, it is said that he "attained [realization] from the Buddha. Subsequently, he had an Arhat perform the "Three Words" ordination for him, as explained below in the *Yinye shu* (Commentary on the Inducing Karma).
This requires five conditions: first, identity of form, as the text says, "shaving the head and donning the robes"; second, the presence of one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the instruction;
third, the existence of a seeking mind, as the text says, "desiring to go to the Buddha's abode"; fourth, the convergence of mind and object; and fifth, the completion of the ritual.
Regarding the five types of *śrāmaṇera* who perform the work, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that receiving the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera* is also called "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*).
To cease slander is as cited above. Furthermore, the Buddha is the Dharma King and acts as the great guide for all sentient beings.

Question: All the following sections are provisional designations used to challenge the reality [of the matter].

Suppose a person who has already received the Buddha’s precepts violates a grave prohibition (*garukāpatti*), abandons the precepts, and then returns wishing to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) again; because this person’s transgression is heavy, they are called one who stands outside the ocean of the Buddha.
It is impossible to re-enter the ocean of pure precepts. Now, the hypothetical establishment of the cases of killing and stealing is intended to give rise to a subsequent objection.

Regarding the phrase "If that were so" (*yadi evam*), one should first provide the answer: "Even if killing and stealing were to constitute a transgression (*antya-avadya*), what fault would there be?

Only then should one take up the words of the objection beginning with "If that were so. This means that according to worldly convention, a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) possesses both karma and precepts; thus, his acts of killing and stealing would be identical to those of a monk.

Is it the case that [the term] "extreme" (*anta*) refers to this meaning? It is not so. Furthermore, if it were established below [in the text] that the name "extreme" cannot be applied to one who has received the full precepts (*upasampadā*) when viewed in light of having committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), then it would follow that those such as those who have defiled a nun (*bhikṣuṇī-dūṣaka*) could all be termed "extremes," because they likewise do not obtain the full precepts.

Alternatively, if it is said that the name "extreme" is established for those excluded from the pure Saṃgha, then consider, for instance, the case of one who has been subjected to the penalty of expulsion (*pravrājana*).

If it were the case that a person could be so [treated], then since a person who has not yet undergone the formal act of *pravāsanīya* (banishment) should not be considered a "border-dweller" (*pratyantaka*), and furthermore, if the designation "border-dweller" were established based on the charge of a *pārājika* offense, then a *śrāmaṇera* who commits sexual misconduct, theft, or the like should not be considered a "border-dweller," because as a member of the lower assembly, he commits only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Why, then, does the treatise state: "Among the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*, if one violates a grave one..."?
Regarding the "offense of a limit" (*antimā āpatti*) mentioned here, the text of the response below is concise and its meaning is obscured; I shall now analyze it to clarify it.

Since this refers to violating the Buddha’s established precepts, and furthermore, since those who have not yet received the five or eight precepts as laypeople do not incur the offense of a limit, and since defiling a nun also applies specifically to those in the secular world who have not received the five or eight precepts, such individuals should instead be subject to expulsion.
Originally, one who is to be expelled is not termed a "limit" (*anta*); there is a specific procedure for expulsion itself.

Therefore, since a śrāmaṇera takes only the violation of the root precepts as the limit (*anta*), how could the designation "limit" be fixed based on the distinction between *pārājika* and *sthūlātyaya*?

Thus, we know that the meaning established for the term "limit" across these various ranks is not appropriate. If one does not commit [the offense], then it simply does not exist; to say it does not exist means it cannot be called a "limit.
The subsequent sentence is the inverse of the preceding one.
Question: If it is said that violating the Buddha’s prohibitions constitutes a *pārājika* offense and results in expulsion, is this not itself a violation of the Buddha’s prohibitions?

Why then is it not called a *antika* (boundary) offense? Furthermore, should the *antika* offenses also be termed "expulsion by extinction" (*nirvāsanīya*), since the commission of a grave offense (*pārājika*) and the violation of a prohibition are identical in nature?

Answer: The first phrase of the response, "In reality... (*zhong shi*), is a concessive statement (*yong*), while the subsequent phrase, "But... (*dan...xia*), is a refutation (*duo*). According to the underlying principle, the commission of a grave offense is indeed [a violation].
First, it may be said that "limit" (*anta*) refers exclusively to those who have committed a *pārājika* offense;

this is because the Buddha established the rule for those who, having previously received the precepts, committed an offense and then abandoned them, only to return later—such individuals are deemed incapable of receiving the ordination again and are thus called "outsiders beyond the limit" (*antagrāha*). Since the present case involves expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), this specific meaning does not apply.

Therefore, these two types of persons—those who have committed a *pārājika* offense and those subject to expulsion—both constitute offenses of the limit. This is because the single status of expulsion exists within the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*).

After committing a grave offense (*pārājika*), one is subject to formal legal expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*); this is what is meant by a "limiting offense" (*antāpatti*). It is not so for other offenses, as there is no such formal expulsion.

Rather, it is called a "limiting offense" because it is designated by the name of the specific grave offense originally committed; thus, it is said to be named according to its origin. In this way, each follows its own particular meaning so that a distinction may be made.

Because the Arhat has completely severed both the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms, and because the Anāgāmin has exhausted the nine grades of desire-afflictions, their sense of pleasure is already forgotten and they are entirely in a state of purity;
thus, for these individuals at the initial, middle, and final stages, even a slight defilement constitutes a difficulty.

Only the Sakṛdāgāmin severs six grades of desire-afflictions, while the Srotāpanna, though having severed the afflictions of view, has not yet severed any of the afflictions of thought; thus, their sense of pleasure is not yet interrupted at the beginning.

If a person becomes defiled after [the object] has already ceased, there is no transgression; this applies equally to ordinary persons who maintain the precepts at the beginning and end. The intent of the question is as follows:
Since the objects of an Arhat or Anāgāmin belong to the realm of the Noble Ones (*ārya*) and thus cannot be destroyed, how can it be said that they are "destroyed"?

Regarding the nun’s case, because the previous object was a Noble One, the karma of pride and defilement is established; it does not depend on the prior destruction of the object for the precept to be violated. This is stated in contrast to those who take pleasure in attachment.

If one forces a layperson’s garment upon a nun and commits sexual misconduct with her, it constitutes an *antarāyika-dharma* (an obstacle). Thus, the *Daichao* states: "If one forcibly makes a nun wear white lay clothing and then engages in sexual intercourse, it constitutes an obstacle.

Furthermore, although it is said that wearing such clothing oneself does not obstruct ordination, according to the principle of the Great Master [Vasubandhu], if one knows that the conditions for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) require it, yet one wears lay clothing, this too should constitute an obstacle; however, this concerns the destruction of the object of purity (*viśuddha-viṣaya*) and is not otherwise discussed.

One who knows purity and impurity but has not yet reached fulfillment is a *śikṣamāṇā* śrāmaṇerī. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one violates a bhikṣuṇī, it does not obstruct [one's] renunciation;

the same applies to the two lower assemblies. All such texts merely speak of violating a bhikṣuṇī without clarifying whether the offense is grave or light across the three groups, nor do they specify the four, five, or ten recensions of the Vinaya.
Regarding the judgment in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Daizhao* (Great Commentary) states that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other codes are all...

Regarding the statement, "Because one does not clearly distinguish between the pure and the defiled, those who engage in worldly affairs ask: 'Have you not committed an offense against a pure nun? This question is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Furthermore, the *Yejieshu* (Exposition of Karmas) states: "None of the three Vinayas provide a definitive resolution; these are therefore texts of incomplete clarity.
One should employ the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to clearly adjudicate purity and defilement."

The intent of the question is as follows: If even killing a Pratyekabuddha who has attained the three fruits does not constitute a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense, why would defiling a nun—who, though still among ordinary beings, is pure—constitute such a grave difficulty?

Furthermore, regarding the destruction of merit: because humans, devas, and those equal to them obtain great merit by making offerings to those in the four fruits, they are the ultimate field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);
thus, killing them constitutes a *ānantarya* offense. The three fruits are the opposite of this; moreover, so too is the Pratyekabuddha.

The purpose of transforming others is meager; therefore, because it does not constitute a direct transgression (*ānantarya*), it must be distinguished [from such]. This is because it defiles and insults a pure object.

If even an ordinary nun commits an offense when she possesses the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*) capable of projecting karma that leads to hell, how much more so for one who has attained the three fruits of the path? Answer:

Below, it is explained that while an ordinary nun possesses the afflictions of views and thought which are fully capable of projecting karma leading to hell, the two nuns in question possess only the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) to moisten karma, and lack the afflictions of views.

Therefore, it merely incurs a separate retribution (*vyavasthita-vipāka*) and lacks a collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*) that would correspond to entry into hell. For this reason, the simultaneous occurrence [of both offenses] is not established.
The mundane interpretation below states: A secular man may commit the offense of violating a nun, but a secular woman should not be able to commit the offense of violating a nun;

hence it is called "one side. If one were to challenge the above by descending to this lower point: if violating [a nun] on one side does not constitute defilement, then it should also be possible to break the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act).

Regarding the two types of *saṃghabheda* (schisms), is there no schism of the Wheel (*cakrabheda*) among *bhikṣuṇīs*, and should they not also commit the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*? The *Jiesu* (Exegesis on the Precepts) explains:
"For *bhikṣuṇīs*, although there is no actual substance of a schism of the Wheel when they commit this offense together, the status of 'principal' and 'companion' can still be established.

Because they may use the five dharmas to entice others, they must also be admonished; therefore, it is said that the 'dharma of admonition' is universal. Furthermore, the subsequent explanation follows the *Dacao* (Great Commentary).
First, it was asked: "Why does one not say 'a monk who has fallen'? This is answered by extending [the principle] to the "one about to fall" (*bhetsyamāna*).

Regarding those who have not yet received what they ought to receive, the Great Master (the Buddha) judged this based on their lack of understanding; even for one of sharp intelligence, it would not be permissible upon a single hearing.

This section below concerns cases that are not subject to formal monastic procedures (*saṃghakarma*), as they pertain to the individual; therefore, they do not constitute an obstruction to the precepts. Alternatively, [this applies when there are] four or more persons.
Other combinations of harmonious factors do not constitute a *kaṭhina* offense if the *karmavācanā* has not been performed; this is difficult to establish.

Question: The lower section of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on Precepts) first establishes the principle that although the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) precepts and vows are not yet the complete dharma, there is no offense even if one violates them.
However, when the *Shuochao* (Explanatory Notes) poses this question, it distinguishes between "great" and "small," where "great" refers to the *bhikṣu* and "small" refers to the *śrāmaṇera*.

The term *huangmen* (eunuch) was an office of the Qin dynasty, which the Han dynasty inherited. The *Hanshu* states that the forbidden gates were called the "Yellow Gates" (*huangtai*), and because those within them served the sovereign, they were designated as *huangmen*.
Although in antiquity castrated officials were employed, in the present day the term *huangmen* is also applied to those who have been deprived of their male organs;

thus the compiler of the notes says: "A *huangmen* is one with the physical characteristics of a non-male. The phrase "one degree lower" refers to those who from birth were incapable [of sexual function].

1. The "two-month impotent" (dvimāsa-paṇḍaka): one who is potent for half a month and impotent for the other half. 2. The "seeing-impotent" (dṛṣṭi-paṇḍaka): one who becomes potent only upon seeing another person engage in sexual misconduct with a non-genital part.
3. The "stimulation-impotent" (sparśana-paṇḍaka): one who becomes potent only when his own genital organ is stimulated by another person's sexual act.

4. According to that Vinaya, the "seminal-impotent" (śukra-paṇḍaka) is simply called *śukra-paṇḍaka*. 5. The "decayed-impotent" (jīrṇa-paṇḍaka): this refers to those such as those who are decayed or rotten, including those whose [semen] has fallen away or is consumed by worms. The following section provides a detailed analysis.

Regarding those four types who should not be granted the going-forth or full ordination—namely, one whose semen is produced through envy, one whose semen is produced through half-envy, and so forth—if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, they should be expelled, because they do not give rise to my *vinaya* of wholesome dharmas. As for the fifth, the sick eunuch:
if he has previously gone forth and received full ordination, but then becomes impotent, withers away, is consumed by worms, or becomes incapable of movement [he too must be expelled].
Even if one remains listening without wavering, if they abandon the precepts and wish to return to the household life to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they should not be granted it;

if they are granted ordination, they should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*). Second, according to the main text, those who have become wives or concubines and give birth to children, yet harbor mutual jealousy toward one another.
In childhood, they were crushed; now they are called "husbands" (*pati*), which is an error for the arising of the male organ (*puruṣendriya*).

As for the phrase "due to another," it means that because of the touch of another person, the organ arises. Regarding the five lower views: first, one sees another performing improper acts, and subsequently the organ arises.

The first three arise spontaneously through crushing and cutting; the latter three are due to another's jealousy for half a month. *Kliba* (eunuch) refers to having the sexual power removed by means of a knife.
Alternatively, in the *Qiāntōngwén* (General Text on the Qiān), it says: "As for *jiàn* (castration), once born, [the organ] is completely cut off. The Great Master said:

"In the present age, some may have their organs partially removed, yet their fundamental nature remains unchanged; furthermore, those who possess great integrity and lofty ambition should be treated according to the *Wǔfēnlǜ* (Five-Part Vinaya), which states that one becomes a *huángmén* (eunuch) upon losing the male organ while engaging in sexual intercourse with another. This occurs due to adverse conditions. And so forth.

In cases such as being attacked by enemies, predatory beasts, or falling [into a pit] due to karmic retribution, one should follow the same rules as for a bhikṣu regarding self-mutilation. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* does not clarify the specific limits;

however, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if the organ is completely severed, one is subject to expulsion (*pārājika*). If only one testicle remains, one may repent according to the specific category of offense.
Because one treats those below as inferior and regards them with a different mindset, one does not conceive of them as parents.

According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, if they are actually one's parents but one perceives them as not being so, killing them still prevents one from leaving the household life. Regarding other circumstances, it is asked:

"If one employs a means intending to kill someone who is not one's mother, but ends up killing one's own mother instead, does one incur a *pārājika* offense as well as the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)?"

Yājñavalkya replied: "One does not merely incur a *stūlātyaya* offense; furthermore, if one personally takes another's life without any other intention or alternative means, such a person should not be granted ordination."

In the *Jiàxià* (伽下), it says: "If one intends to kill an ordinary person but instead kills an Arhat, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (偷蘭遮) offense, yet the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) is not incurred.
From this, we know that [the recipient] may receive the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*. Below that, there are four phrases that distinguish and clarify: 1.

An offense of the root nature that is not a crime of immediate retribution (this refers to killing a Pratyekabuddha). 2. An offense of the root nature that is also a crime of immediate retribution (the *Chāo* [Commentary] cites this phrase, hence it says: "This is both an immediate retribution and a root offense"). 3. Not a root offense, but is... [text fragment].

"Rebellion" (ānantarya) refers to slandering the Dharma by exposing its faults and evils; these are the four [rebellious acts]. Those that are not fundamental rebellions refer to killing other classes of beings. The detailed explanation of the second phrase states:

"If a person who has left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) takes the life of one who has attained the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), this is called a rebellious offense and is also a fundamental sin.
Such a being should be expelled from within my disciplinary code (*vinaya*)."
Therefore it is said that for these persons, the three fruits do not constitute an obstruction because their field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) has not yet reached its ultimate limit.
