The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states: "On that very day, one should accept and maintain one bowl; as for the others, they must be purified."
Regarding the title "Bhikṣu" used for the donor: although he was formerly called a bhikṣu, he is now a bhikṣuṇī; therefore, only one [title] is mentioned.
As for "Nirvāṇa," it is said that the Buddha is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Saṃgha—this refers to the equality of the nature of the Three Jewels across both ordinary and holy beings.

In the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), these are designated as the two types of Saṃgha: the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti). To speak in broad terms, they do not exceed the categories of the ordinary and the holy.

To discuss this in detail: within the one [community], there are naturally many kinds, as is commonly explained. Those who are external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) have not yet seen the principle of the Truth;

thus they are called "external" and have not yet attained the name of "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, because they have not yet attained the true principle, they possess only the concord of phenomena (*dharmasamagra*), which is a conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*) monastic function.

Therefore, regarding the person who practices the five *smṛtyupasthānas*—namely, the distinct-characteristic mindfulness and the general-characteristic mindfulness—one speaks in terms of the phenomena.

Regarding the four types of differences, at this stage there is only the morality of deportment (*airyāpathika-śīla*). As for the "inner ordinary beings" (*ādhyātma-prthagjana*), because they resemble those who have seen the truth of the principles (*satya-dharma*), they are called "inner";

yet, as they have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, they are termed "ordinary beings. These are the persons of the four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*): Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Because they resemble those in accord with the principles of the truths and are free from contradiction, they are called the "harmonious Saṃgha. They are sustained by the protection of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) and the concentration associated with them (*samādhi-sahaja*).
The second is the precept of the harmonious Saṃgha (*saṃghasaṃvāsa-śīla*), also called the "precept of the true Saṃgha.

This refers to the precept shared with the path attained by the four types of noble ones (*āryapudgala*) who, through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), clearly perceive the principles of reality and undergo no further change;

it is thus termed the "true Saṃgha," and the precept obtained together with that path is called the "precept of the true Saṃgha. To speak of "four" refers to the fact that these four types of Saṃghas uphold the Dharma and possess virtuous utility. As the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:

Four people constitute a *saṃgha* and not three; furthermore, within this school, four types of *saṃghas* are discussed—namely, a *saṃgha* of four, five, ten, or twenty people—which are distinguished according to the specific requirements of the matter at hand.

Below these, ordinary monks lack the merit to be distinguished by other titles, and thus they are designated by the term *karmavācanā*, as the *karmavācanā* is the formal record of the ritual action. It is also...
Regarding the "traces of the teaching" (*jiaoji*), as the *Xuan* states: "The Six Classics are the traces of the former sages. Thus, the teachings serve as the conditions for the capacity to speak.
In the *Lunxing jieshu*, it says: "What is called 'practice' does not exceed the Eightfold Path; using the worldly wheel as a metaphor refers to verbal karma (*vākkarman*)."

The *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) regarding the "Wheel of Life and Equality" states: "The Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma transforms and benefits the three thousandfold world system, encompassing both monastics and laypeople;

therefore, this is the correct interpretation. [Conversely,] it says: "When Devadatta proclaimed the five dharmas as being the four reliances, and even when the celestial deities announced throughout the three thousandfold world system that meditation and recitation were no longer to be practiced—this is the incorrect interpretation. This "untainted contemplation of emptiness" refers here to the principle as that which is realized.
In essence, because they are all capable of transforming the ordinary and grinding away afflictions to reach the Path of the Sages, they are called "wheels" (*cakra*).
Regarding the harmony of affairs (*karmārtha-sāmagrī*), the *Karmasūtra* states: "The harmony of affairs reveals the manifest form; it refers back to the universal Dharma.

It must accord with the characteristics of the Dharma, such as the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and all must revere it together like water and milk, being non-dual. As for the harmony of principle (*dharmatā-sāmagrī*), the *Sūtra* says: "Principle takes the realization of the correct as its standard, not exceeding it."
It is the Eightfold Noble Path; therefore, the following citation from the *Śāstra* provides dual proof for both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).

Based on this, one who speaks of "schism in the Saṃgha" must do so by distinguishing between the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Thus, there are two types of concordance: the Wheel of Dharma corresponds to principle, while the *karmavācanā* corresponds to phenomena.
Regarding the false speech [of Devadatta], it refers to Devadatta’s proclamation of the five points to subvert the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*). Devadatta said: "Butter..."

Excessive saltiness and the spoiling of fish and meat—these two constitute false speech. Furthermore, establishing the three practices of begging for food, wearing rag-robes, and sitting in the open as being similar to the Buddha’s four reliances constitutes "similar speech.

Regarding the phrase "not by the five dharmas," etc., it means that breaking the essential rules of the Saṃgha—specifically by performing the *śīla* (precepts) and *karma* (formal acts) separately at two different locations—is what is called "breaking" [the Saṃgha], not by the five dharmas. This results in the loss of understanding; one loses [it].
This is the correct interpretation: it refers to the time when the Saṃgha was first split. At that time, [Devadatta] imitated two of the Buddha’s dharmas to simulate his own false teachings:

first, he established five wrong practices as his method of conduct to replace the four right supports; second, he established illegal *karmavācanā* (formal acts) as the community's method to replace the legitimate *karmavācanā*.
Thus, at the time in Rājagṛha, the acceptance of these five practices constituted the actual breaking of the conduct; subsequently, at Gayā, the *karma* was performed.

Since it is only when one grinds away the recitation of the *Poṣadha* that the breaking of the communal Dharma (*saṃgha-dharma*) begins and reaches its ultimate point—the breaking of the Wheel of the Dharma—it is known that the loss of understanding is merely the breaking of practice.
If the breaking of practice were itself the ultimate breaking of the Saṃgha, why wait for the mountain of Gayā to separately realize the precepts for oneself?
By this evidence, it is proven that the breaking occurs at Gayā.
There are two matters: first, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), and second, the *śalākā* (voting tally). The *Vinaya* states: "Upāli, there are further two matters by which the Saṃgha is split:
when those four persons or more carry out the split of the Saṃgha by means of the *śalākā* and perform the *karmavācanā*; this is what is meant. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When Devadatta proclaimed the five points during the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, five hundred people took up the voting tallies; only Ānanda..."

It is difficult to reach the stage of a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who does not grasp at a beginning or an end; "breaking" begins with the breaking of conduct and ends with the breaking of the assembly.
If one follows the eightfold noble path—which is to be emulated and taken as a standard—one can transform the mundane into the noble, serving as the cause for becoming a *saṃgha*.

Now, because this Dharma is destroyed, it is called the "Karma of Breaking the Wheel. It is the same in this case: one merely breaks the internal rules of the *karmavācanā*, yet there is no separate *karma* [for the act itself].

"Grinding the Saṃgha can break it"—the "two" here specifically refers to the two aspects of the substance of breaking the Saṃgha: the agent and the object. Therefore, it cites the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), saying:

"Neither matter nor mind," and so forth. Now, the *Jingye Shu* (Commentary on the *Karma-sūtra*) states: "There are those who, based on the Vinaya and in accordance with the śāstras, adopt the intent of the *Tattvasiddhi*:

just as grasping fingers forms a fist and grasping the aggregates forms a person, the 'person' is the conventional body while real dharmas have no [independent] function; thus, the four persons are merely conventional."
Taking this as the substance (*tattva*) of the Saṃgha, its function possesses no separate substance; rather, it takes the four persons who constitute the underlying basis as its substance.

In the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, it is stated that there are people below [the level of] the *vinaya-mūla*; relying on the *vinaya-mūla* and clarifying the substance by way of number, it means that from one person up to many, reaching as far as four persons, if they all possess the purity of the three roots and are free from any non-Dharmic characteristics, they thereby constitute the substance of the Saṃgha.

There are three [components], namely the three categories explained below. The phrase "by means of these" refers to the application of these eightfold right paths as a metaphor for the worldly wheel (*saṃsāra-cakra*).
A worldly wheel must possess three elements: the hub, the spokes, and the rim.
Laozi said, "Thirty spokes converge upon one hub," and Wang Bi remarked that the hub is that which is able to govern the thirty spokes; here, precepts are taken as the hub and wisdom as the spokes.
The spokes converge at the hub, yet even the spokes of wisdom may still scatter; therefore, the rim of meditative concentration is established as the outer boundary for support.

Although these three are complete, if there is no diligence (*vīrya*), how can one travel far? Thus, the sixth, diligence, serves as the driver of the wheel. First, it is explained in terms of practice;
next, it is explained in terms of understanding, because one must attain what is appropriate. Conversely, through perverse conduct and delusion, one fails to attain it.
Furthermore, because it ought to be resolved, one instead uses false resolutions to cause confusion and loss;
thus, if one were to say that losing resolution is called "breaking" (bhaṅga), then attaining resolution should be called "harmony" (saṃgha).

Should not the *vinaya* employ a single formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha? Looking at the teaching, the teaching establishes a single boundary for common observance; now, since each acts separately, this makes it clear [that they have lost harmony].

To resolve a schism, one must employ *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) for reconciliation; one cannot use reconciliation through principle (*yukti*), because principle belongs to the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
As explained previously regarding the "inner ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*), when understanding cuts off all opposition, it is called "reconciled harmony" (*saṃghasāmagrī*).
Regarding the four companions: first, Śrutadatta; second, Khandadrava; third, Kauṇḍinya; and fourth, Kālodāyin. Question: If it is said below that there were five hundred bhikṣus...
Regarding why the Vinaya states that there were five hundred companions among those to be defeated: this indicates that the companions also belong to the side of the defeater.

Thus, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "There are other companions, even up to an infinite number. If it is asked how this does not contradict the Vinaya, the answer given below is that when Devadatta first proclaimed the five points and broke the wheel of practice, the five hundred still belonged to the side of those to be defeated; therefore, [the Vinaya] does not [contradict this].

Regarding the "Contradictory Question" (*xiāngwéi wèn*) below: If this refers to that which is to be refuted (*suǒpò*), why did Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana lead five hundred bhikṣus back [to the Buddha], and why did the Buddha say, "They should be taught to perform repentance for a *sthūlātyaya* offense"? The second [interpretation] explains:

Although the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) do not exist [in this context], the first *sthūlātyaya* is treated as the first; thus, what is called the "second" refers to the fact that the offense incurred is equivalent to the second [of those heinous crimes].

Furthermore, the initial [act] belongs to the five hundred who have not yet entered the formal count of the schism; because they subsequently participate in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) that effects the schism, it is called the "second" [offense].

If this is the case, then even when looking back at the time of the subsequent schism, those five hundred were included within the group; since they also belong to the side of the schismatic, they incur the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression).

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the *karmavācanā*-schism, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*," as recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*) regarding Devadatta’s conduct during the schism of the Sangha through the drawing of lots (*śalākā*).
When he announced, "Endure these five matters," and they proceeded to take up the voting sticks (*śalākā*), five hundred ignorant ones took them up. Ānanda said to the bhikṣus:
"These five matters are contrary to the Dharma. This constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense for violating the admonition of Nandika (Ānanda).

Because the procedure (*karmavācanā*) being performed is based on what is contrary to the Dharma, and because it subverts that correct Dharma procedure, it retains its original name [of "unlawful procedure"].

Regarding the phrase "now looking toward the four companions of Devadatta": when they first acted as the destroyers of the wheel of practice (*cakra*), they still retained the name of what was originally to be destroyed.
As for "originally one, now separate," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Originally they were one in harmony, but now they are divided into two distinct parts;

this is because the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) reaches the three thousandfold world-system, encompassing both monastics and laypeople. Because they have now become fragmented and dispersed, it is called [the breaking of the wheel].
The "three persons" refers to those at the three stages [of the path]; the "Saṃgha" refers to the remaining pure monks. As explained extensively in the twenty-fifth fascicle:

Ānanda and a certain Srotāpanna bhikṣu, having not yet received their voting tallies (śalākā), immediately departed for the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke this verse: [The verse follows. (Note: The specific verse is not provided in the source text, so it is indicated here as a placeholder.)

"It is easy for people to assemble with those who are evil, but difficult to assemble with those who are good; it is easy for the wicked to assemble together, but difficult for the virtuous to assemble with the wicked.
When Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana heard this matter, they went to that place and returned with five hundred bhikṣus (and so forth).
The *karmavācanā* (formal act) for schism in the Saṃgha also applies to Bhikṣuṇīs; however, they cannot cause a schism in the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Bhikṣuṇīs are of female retribution and lack faith in the Buddha; furthermore, since neither of the two wheels can be split by laypeople, there is no principle for them to be confused [with monks].
Within the monastic community, even those such as śrāmaṇeras who possess the precepts cannot cause a schism; thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "It is the bhikṣu who destroys the Saṃgha."
It is neither a householder, nor a śrāmaṇera, nor a bhikṣuṇī. [This refers to] the passage in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature" cited below, which states in full:
"I have further manifested the attainment of Buddhahood in a female body within Jambudvīpa, and all people said, 'How extraordinary!
A woman can attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Yet, the Tathāgata ultimately does not undergo such [transformation]."

Question: Since that sutra states that one manifests in a female form for the sake of taming immeasurable sentient beings through the female body, and thus establishes that there are those who attain Buddhahood as women, why does the *Pañcavastuka* say that women face five obstacles and cannot become Dharma Kings? Answer:

For now, this [text] relies upon the fact that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood as a male during his single cycle of transformation; it is for the sake of establishing this specific principle that it does not [mention female Buddhas].
Regarding the statement that women attain *nirvāṇa*, although it is spoken of, how could it be limited to the present alone? Thus, that sutra says:

"I have already accomplished what was to be done throughout immeasurable kalpas; yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, I even manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in a female body within Jambudvīpa.
Therefore, it is said that this is a provisional teaching concerning the past and so forth. Furthermore, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the dragon girl attains [Buddhahood].

At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a male, complete with the practices of a bodhisattva, and immediately proceed to the Immaculate World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, her attainment of Buddhahood was as a male;
what is now called "the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood" refers to the result by means of the name of its cause.

In the *Karmavācanā*, one does not falsely claim the title of Buddha; furthermore, because a Buddha does not participate in the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha, the thirty marks [of Devadatta] were lacking only the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the mark of the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "My thirty marks are not much inferior to those of the Buddha. If my disciples had not yet gathered and surrounded me..."
How is it that the Buddha, with no other intention, broke the Saṃgha and claimed to be the Buddha himself?
As cited in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (the "Miscellaneous Mind" treatise) below, there is also the case of one who was a Tathāgata;

this is because, among the assembly being broken, the True Buddha was employed as the leader of those being broken. Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "The Wheel of Dharma is destroyed in Jambudvīpa, not in other places."
Thus, where there is one who possesses the Way, there are those with divergent ways; where there is one Great Master, there are teachers of divergent schools.
At the very minimum, this extends to nine persons; hence the verse says: "In three directions, the minimum is eight. This refers to the degeneration of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

When it reaches nine in Jambudvīpa, the Wheel of the Dharma degenerates. Why is ten not mentioned here? The Buddha’s subsequent response clarifies this. Furthermore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
The Great Master was present among the assembly, and since they lacked any majestic radiance, it was on this basis that he could not proclaim false teachings.
However, if Devadatta had not falsely claimed [the title], how could he have been refuted? Now that he has made such a false claim, he cannot be treated as an example of the True Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "breaking below," it refers to breaking the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action). Since there is no fault when two assemblies perform different rituals within a single boundary (*sīmā*), this does not extend to those outside.

Those who are "broken" and extend beyond [the boundary] are those who have received false teachings outside the boundary; furthermore, this prevents the Wheel of the Dharma from turning throughout the trichiliocosm.
In this context, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) adopts this interpretation, stating: "The breaking of the Saṃgha regarding the Wheel of the Dharma is first [discussed here]."
When upholding the Dharma, it applies only within the boundary (*sīmā*); later, when the schism occurs, the practice of the Dharma extends both inside and outside the boundary.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Wángshè xià záxīn) states: "It means that a bhikṣu gives rise to such an aspiration: 'Devadatta is my Great Teacher, not Gautama;
the five dharmas he has established are the Path, not the Eightfold Noble Path'; he proclaims the Truths as if the Buddha had done so when he first attained enlightenment for the sake of Kauṇḍinya."

After the Wheel of the Four Truths had been turned, the Earth Deities informed the Sky Deities; the Sky Deities informed the Celestial Deities, and so on, until it was known throughout the Brahma Palace that the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma.
Since this was already known, why could [the assembly] not provide an answer? The commentary on the text can be understood as not requiring the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha;

for as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* (Zhenglun) refutes the schism of the Saṃgha, it states that such a schism must rely upon the formal procedures performed by that assembly. The *Śīla-śāstra* says:
The essential point is that within a single *sīmā* (boundary), two assemblies should act separately; this is not the case here.

Rather, the provisional *karmavācanā* rite merely assists in the act of schism, because that which is being split extends beyond the boundary. If one were to first provide a further explanation of the reason for this, it would be as follows:
if one does not rely on the provisional *poṣadha-karmavācanā*, then the schism is not yet complete. Thus, if the Wheel of Dharma is split, it is possible for the *karmavācanā* to also be split.

Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) certainly does not break the Wheel of Dharma, yet the Wheel of Dharma delights in breaking the *karmavācanā*.

This means that because worldly people possess the four roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth, while still dwelling in the outflowing (*sāsrava*) state where the Noble Path has not yet arisen, they are called "worldly" (*laukika*).

When the Noble Path of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is attained, it increases and excels; thus, there is a "disturbance of affairs," which refers to [the situation] regarding the matter of the *karmavācanā*.

There may indeed be confusion regarding this. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "In the case of a noble person (*ārya*), if confusion arises, it is possible for a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*) to form;

this is considered 'non-dharma' (*adharma*) within one's own category (*svabhāga*). From the initial stage where a person of good roots attains the precursor to the fire of wisdom, they cultivate the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) through the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) as their own category, continuing up to the 'Supreme Worldly Dharma' (*laukikāgra-dharma*), which can, in a single moment of mind, possess the function of a Great Man (*mahāsattva*), thereby departing [from the mundane]."

The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). To negate and destroy the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and enter the gate of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one repeatedly contemplates a single practice for a single moment;
these are all considered "one's own portion" (*sva-bhāga*). However, in relation to that which has not yet been attained—the untainted [state]—these are "another's portion" (*para-bhāga*).

For one who has seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), the untainted noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*) consisting of the first fifteen moments of mind, such as the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

This means that because one is able to investigate and clearly perceive the principles of the truths (*satya*), and because the meaning of having attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) is supreme, it cannot be refuted by either its own category or another category.
When the Sūtra says "I," it refers to the *Nirvāṇa*; its full text states: "I also manifest in Jambudvīpa to break up harmonious assemblies."
The monastic community and all sentient beings all claim that I am one who has split the Saṃgha; yet I observe that among humans and devas, there is no one capable of splitting a harmonious Saṃgha.
The treatise refers back to the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, stating that because one should have attained [the fruit] but did not, it is called "splitting";
thus it says, "the realization of what was not yet attained. Furthermore, because Nirvāṇa is the ultimate consummation of the Mahāyāna and manifests its secret excellence, it is called "ultimate."

Regarding "No destruction" (aprahaṇa) and the two [categories] below: since this treatise belongs to the Hīnayāna, it speaks of "actual destruction" (*bhūtavyavasthāna*) and "provisional, temporary demonstration of destruction.

From the stage of "patience toward others" (*parabhāga-kṣānti*) upward is termed "patience toward others. The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "An ordinary person who has attained patience cannot be destroyed, because they have already entered the definitive assembly of the noble ones (*āryasaṃgha*).
Thus, being indestructible by self or others means that both one's own part (*svabhāga*) and the part of others (*parabhāga*) are [indestructible].
It is indestructible. Regarding the realization of the true nature of the mind of wisdom, a sutra states:

"If a person, with respect to the Dharma, is able to observe and endure it with even a small amount of wisdom and finds joy therein, this is called 'practice through faith' (*śraddhācārī*). It further states: "This person, while within the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, correctly contemplates all phenomena;
though they have not yet attained the wisdom of emptiness and non-self, they are able to give rise to a mental state that resembles the dharma of patience within the world."

From this point onward, one is said to have transcended the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*). If one lacks the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā-ādīni pañcendriyāṇi*), that person remains among the external ordinary beings;

because they gradually practice and attain the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages through cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), they still retain their original name and are thus called those who "practice by faith" (*śraddhā-carita*).

[The phrase] "not breaking the lower" should be joined with the three characters "having the portion of others and breaking," which are omitted from the text. Below the section on the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this refers to the person (*pudgala*).

The attainment of the wisdom of non-self within the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Peak (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) constitutes practice in accordance with the Dharma;

that is to say, the practices of emptiness, non-self, and so forth are termed "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*). In these stages, one cannot be refuted by either one's own side or another’s side.

The above citations are all from the first fascicle of the text. Furthermore, below that, it refers to the text of the eighth fascicle, which asks: "How many factors constitute the schism of the Saṃgha?"
At that time, he replied: "The Dharma will not abide for long; it shall not even pass through one night.

Thereupon, the Brahma King, the various devas, Śāriputra, and the other great disciples immediately returned to harmonious accord. Some say that these five hundred bhikṣus received this retribution because in previous lives they had obstructed others from attaining roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it was spoken because the minds of ordinary people are fickle and restless.
It may be refuted if one has attained mundane emptiness and so forth as an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) on the stage of inner cultivation;

however, it cannot be refuted by those who have already seen the Truths (satyadarśin), for they are noble ones (ārya) possessing untainted (anāsrava) realization. As for "endurance" (kṣānti), because ordinary persons have not yet fully perfected the power of the Path, they may tolerate false teachings;
this is not the case for the noble ones, and therefore [their realization] cannot be refuted.

Regarding the statement that "among ordinary and sage beings, the sages should have affairs and disturbances," this is correct. First, because their capacity (*indriya*) is fixed, it cannot be altered;

moreover, having heard the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma, they have realized it through both hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī* prajñā), and thus it is absolutely impossible for them to be overturned.

Second, even if there were the external conditions of Devadatta’s perverse attachments and powerful influence, when compared to the hearing of the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma, [the former] is utterly insignificant.

Because there must be that which is to be realized but has not yet been realized, the capacity [of the faculties] is indeterminate; those who were defeated by Devadatta—namely the five hundred and so forth—are such individuals.
"If one kills" refers to the nine grades of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) abandoned when one has already attained the third fruit and is proceeding toward the fourth stage.

The uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the final, lowest-of-the-low grade of the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation is called the "final mind" (*paścima-citta*), as it is capable of destroying all afflictions, much like a worldly diamond.
Compared to the subsequent state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it possesses only a small portion of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

When the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayaprāpti*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arise together, if one kills such an Anāgāmin, could this also be considered killing an Arhat—namely, the failure to obtain what ought to be obtained? The answer is: No. This is because [the Anāgāmin] still possesses the higher grades of defilements.

The refuter speaks from the perspective of the object to be refuted; therefore, they include ordinary beings while excluding noble ones. However, if one speaks from the perspective of the perpetrator, since both three and four [people] can be killed, there is no need for such distinction.
Regarding the offense of causing schism and the offense of destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, these concern the Three Jewels collectively.

Although it is specifically the Saṃgha that is being split, the Three Jewels are equally damaged, just as when Devadatta proclaimed the "Five Dharmas" to disrupt the correct teachings and caused the Saṃgha to fall into confusion.
In the case of killing, it is not so; because one abandons the previous fruit and moves toward the subsequent fruit, it is said that "it is also not shared with the subsequent [moment].

The phrase "in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) expresses its swiftness. This is because in one *kṣaṇa* the preceding [state] belongs to three fruits, while in the subsequent *kṣaṇa* it immediately belongs to four fruits.
Therefore, at the time of a single thought-moment within a *kṣaṇa*, its destruction cannot be described. The intent of the question is to refute the notion of an ordinary monk (*pṛthagjana-bhikṣu*).

If failing to attain what one ought to attain is called "breaking the Wheel of Dharma," could it also be that making offerings to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) results in the merit of a noble one (*ārya*)?

If that were so, since making offerings to ordinary persons below does not result in the merit of a noble one, this would conversely imply that breaking ordinary persons does not involve breaking the noble ones.

Why then do you say that failing to attain [the fruit] in another's portion is called "breaking"? Answer: Because if one has already attained resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), such a person cannot be broken; therefore, one must refer to the case of ordinary persons.

Whether one attains [the fruit] or not can be refuted by this argument. Furthermore, if we discuss the nature [of the Saṃgha] in a restricted sense, the two types of Saṃgha—the ordinary and the noble—are categorically distinct;

how then could it be said that by making offerings to the ordinary, one obtains the merit of the noble? This interpretation is incorrect. As for the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (the *Zaxin lun*), it states:
"In the three directions, the minimum is eight; thus the *karmavācanā* is maintained. In Jambudvīpa, it reaches nine."

This constitutes the destruction of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "That which is destroyed by *karmavācanā* pertains to all three continents; the destruction of the Sangha by means of the Wheel of Dharma is restricted to Jambudvīpa.

This is consistent with both the [Abhidharma-]kośa-śāstra and the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. In that latter work, it first asks: "In what division does the Sangha abide so as not to be destroyed? It answers: "Before the boundaries have been established (*sīmābandha*)."

Before and after the Muni had entered parinirvāṇa, while the *piśita* (cankerous growth) had not yet arisen, and when there was no "foremost pair"—during these six periods, the Wheel of Dharma could not be destroyed.
(The meaning of these six periods is fully explained in the cited passage from the *Fahui*). The intent of the question is:

Are these two periods distinguished based on the temporal sequence of the destruction [of the Dharma], or are they divided into two times based on whether it is before or after the Buddha? In the response, the first interpretation is adopted.

The breaking of the preceding [period] and the breaking of the succeeding [period] constitute two distinct times; it is said that during these two times, there is no such breaking. Regarding this, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) raises a specific objection:
"If that is so, why is it that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs throughout all ages? The answer is: "It can only be achieved through expedient means and is never ultimate.

In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the explanation of the preceding and succeeding periods states: "The 'former' refers to when not long after the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; the 'latter' refers to when the Buddha is about to enter Parinirvāṇa. The second [period] is as follows.
At that time, because the great assembly was practicing a single flavor (*ekarasa*) without any schism, they did not expect two Buddhas [to appear].

This refers to the fact that they did not accept the presence of a Buddha before or after [the first], nor did they accept the common teaching of a period without schism. If one were to hear of a schism occurring during the interval, or if one were to establish a period without schism after the Buddha’s passing as being "at one time," the treatise states:
"The Muni has already entered *parinirvāṇa*; its meaning is already encompassed. There are only five periods. Therefore, this [latter view] is not accepted.

Regarding the phrase "breaking [the Dharma]," the text below is abbreviated; the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) fully enumerates nine meanings: first, using the correct to break the correct refers to using the Wheel of the True Dharma (*dharmacakra*) to break it, or using the false to break the correct;
second, merely losing the benefit of the matter involves minor faults and light transgressions, whereas breaking the Wheel of the Dharma is grave because it results in the loss of understanding;
third, breaking a teacher by a disciple is grave, while mutual breaking among fellow disciples is light; fourth, merely breaking a practitioner is light.

1. When both principle and practice are violated, the offense is grave; it harms only those who have left the household life. 2. When the path is slighted, both monastics and laity are equally harmed; this is a grave offense. 3.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), when the intention deviates from the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), both the intention and the rite are lost; this is a grave offense. 4. Regarding the *karmavācanā*, when the two assemblies are separated, the Wheel of Dharma is broken; this is a grave offense. 5. Regarding the *karmavācanā*, when the seven classes of followers are divided, the Wheel of Dharma is broken;

this is a grave offense. 6. Regarding the *karmavācanā*, it certainly does not break the Wheel of Dharma; for the Wheel of Dharma easily breaks the *karmavācanā*, this is a grave offense. 7. Regarding the *karmavācanā*, it harms only the Sangha.

Regarding the question concerning the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) as pertaining to the Three Jewels: the intent of the question is that since the wheel belongs to the Dharma and the interpreter belongs to the person, and since the Dharma and the person are distinct, should two offenses not be incurred?

The answer below states that because the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma necessarily involves the breaking of the interpretation of the Dharma; the rest is as stated in the text. These four are the four types of Saṃgha. "The other" refers to Devadatta.

As for the term "Jewel" (*ratna*) in "Saṃgha-jewel," it pertains exclusively to the category of the Noble Ones (*ārya*); whereas as for the term "Saṃgha," [it pertains to both the ordinary and the noble].

Because this concerns both the noble (ārya) and the ordinary (pṛthagjana), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one makes an offering to the Saṃgharatna by placing it within a stūpa, one is making an offering to the Saṃgha of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
if one makes an offering to the Saṃgha [in person], both the ordinary and the noble are included.

Regarding the mind, because the intention (*cetanā*) fulfills the conditions for an offense, it is like the case of performing a *karmavācanā* that results in a schism; even though they perform the same ritual action simultaneously, each is judged individually.

If one obtains even a single minor *kārṣāpaṇa*, one does not expect many small coins in return; likewise, it is with the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* asks: "Among these five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), which is the greatest evil? The answer is: "The false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is the most evil among all karmas. Regarding the thought within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this is said to have the greatest fruit. The treatise itself explains: [The text continues: ...the thought associated with the Peak of Existence is the most powerful of all thoughts. Why? Because its object is supreme, and because it is free from the antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Furthermore, the power of the cause is superior to the power of the object. This is because the cause is the primary factor in producing the result. For example, when a person performs an action with a mind of intense hatred, even if the object is not particularly grave, the resulting retribution is extremely heavy. Conversely, if one performs an action with a mind of great faith, even if the object is grave, the resulting retribution is not as heavy. Therefore, the power of the cause is superior. Moreover, the power of the object is superior to the power of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*). This is because the object is the basis upon which the action is performed. For example, if one kills a human being, the retribution is heavier than if one kills an animal, even if the animal is large and the human is small. Thus, the power of the object is superior. However, the power of the cause is ultimately superior to both the power of the object and the power of the preparatory effort. This is because the cause is the very root that produces the result. Therefore, the thought associated with the Peak of Existence is the greatest evil of all. It is like a king who, though surrounded by many ministers, is still called the sole ruler. Likewise, although there are many types of evil karma, the thought associated with the Peak of Existence is the foremost. It is also like a medicine that, though mixed with many other ingredients, is still called the sovereign remedy. Likewise, although there are many types of wholesome karma, the thought associated with the Peak of Existence is the most excellent. It is also like a lamp that, though its light may be dimmed by many obstacles, still illuminates the darkness. Likewise, although there are many types of ignorance, the ignorance associated with the Peak of Existence is the most profound. It is also like a mountain that, though covered by many clouds, still towers above all. Likewise, although there are many types of afflictions (*kleśa*), the affliction associated with the Peak of Existence is the most difficult to eradicate. It is also like a tree that, though surrounded by many branches, still has a single trunk. Likewise, although there are many types of mental states, the state associated with the Peak of Existence is the most stable. It is also like a river that, though joined by many tributaries, still flows toward the ocean. Likewise, although there are many paths of rebirth, the path associated with the Peak of Existence leads to the most extreme suffering. It is also like a fire that, though fueled by much wood, still consumes everything. Likewise, although there are many types of karmic formations, the formations associated with the Peak of Existence produce the most intense results. It is also like a wheel that, though turned by many spokes, still revolves as one. Likewise, although there are many types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), the phenomena associated with the Peak of Existence are the most difficult to transcend. It is also like a fortress that, though besieged by many enemies, still remains impregnable. Likewise, although there are many types of adversaries, the adversary associated with the Peak of Existence is the most formidable. It is also like a physician who, though attended by many disciples, still possesses the most profound knowledge. Likewise, although there are many teachers, the teacher associated with the Peak of Existence is the most authoritative. It is also like a jewel that, though set among many gems, still possesses the most brilliant luster. Likewise, although there are many types of wisdom, the wisdom associated with the Peak of Existence is the most penetrating. It is also like a drum that, though struck by many hands, still produces the most resonant sound. Likewise, although there are many types of vocal expressions, the expression associated with the Peak of Existence is the most significant. It is also like a cloud that, though accompanied by many raindrops, still brings the most abundant harvest. Likewise, although there are many types of merit, the merit associated with the Peak of Existence is the most vast. It is also like a sun that, though obscured by many mists, still dispels the darkness.
