Likewise, although there are many types of leaders, the leader associated with the Peak of Existence is the most preeminent. It is also like a general who, though commanding many troops, still holds the most strategic position. Likewise, although there are many types of positions, the position associated with the Peak of Existence is the most secure. It is also like a fortress that, though besieged by many attackers, still remains unassailable. Likewise, although there are many types of defenses, the defense associated with the Peak of Existence is the most impenetrable. It is also like a gatekeeper who, though watching many entrances, still guards the most important passage. Likewise, although there are many types of watchmen, the watchman associated with the Peak of Existence is the most vigilant. It is also like a lamp that, though placed in a dark room, still illuminates the most obscure corner. Likewise, although there are many types of illumination, the illumination associated with the Peak of Existence is the most penetrating. It is also like a mirror that, though reflecting many images, still reveals the most subtle details. Likewise, although there are many types of reflections, the reflection associated with the Peak of Existence is the most
Because that thought takes the eighty thousand *kalpas* of lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its retribution, by analogy,
one who causes a schism in the Wheel of the Dharma undergoes suffering for eighty thousand *kalpas*. If one follows the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*,
committing the fourth offense of *sthūlātyaya* results in a lifespan equal to four thousand years in Tuṣita Heaven, which corresponds to fifty billion and sixty thousand years in human reckoning.

Falling into the *niraya* hells is also merely a difference between the sūtras and the śāstras; furthermore, the divisions of *kalpas* vary in weight and number—some being large and others small—and because ten million (*wan wan*) constitutes the measure of a hundred million (*yi*), such distinctions arise.
The ability to refute [the opponent] by means of established reasons refers first to the refutation of their practice-wheel (*caryā-cakra*); yet this is not yet ultimate.

It must reach Gayā to refute their ritual action (*karmavācanā*) before it becomes ultimate. Regarding the acceptance at Rājagṛha, when the five dharmas were first proclaimed, five hundred [monks] accepted them;
thus, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 26, Devadatta fled toward Gayā while the Buddha followed behind him toward Gayā.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, the Buddha told Ānanda, "Go and summon them. They immediately came down from their quarters. Devadatta declined, saying, "I am renowned for my reputation;
the Six Groups [of monks] will say, 'We have established our fame for future generations. While the Buddha was in the world, Devadatta and the Six Groups together caused a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the Buddha heard this in full, Ānanda reported these circumstances to the World-Honored One in detail. The World-Honored One heard it.
Having spoken this verse, the intent of the question is as follows: Once Devadatta has begun to destroy the practice of the Dharma, he has already committed a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense;

even if he is not subsequently summoned to the assembly, there is no offense of performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) apart from the group. However, if his followers have not yet committed the *ānantarya* offense, would one now incur the offense of "separating from the community" (*bhedaka*) if one does not summon them?
The answer below is that it is not because their commission of the *ānantarya* constitutes a grave offense [that they are exempt]; rather, it is simply...
There is no offense; it merely anticipates that after the schism between the leader and his followers, the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox will diverge.

Thus, there is no fault of the orthodox being distinct from the heterodox. This is not like what is stated in the *Śīla-prastāva* (the introductory section on precepts), nor is it as taught by the Tathāgata.

Establishing one's own [view] as the correct text, it briefly omits the thirteen *aniyata-dharmas*, the *nissaggiya-pācittiya*, the *pācittiya*, the *pratideśanīya*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha*. Therefore, it says "up to the settling of disputes," following the subsequent [text].

These include the *dharmas* for practicing in accordance [with the rules], such as the confession (*pratideśanā*) for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the treatment for concealment (*channapraticchādana*). Furthermore, there are the *dharmas* for practicing in opposition [to the rules], namely the seven types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for treating individuals.
All of these refer to what the legislator (the Buddha) did not prescribe, yet was prescribed; and what was not prescribed, yet was prescribed.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, only the *dharmas* for practicing in accordance are explicitly stated, while the *dharmas* for practicing in opposition are omitted and subsumed within the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*). From the words "Furthermore, moreover" down to "is not the same," this is the current Master’s [interpretation].

Regarding the path for both the ordained and the laity, it is said that those who dwell at home and those who have left home should practice the Dharma together, namely the ninefold division of the scriptures (*navāṅga-buddhavacana*):
*sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, and *adbhutadharma*.
To alter these ninefold scriptures by composing different phrasings and so forth is entirely contrary to what the Tathāgata has taught.

Since it has already been explained above that the various *saṃgha-dharmas* applied to the assembly differ according to whether they pertain to the confession (*poṣadha*) or its opposite, I have not yet understood how the *karma-vācanā* *saṃgha-dharmas* applied to the assembly further differ.
It may be that what follows below is an explanation of these two types of *dharma*: namely, the *pratipatti-dharma* (the dharma of practice) and the *saṃgha-dharma*.
The passage beginning with "出下古謂" (The ancient [commentators] below say regarding "emerging") means that drawing blood is merely a preliminary expedient (*upāya*) for killing.

Because one seeks to kill the Buddha but does not yet achieve the final act, it is still the very first stage and thus not an offense; this is because there was as yet no prohibition, and thus the contrary teaching could be transgressed. The question following "問下意云" (The meaning of the subsequent question says) is:

Although there is no teaching permitting the transgression of drawing blood, the phenomenon of drawing blood belongs to the category of killing. Since killing was already prohibited previously, [how can it be done?]

If blood is drawn only after one has received the precepts, is this not also a violation of the prohibitions against taking life? However, while the precept against killing is grave, the act of drawing blood is light;

why then do you say there is no teaching to violate? Answer: In ancient times, it was said that [the offense] could be expiated when contrasted with what is not a *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression, as this was spoken in reference to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

One may say that prior to the second [offense], there is killing that can be violated and thus can be expiated; however, this is not the case for an *ānantarya* transgression committed against a Buddha.
Therefore, one cannot say that prior to the second [instance], there was no shedding of blood from the Buddha.

Question: If it is said that killing the Buddha constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, and thus there exists the principle of a "first-time non-offense" distinct from others, would it not also follow that killing one's father or an Arhat—though these are also *ānantarya* offenses—likewise possesses the principle of a "first-time non-offense"? Answer: Although killing one's father is indeed an *ānantarya* offense...

Because it can be repented in the same manner as the Buddha [taught], there is no distinction; thus, there was no initial transgression. Second, that which is different cannot be repented and constitutes a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense.

Since the *Chih-lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states that one is "pure," we know there was no initial transgression. Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), if it is said that "the first is not a *sthūlātyaya*," this may be so;
however, does this not mean that there was no transgression of principle or the commission of a heinous karma? If there were...
What is meant by the "nine pure persons"? Aṅgulimāla—translated into Chinese as Zhǐjì (Finger-Topknot)—is mentioned in that sutra:
there was a village named Sona where lived a poor Brahmin woman named Bhadrā. She gave birth to a son named Sarvalokapratyakṣa (Manifest to All the World).
At a young age he lost his father; at twelve years old, being intelligent and possessed of eloquent wisdom, he received the Brahminical teachings and [was instructed] to kill.
Having killed a thousand people, he made finger-rings from their fingers to wear as a crown upon his head and returned, having attained the status of a Brahmin.
For this reason, he was named Aṅgulimāla. He then proceeded to kill a thousand people, falling short by one.

At that time, seeing his mother grasping a sword and intending to go forward and end his life, he was ten *yojanas* less one *zhang* away from Śrāvastī. The Buddha, knowing this through his omniscience, immediately came and touched him.
As Aṅgulimāla held his sword, intending to harm the Buddha, the Buddha manifested the appearance of evading him. At that time, he spoke this verse: "Stop, stop, great śramaṇa!
Son of King Śuddhodana, I am Aṅgulimāla; now I shall speak of the 'one finger' and so forth.
Then the World-Honored One, walking like a king of geese for seven steps, looked back and spoke this verse: "Stop, stop, Aṅgulimāla! You should abide in purity."
"I am the Fully Enlightened One; I bestow upon you the sword of wisdom. I declare that I abide at the limit of non-arising, yet you do not perceive it.
[He continued] until he said: "You should cast away this sharp sword and quickly come to take refuge in clear wisdom. Do not follow evil teachers who mistake what is not the Dharma for the Dharma.
Thereupon, he immediately cast away the sword, left the household life, and studied the Path, as described in detail in the first fascicle of that work.

Question: Regarding the passage below which states that Aṅgulimāla was pure, yet those among the non-Buddhists who kill their parents receive no benefit and are immediately expelled—how is this to be understood?
Answer: It is not said that he was expelled because his offense was identical to that of the second person [who killed his father];

rather, it is because, from the perspective of killing one's own parents, such an act violates the principle of reality and constitutes a grave misdeed, and thus must be expelled. (The section on "Shou" follows the *Jieshu*).

This belongs to the doctrine of the present master. He says: "The current interpretation is not so; if the offense of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) has no beginning, then how can it be that one only breaks the Saṃgha by shedding blood?
It is the same as this [case]. Answer: In the case of killing one's father, there is a formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) that can be violated;
however, in the case of shedding blood, there is no such exclusion that can be violated. Therefore, it is said to be pure.
Regarding the four individuals mentioned in the Vinaya who conspired with King Ajātaśatru— where it is said, "You shall assassinate the father-king, and I shall assassinate the Buddha"—
and where they first dispatched two, then four, then eight, and so on up to sixty-four people to harm the World-Honored One:

since these constitute the preparatory offenses (*prayoga*) of the precept against killing by dispatching messengers, the existence of such preparatory offenses places them at the same level as the second category of transgression.

Why is it called "pure"? It is not because one does not uphold the five categories of offenses, nor is it because one generally upholds the five categories and remains equal to those who do not transgress;

thus it is named "pure. Furthermore, below this, another interpretation is presented: the meaning is that although Devadatta also committed the *pārājika* offense of drawing blood and the *ānantarya* of breaking the practice by proclaiming the five points, his breaking was not yet ultimate;
he was able to enter the number of the *karmavācanā* monks, and it is with reference to this that [he is considered pure].

Because it is called "pure" by virtue of upholding [the precepts], there can only be a violation; if one were actually in contravention of a proscribed offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), it would not be pure and thus a violation could not occur.
Therefore, it is said that this is the reverse of the former case.

To commit a grave offense is precisely to incur *pārājika*. Since one has already addressed the Buddha, this constitutes a great falsehood; logically, the grave offense is already established—how then can one remain pure?

Regarding the person who causes a schism in the Sangha, the answer below uses the term "to adjust": if one says, "I shall become a Buddha," this is not yet a definitive claim, and thus the grave offense has not been committed.
If that is so, then if one says, "I shall become a Buddha," one is not yet a Buddha; how then could one cause a schism?

"Ya," this [query] is also missing an answer within the text; the present response states: "If he were a true Buddha, there would be no schism (*bheda*); because he is not a Buddha, it is said that a schism occurs.
Previously, it was also stated that Devadatta styled himself as such, yet his essence was not that of a Buddha; thus, he is included among the nine [categories]. Furthermore, it says:
"If Devadatta had not committed a schism in the Saṃgha, how could he have again relied on the lower to connect with the upper? This is stated because of the intended meaning of the response.

Furthermore, based on the aforementioned thought, "I shall become a Buddha," one does not commit an offense; and now, based on the treatise stating that the Buddha has no faith, one does not commit a grave offense.
Whether it is grave or not grave, in both cases it is said that there is no offense of the *pārājika* for a great falsehood.
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are as clarified in the usual explanations.
Regarding the three immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) that constitute *pārājika*: these refer to killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, and killing an *arhat*.

These involve a violation of the established precepts and are the most extreme forms of gravity. However, even if one commits these, one cannot subsequently cause a schism in the Saṃgha, because such a person is no longer pure.

Furthermore, acts such as drawing blood [from a Tathāgata] or breaking the practice (*caryā*) are grave violations of the practice itself; yet, for these, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense, which is a formal instruction regarding the conduct.

Even a minor offense may be counted as a formal act (*karmavācanā*), for one who upholds the precepts by name should be like those described in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as "the nine pure persons" who can cause schism;
however, the evidence below places the shedding of blood first and the breaking of the Saṃgha later. Regarding the intended meaning, the sub-commentary on the Vinaya states:

"With his original intention, he seeks to seize the assembly, destroy the Saṃgha, and sever the Dharma, so that he may return to follow his own views and fill his heart and mind completely, leaving nothing else."
Regarding the second section of the "Explanation of the Lower" concerning the *sthūlātyaya* of approaching [the schism], the question below asks:
since the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha has not yet arisen, why was he preemptively penalized with a *sthūlātyaya*?
Furthermore, below it says that when Devadatta first threw a stone at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and drew blood, the Buddha ordered Śāriputra to be dispatched to inform the lay followers.

Suffering from ill repute and the loss of gain, he went to the five families of his own kin to beg for alms. Consequently, the Buddha established the rule against eating in a separate group (*pṛthag-bhaktika*).

Furthermore, Devadatta conceived this thought: "Gautama has cut off the people's food; I shall rather cause a schism in the Saṅgha. He then formulated the three requests and proclaimed the five points.
Although admonished, he did not relinquish them. Only then did the Buddha declare: "In Niraya hell for one kalpa"—this was to manifest the origins of his transgressions.
It is gradual, not entirely unarisen.

Regarding the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for disregarding admonition, the following passage in the text—where the Buddha commands the bhikṣus to admonish [the offender] through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations)—states:
"I have already completed the motion; there remains the *karman*. You should now abandon this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform the *karman* against you."

[If one] grinds [it], one further commits a grave offense (the above is from the Vinaya text). Since it is called a "grave offense," it should likewise be subject to the Buddha’s rebuke as in the second case.
Why, then, does the end of the precept state that there is no offense in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established?

The answer is that, regarding Devadatta’s initial actions, this is based on the Vinaya which first prohibited eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*) in order to manage those who are difficult to discipline, fearing they might cause a schism in the Saṃgha; subsequently, [the rule was relaxed].

Once the five factors have been proclaimed that break the harmony of the Saṃgha, the Buddha declared it a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) with a retribution of one *kalpa*; thus, cause and effect are made manifest.

As for the name, because the offense is exclusively a *pārājika* (defeat), its designation is restricted. However, when the name is applied broadly—as when, after the first proclamation is finished, one warns:

"Do not let the Saṃgha’s *karmavācanā* lead to further commission of a grave offense," and even down to the completion of the first or second *karmavācanā*, one likewise says: "Do not let the Saṃgha perform [the act] again"—the name is used in a general sense.
If one commits a grave offense through *karmavācanā*, this is termed "universal" (*sāmānya*); yet even when dividing the offense, there is no absence of degrees of lightness and gravity.

As the Vinaya states: if one abandons [the intention] before the *jñapti* is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one abandons it after the *jñapti* is completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya*; if one abandons it after one *karmavācanā* is completed, it is two *sthūlātyayas*;

if one abandons it after two *karmavācanās* are completed, it is three *sthūlātyayas*; only upon the completion of the third *karmavācanā* does it become a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Furthermore, because the Saṃgha has not yet clearly manifested the cause and effect, it constitutes an offense.

It is not the second [offense]. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of the subsequent text, it follows the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) by adding the following at the end of the section:

"Regarding the second [point], 'not admonishing during the time of admonition'—because one fails to admonish when there is resistance to admonition, this resistance constitutes the initial *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This is the primary point of understanding. The remaining four [offenses] are:
killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an *arhat*, and shedding the blood [of a Buddha]. As for "relying upon," the Vinaya states that Devadatta said, "The Tathāgata is constant..."

Regarding those who preach the dhūta practices, few desires, contentment, and the joy of renunciation, I now have five dharmas which are likewise superior dhūta practices for those with few desires, contentment, and the joy of renunciation;
these are so-called "resembling words" (*sādharmya-vākya*) and the like, by which one relies upon them. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"As for the schism of the Saṃgha, one relies upon the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) and the eight right paths; therefore, the Buddha first rebuked and admonished those who would oppose [the teaching]."
The offense for failing to provide admonition is the second [category]. Now, below, the remaining four [categories] are shown as a summary of what was previously explained extensively.

Regarding those offenses that have a "first instance," this is in view of not violating the formal regulations (*śikṣāpada*); it does not concern the nature of the transgression as a fundamental sin (*pārājika*). Thus, the *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma) states:

"If one discusses the name 'transgression' (*ānantarya*), it refers to karma arising from specific events; there is no formal regulation (*avijñapti*) to be violated. Therefore, in the Vinaya, when non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) kill their parents, they are considered to have no basis for growth [in merit]."
"Yi (益) then immediately executed the expulsion; how could he have hoped to violate the teachings? (The above is the original text).
Regarding Ajita, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder named Ajita.
He committed adultery with his mother; for this reason, he killed his father. His mother, in turn, [committed adultery] with another man."
Once he had learned of his common son, he killed him as well. There was an Arhat who was his spiritual friend; feeling shame before this friend, he then killed him too.
Having committed these murders, he went immediately to the Jeta Grove Monastery seeking to go forth [into the religious life].
At that time, the bhikṣus fully knew that this man had committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma), and none dared to grant him admission. Why? Because of this.
Because he heard this, his anger redoubled; that very night, he set a great and fierce fire, burning down the monastic quarters and killing many innocent people.
He then went to Rājagṛha and approached the Tathāgata, seeking permission to leave the household life.
The Tathāgata immediately granted it and preached the essentials of the Dharma for him, causing his grave offenses to gradually diminish until he resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Regarding the "thought of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," since this is stated here as a grave offense, it is certain that there is no such thing as a first offense;

this is the second [category]. The five types of benefits (*pañca-lābha*) are: keeping extra robes (*dīrgha-cīvara*), staying overnight separated from one's robes, refusing an invitation, eating in a group apart from the community, and visiting the homes of others before or after a meal.

In these cases, for those who possess robes, there is a period of five months; for those without robes, it is only one month. This is as explained in the section on the distribution of robes (*cīvara-vibhāga*) following the *Vilana* [incident].
After the Buddha accepted the invitation of the brahmin Vairaṇyā, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, he intended to travel through the human world.

The brahmin offered three robes as a gift to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, and gave two pieces of woolen cloth for the summer robes to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus did not accept them and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I permit you to accept them; this is called a 'timely gift. As for those who divide the robes into four parts, this also refers to the method of distributing the robes."
The text simply states that to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) during the summer retreat without being prompted by the labor [of robe-making] is called "untimely" (*akāla*).
As cited in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, Part II, in the *Cīvara-vastu*: "The two groups each held their own views and split into two factions.

This refers to cases where the formal act is not performed before the assembly (*sammukhībhūta*) at the proper time; rather, the distribution follows the number of monks present in each of the two factions. The opposite of this constitutes the proper procedure.
The methods for the correct and the heterodox differ. If one obtains a large quantity of robes, they are to be divided into two portions. Thus, in the *Cīvara-vastu*, it says:

"At that time, the monks obtained a large amount of divisible robes, and the Saṃgha split into two factions. The monks informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: 'They should be divided into two portions.
If the Saṃgha splits into two factions before the divisible robes have been obtained, the Buddha said:"

"One should ask the donor, 'To whom should this be given? (The above is the original text). This refers to the passage from the Vinaya cited below concerning the time when the Saṃgha receives [offerings], which should be compared with the textual details of the bhikṣu receiving a gift.
The term "etc. includes the method of distributing by casting lots (*śalākā*). Regarding that, the Buddha said: "One should not cast the lots oneself;
one should have someone who is not present cast the lots. If it is an offering made at an improper time, it belongs to the Saṃgha.
When a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) has been performed and the object [of the gift] is already distributed, it must be determined by means of the Dharma.

Even if the *karman* has been concluded and the assembly of monks has not yet dispersed, they may still receive a share of the benefit; conversely, if this is not the case, they do not receive it. This concludes the preceding section.

Below, the *Daocao* (Great Commentary) on the two divisions of the Sangha—monks and nuns—states: "The mutual rectification between the two divisions also has four types: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, and if the distribution is compared..."

If there is not even a single *śrāmaṇera* among the monks, or if there is not even a single *śrāmaṇerī* among the nuns—and thus the five groups of practitioners take [the precepts] from one another at the monastery without distinguishing between monks and nuns or other categories—all are considered monks present before them; they collectively and jointly receive [the precepts].
Therefore, the meaning of "receiving by category" (*jùlèi jiāshòu*) can be understood in this way.

"Non-procedure" (*akriyā*) refers to the distribution [of robes] directly without the necessity of performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*). Regarding the four kinds of "certainty" (*niyama*), this is discussed here in terms of the present time: first, certainty of time;
for example, on the same sixteenth day of the seventh month, if one receives the robe before the summer retreat has ended, one incurs an offense.

Second, certainty of place; for example, within the same boundary (*sīmā*), those who have entered the prior retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*)... Third, certainty of persons; for example, three people who are not from outside the boundary... manifest.

Regarding the four dharmas for the preceding *pūrvavāsa* (prior retreat): in all cases, the number of people must be counted directly as they participate together in casting the voting sticks (*śalākā*) to divide [the robes].

For the *akāla-pratyakṣa* (non-seasonal presence), one simply changes "the seventh month" and so forth to "non-seasonal," removes the phrase "prior retreat," and performs it [in this manner]. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that these all refer to the opening passage of the *Cīvara-vastu*;

the explanation below clarifies the meaning of "joyful. Because one receives [the robes] in their entirety, it is given the name "joyful. The three utterances are the same as the three recitations of the mental vow (*manasikāra*), as explained below.

Furthermore, to clarify the ritual procedure: it is to be carried out using the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) to resolve matters before the assembly, following the precedent of the rules for distributing the minor belongings of a deceased person.
As for the four cases below, both the location and the persons involved are indeterminate.

However, the *Vinaya* states that when there are two separate monastic communities in different locations and a large quantity of robes to be distributed, if the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) is numerous while the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇīsaṃgha*) is few... [the monks] should [act as follows].
The Venerable Kāśyapa did not know how to report this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "It should be divided into two parts...
[and so on] ...even if there are no bhikṣuṇīs and only śrāmaṇerikās. The Buddha said: "It should be divided into two parts; therefore it is called 'equal property' (*samasama-vastu*).
Although at that time it was briefly categorized as half-and-half, one must ultimately divide it according to the respective groups by performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for each.
Regarding the provision that remains until the non-time period on the sixteenth day of the eighth month, it is treated as the "Non-time Monastic Gift" (*akāla-saṃghalābha*).

Below, two interpretations are evaluated: the Master [Xuanzang] takes the latter interpretation as definitive, while our present Master takes the former interpretation as definitive. The following arguments by way of concession and refutation explain this:
if one were to rely on the "Time Monastic Gift" (*kāla-saṃghalābha*) as being restricted solely to rewarding labor during the summer retreat, then there would be no such labor [to reward].
It is not appropriate to accept gifts as if they were not subject to the rules for adding [merit], for since the intention to give is universal and encompasses all beings in the transformation,
one must employ the first principle so that there may be a definitive limit through the severance of dharmas.

Regarding the mutual entrustment (*parivāsa*) within the Vinaya concerning robes obtained during the summer retreat that have not yet been distributed: if a bhikṣu departs, the Buddha said, "Wait for his return," or "First entrust it to one person.
Since this does not reach the point of the formal ritual motion (*jñapti-karman*), how can the distribution be effected?

First, because it belongs to those within the same boundary (*sīmā*); thus, although he has now gone outside, he is considered to be in common residence. Second, because the robe was originally bestowed [upon the community].
At that time, because they were within the same boundary (*sīmā*), one who was departing from below should first ask:

"Since he already possesses a share, will you not take his share when you depart? The answer from below is: "I shall take my share. Because a monk might have doubts after the distribution has been completed, the Buddha was informed;

the Buddha said: "The distribution is valid, for it was accomplished through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Furthermore, departing possesses three conditions; moreover, two conditions—waiting and entrusting—are opened up, which are as stated previously.
Regarding the second point, "giving at the proper time" means giving when the recipient is present before one; it does not mean to simply take [the object] oneself.

One should follow the original Vinaya rule regarding a single person receiving a gift: one should mentally reflect and verbally say, "This is my portion. To arouse the thought and bring it forth is what is meant.

As the poem says, "Rising early and sleeping late"—the ancients referred to the thought that something belongs to oneself as "mental reflection" (*cittābhoga*). Now, the Master must transmit this orally.
If one’s intention is as if performing the *cetanā-śuddhi* (purification by mental resolve) within a *saṃghārāma*, yet one does not speak it aloud, this is called "unlawful" (*adharma*).
First, regarding the case where one has previously resided here and likewise obtained a share: this refers to waiting for an entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇa*).

The *Pañcadaśavidha-vāda* (Treatise on the Fifteen Kinds) states that there are fifteen locations for receiving offerings: first, the boundary of the *sīmā*; second, the precinct (*viṣaya*)—or the lecture hall; whether the boundary is large or small, all have the "stone-throwing boundary" (*pāṣāṇakṣepa-sīmā*), and when a *bhikṣu* enters...
All obtain a share. (1) The boundary for the common *poṣadha*; (2) the boundary for not losing one’s robe;

(3) the *rāva* boundary—when a king or minister has established a residence for a bhikṣu, whether it be ten *yojanas* in extent, or defined by the planting of pillars or boundary markers, whatever is offered within this area belongs to us; (4) the village boundary;

(5) the town boundary (a place with a market is called a *grāma*, while one without a market is called a *nigama*); (6) the kingdom boundary (which includes cities and towns); (7) the *araṇya* boundary (the forest hermitage boundary); (8) the water-throwing boundary.

(1) The boundary of a ship; (2) the boundary of a village district (a "district" is named according to the east or west of a city); (3) the boundary of a *roṇa* (the boundary of a kingdom); (4) the boundary of an *araja* (a kingdom ruled by a single king);
(5) the boundary of a continent (one continent within the ocean); (6) the boundary of Mount Cakravāḍa (this refers to a single Cakravāḍa).

Among these fifteen boundaries, if one says, "I give [this as] a *śīma* for the observance of the precepts (*śīla-kṣetra*) and the *poṣadha*," it is not permitted even up to the point of establishing the *poṣadha* boundary.
Regarding the distribution of offerings to the Saṃgha of two continents—Siṃhala and Jambudvīpa—according to their respective numbers, it is divided into three parts.

The lower portion is determined by *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) and returned to the present Saṃgha through two methods. Immediately, the Saṃgha obtains [the share] at the proper time and the Saṃgha obtains [the share] at the improper time. This constitutes one section.

Regarding the two assemblies, there are two divisions each for monks and nuns—namely, the heterodox and the orthodox. According to whichever division’s assembly reaches the required quorum, they cast voting sticks (*śalākā*) by means of *karmavācanā*.

If there is dissatisfaction, then the mental recitation and the face-to-face methods are all distinct, as described above. One should thus count the number of people, observe their qualities (good or bad), cast lots to determine shares, and take possession for oneself.
Having performed the formal act of taking possession (*dhāraṇā*), one may either designate a steward for the purification (*śuddhi*) or transfer the gift to another person.
As for others who arrive—specifically those coming from outside the boundary—if the act of taking possession and so forth has not yet been completed here, [the procedure remains as follows].
One must divide [the robes] as described above; this is because all four [cases] require the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding the differences among the three masters of the past and present concerning this point: the first master [proposes] three methods, the second master one method, and the third master two methods.

First, to indicate the initial meaning: within the ritual for robes (*cīvara-karma*), there is only the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) for the entrustment of the robe.

Regarding the two procedures for the distribution of property before and after [the *saṃgha*’s formal act], they do not appear in the *Karmavācanā* (ritual texts). Although the text is brief, the meaning is necessarily complete;
for the text states that one monk is to be appointed, and further mentions that the appointed person performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the division into two parts.

Furthermore, in the subsequent section, the Master points out that the meaning derived from the *Vinaya* includes the entrustment of the distribution. Therefore, the five virtuous qualities (*pañcaguṇa*) need not again perform the ritual for the distribution, as the underlying conditions refer to the *saṃgha*.
Now, the formal motion for entrustment is presented to [Name]; he shall then distribute it to the Saṃgha. This is simply a single procedure.
Although no response is provided here regarding potential external objections that might arise below, we shall now address them:

although the entrustment is performed by an individual, the distribution rests with those possessing the five virtues (pañca-guṇa). Since they receive the entrustment and perform the distribution on my behalf, the assembly already knows this through delegation.
What is the fault in this abbreviated division? Furthermore, the third master below follows the second master’s method regarding the non-performance of the formal act (*karmavācanā*);

it further requires the performance of the appointment (*niyoga*), thus constituting two formal acts together, because the Vinaya states that "one person is to be appointed. (The present master adopts this view; the records of the ancient masters’ *Vinayavibhāṣā* treat the second as the third, which differs from this listing.

Since the Vinaya contains no specific rite for appointment, if one were to perform it now, one must add the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation). Within the motion (*jñapti*), there should be only four phrases.

To establish the third preparatory rite (*pūrvakṛtya*), it is said: "The Saṃgha appoints the monk so-and-so to act as the distributor of robes. (The *karmavācanā* follows this pattern and is to be recited when the time comes. The *Daichao* states:
"In current practice, one simply selects someone who understands monastic affairs, or appoints them orally according to the occasion, without using the *karmavācanā*.

Since this violates the Dharma yet is generally accepted, we know that only by performing the formal appointment through the *karmavācanā* is one free from violating the Dharma. This was established by the former masters of the lower and upper [traditions]."

Regarding the two methods for the *śalākā-vibhāga-karman* (the ritual of distributing voting sticks), ancient masters erroneously claimed that after the distribution of sticks, it might be difficult to reach a final decision if more monks arrived;

therefore, they performed the *karman*. Our Master, however, does not hold this view. In the procedure for distributing sticks, there are two types of *sammukha-karman* (face-to-face rituals) specifically applicable to both cases.
For individuals, if there is only one person, one adds the *manasikāra* (mental recitation); for two or three people, [the appropriate ritual is applied].

One must perform the formal procedure before another person (*pratimukha*), as detailed in the *Mahāśrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada* (Dà chǎo), where the *Mātṛkā* is cited within the section on the two robes to provide the wording for the addition of the acceptance (*parigraha*).

According to the Vinaya, however, it merely states that one accepts with three utterances; thus, when dividing [the robes] together, there are no specific phrases. From the division of summer robes downward, all are the formal texts of the *Cīvara-vastu* (Yì jiàn dù).
The "etc. (*zhí'ěr*) refers to the inclusion [of other items]. This is the interpretation of the Master Shou; above, it was also judged that this is the meaning of Master Shou.
The determination of the meaning based on later principles accords precisely with this interpretation. Now, the Master must establish the method for dividing [the property].
If someone has not yet received their share, because they have not yet taken possession, they do not obtain a portion upon death, nor is it said that it is severed and returned to the Saṃgha.
However, if there is a gift made in the presence of ten or a hundred people, each has a share; even if it has not yet entered their hands, should they die, [the share remains theirs].
One portion is returned to the deceased, and then the remainder is sought out for entry into the Saṃgha, where it is adjudicated according to its gravity. Thus, the *Wǔbǎi wèn* states:

"If there are remaining offerings and the original practitioner has already departed, or even if one knows they are dead and yet takes them, one commits the offense of abandoning property belonging to the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, the lower fascicle of the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) records that when bhikṣus divided food obtained during the summer retreat, they informed the Buddha; the Buddha said, "It should not be divided."

Regarding the rule that one should eat according to what is offered, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Other bhikṣus, while traveling through Kośala, arrived at Śrāvastī and asked those residing there, 'Is there any food for the Saṃgha?
They replied, 'There was originally some, but it has already been divided and taken away after the summer retreat ended.

Those of few desires reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, 'Food belonging to the Saṃgha should not be divided; if it is divided, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. At that time, as for the distribution among those present, it should be done according to the text."

Having understood that it is not the case that the manifest signs appear simultaneously, one proceeds to distinguish them by repeating the address "so-and-so. Such is the wording of the Vinaya text for the purpose of distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox.

Thus, when one person among five virtuous ones dies, the remaining four are permitted to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act); this refers to the five members of the community dwelling together.

Once the three [surviving] members have reached a consensus regarding the distribution of the deceased's robes and bowl value as a reward for their labor, the other minor items are to be dealt with according to the *Mātṛkā*.

In the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the four persons to directly divide the robes, the words "the Sangha now takes these robes and garments and gives them to so-and-so, who shall in turn return them to the Sangha" are excluded; the remainder is the same as before.
Regarding the prohibition against "successive transmission" (*kṣepa-krama*): according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, two or three people may perform successive transmission;

for four people or more, it requires a formal ritual (*jñapti-karman*). This is divided into two methods: first, the distribution of rewards (*lābha-vibhāga*), and second, the distribution of property (*dharmavibhāga*). Regarding the case where four people perform only the single method of distribution:
as for those corresponding to the numbers two, three, or four, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that when two bhikṣus live together and one passes away, the survivor performs [the distribution].
Thinking, "The property of this deceased bhikṣu should belong to me," that person alone obtains it, while those who arrive later do not;
this is called the method of single correspondence. When three people live together and one passes away, the other two should speak to each other in turn:
"Venerable sirs, please remember that this property should belong to the two of us. Speaking thus in turn is called the method of dual correspondence. (4)
When people dwell together and one person dies, the remaining three perform the ritual in succession as described above; this is called the *kamma* of the "threefold correspondence.
That treatise states that within the boundary (*sīmā*), from one person upwards, they may all strike the *ghanṭī* (bell), but they may not perform the *kamma*.

Otherwise, there is an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*). Outside the boundary, with five persons or more, they may perform the *kamma* for distribution [of property], but they do not strike the *ghanṭī*.

Because there is no formal boundary (*sīmā*), if there are four or fewer persons, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for distribution cannot be performed. If it is distributed, one commits an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*) and should immediately go before the Saṃgha.
Regarding the performance of the ritual by a single person: among three persons, only one person recites the words and phrases while the others do not need to respond face-to-face.
Each may speak individually; furthermore, it is accomplished by a single recitation, and it is not said that it must reach three recitations. They perform it alternately for one another.
It is so stated.

Why is it that while the lower section says "one person performs the ritual action and it is accomplished," the explanation of the *pravāraṇā* for individuals (*pratyekapudgala*) does not state the same, but rather says each person recites it three times?
That lower section is the explanation. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are generally two sections; the first says to strike the *ghanṭī*.

When the assembly had gathered in harmony and the distribution of goods was completed and they had risen, at that time the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks came from outside the boundary and said to the bhikṣus, "I shall share in the division of whatever property this saṃgha possesses.
One said, "It has already been divided. Then the group of six came from within the boundary and sought to share in the division.
They reported all these matters to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If the ghaṇṭā has been struck and the saṃgha has already finished distributing the goods and risen..."
If a bhikṣu from outside the boundary comes and wishes to give [a portion], one may give it; one must not forcibly divide the assembly’s share of the robes, for this constitutes a valid distribution.
Although there is no explicit text regarding this in that Vinaya, it is a ruling by the Great Master [the Buddha].

Since it states that one "must not forcibly divide," we know that the method for distributing within the boundary is established as a matter of course through the prior striking of the wooden gong to assemble the community; thus, he cites that [text] in turn.

The Buddha’s words provide the lower-level proof. Regarding the meaning below: if a bhikṣu is within the boundary (sīmā) and does not know [of a distribution], yet later desires to claim a share—according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says:

"If one wishes to give, one gives; if one does not know at the time of giving, may the formal act (*karmavācanā*) be performed again to divide [the property]? Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* below:

if one refers to the principle of one's own school, the formal procedure must necessarily be performed again to divide [it], because dividing robes with a separate group does not constitute [a valid division]. Thus, there is a comparison.
This refers to when one forms the perception that there are no bhikṣus where there actually are none.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is not necessary to forcibly divide [the robes], for it states that even if they are given, they must be distributed harmoniously according to the occasion. Since there were in fact no bhikṣus within the boundary, the division of the robes was naturally valid.
However, because one now acts contrary to this by failing to seek out [the truth] despite having formed the perception that they exist, one must undergo the *kṣudraka-āpatti* (minor offense).

Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.

Regarding *pārājika*, according to the meaning of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it refers to the ultimate evil. This is explained through three points: first, regarding "retrogression and submergence," because one has violated this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path;
second, regarding "not dwelling together," it is not merely a loss of the Path, but one no longer enters [the community].
Regarding the three types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there are two kinds of monastic communities (*saṃgha*). First, "falling" refers to falling into the Avīci Hell after discarding this body;
thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* uses the analogy that it is like severing a person's head, from which they cannot rise again—this is derived from such a metaphor.

Furthermore, it is said that "without remainder" means being severed from the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*); this section is distinct from the eight heavy offenses of the nuns, hence it is called "four."
"Poison" refers to the three poisons; "karma" refers to the three types of karma. To seek one's own benefit as pleasure is to indulge solely in self-satisfaction.

Furthermore, this single precept is the root of defilement from time immemorial, and its affliction is most grave. Regarding the "three matters," they are the three poisons. Although they arise because of the three poisons, their completion necessarily occurs within greed.
As for "the meeting of objects": externally, forms intersect; internally, the emotions flow in harmony. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The meeting of objects..."

Internally, because they do not accord with non-greed and lack discernment, they are said to "obstruct thought. As for "resolving matters," "deciding" means to accomplish them. What is this "non-greed"?

Furthermore, delusion belongs to confusion and anger belongs to resentment; therefore, neither of these two can be established [as the basis]. Regarding harm and benefit: for example, killing or stealing and obtaining profit that enters one's own possession is called "benefit"; the opposite of this is "harm.
The following statement—that [these actions] also arise from the three poisons and also reside within the three poisons—is likewise [to be understood].
[The act] is established. As it is stated extensively below: "If one takes the property of another for the sake of oneself and one's kinsmen, this is called [killing] proceeding from greed;
if one steals the property of an enemy, this is called [killing] proceeding from hatred; if one robs those of low status, this is called [killing] proceeding from delusion.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Regarding parents who are old or ill, killing them is said to be without fault. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, relying on the ancient laws of kings, maintains that a person may be killed based on their crimes.
To claim that one is without fault is entirely the act of a deluded person. One who possesses the conduct of hatred and greed may commit killing;

this can be understood by analogy. A *māmaka* (manager) is one who administers affairs; because they do not understand the characteristics of the teachings, they commit offenses within a deluded mind.

Because greed and delusion arise from the pursuit of profit, such false claims are driven by greed and confusion regarding cause and effect, which constitutes delusion. Furthermore, since delusion is the mother of greed and hatred, these cannot be separated. Even if...

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The precept against great falsehood originally arises from greed and delusion for the sake of one's own benefit; how could it not also include anger? Thus, the *Shansheng* says:
'If one commits it for the sake of wealth and profit or to enjoy pleasure oneself, it is called greed; harboring resentment is called anger; fearing [retribution] is called delusion.
According to this principle, a false claim made to gain profit through greed is grave; a false claim made out of fear of death is light; and anger constitutes the middle degree."
Regarding killing and stealing, these two are performed through both body and speech; they are established through both acting oneself and instructing others, thus mutually completing one another.

However, the body is the root and speech is the branch. Why is this so? Because the destruction of wealth and the taking of life are accomplished by the body alone, without depending on the assistance of words.
Therefore, we know that the body is fundamental. As for the verbal instruction to kill, the act is not yet complete until the preceding severance of life has occurred.
Only then does one incur a grave offense; because that person’s body assists in the verbal transgression committed by oneself, it is known as a secondary factor (*śākhā*).

Since the precept against sexual misconduct involves instructing another to take pleasure while not personally indulging in it, one does not incur a grave offense; therefore, this is not analogous to the case of killing, such as the instances of Xiang Yu or Zhu Faluan.
Regarding the "deep river," the opponent should first raise the objection: "If bodily action must assist [the verbal act], then it is like the deep river."
If one deceives with shallow words and performs a bodily action, and the person dies based on that [deception], why must the body [of the deceiver] be robust?

Now, to explain this meaning, it is the same as the previous answer: death must occur while crossing a river by means of that body for the offense to be established; this can be understood by analogy.

Regarding the distinction between the types of karma, it is because the essential natures of the three types of karma are each distinct; furthermore, even if one allows for the assistance of other factors, a single type of karma cannot be ultimate in itself.

The statement "under the words" indicates that the ultimate meaning is not exhausted; for although it is explained verbally, it ultimately relies upon the body, and thus the vocal karma (*vākkarman*) does not itself exhaust the intended meaning.

As stated above, this refers to the *Dhāraṇī* methods, the "Passing through the Passes," and so forth, which are also cited in the *Sūtra of Harmonious Benefit* (*Andhahṛdaya-sūtra*) and the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*.
Regarding Nārada, the full name is Nārāyaṇa. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When the Great Sage is angry, he can cause [even] a great..."

The destruction of a nation and the intent to kill are fundamentally bodily karma (*kāyakarma*), yet because they are now produced by the mind, they are mutually inclusive. Silent falsehood is fundamentally verbal karma (*vākkarma*), yet it is now accomplished by the mind.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* answers this by stating that these three types of karma are all merely the mind; apart from the mind, there is no volition (*cetanā*) and no bodily or verbal karma.
It further states that it is by the power of this mental karma (*manaskarma*) that bodily and verbal evils, and so forth, arise. This is also the case here.

Regarding the "lower" [grade]: for example, there is a person who gives an object and addresses the assembly, saying, "This is a holy man. A bhikṣu harbors a desire for gain and arises [with this thought], which constitutes a great false claim.
This is judged as a case where the body is the branch and the mouth is the root; it is established as a false person of the mouth.
The lower grade should be supplemented with the four characters "if one instructs others" (*jiao ren zhe*) to be complete.
Regarding "Great Falsehood": if one instructs another to claim oneself as a saint, and there is benefit or gain resulting from it, it is also grave.

"Self-creation" refers to reaching that object oneself; "other-creation" refers to it occurring in relation to one's own object. The case of the "weak-spined bhikṣu" is an example of this. All three types of offenses constitute *pārājika*.

As for the remaining two [offenses], "other-stealing" refers to stealing what belongs to another, while "self-stealing" refers to stealing what belongs to oneself. If the object differs from the original intent—such as intending to steal that [object] but instead stealing something else—it remains [an offense].

Because there is a discrepancy regarding the arrival of the object, it is called "tying the orchid" (*lan*). If one takes the example of giving to oneself—since giving to oneself does not constitute an act of giving, how could stealing from oneself constitute theft?
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "If one is stingy with oneself, it constitutes stinginess;

because one protects and cherishes one's own property, giving to oneself does not constitute giving, and greed for oneself increases. Regarding the tenth [case], it says: "Is there such a thing as killing a person without committing an offense?"
*Yiye* means suicide. *Shunzheng* refers to the *Shunzhenglilun*. Regarding the current passage in the *Jieshu*, it says:
"Some interpret this as not establishing 'progressive advancement' (*jinqu*); if that were so, it would not be the original text of this school. Furthermore, the commentary states:

"Even if one were to establish the meaning of 'progressive advancement,' there would be no fault, because the *Tiaobu* contains the sense of 'formal meeting' (*juelan*). The *Shu* further states: "As in the Vinaya itself..."

If one kills a *laṇ* (a woman in menses) but the act is not completed due to a discrepancy, it constitutes a formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). If she dies, because the causal conditions are identical to those of the preceding case, it is classified as such.

Generally speaking, "progressing toward" (*abhipravartana*) refers to the movement from cause to effect without cessation; since the intention to harm here corresponds to the object, it fulfills the meaning of "progressing.
However, because life has been cut and the precept has lapsed, the full offense of *pārājika* is not incurred; yet the prior offense is not non-existent.

Progressing [toward the goal] is caused by transgression. Striking oneself or slandering the meaning [of the Dharma] rarely constitutes an offense. Regarding self-concealment, according to the Vinaya, concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) committed by another incurs a *pārājika* offense;

however, if one conceals it oneself, although a *duṣkṛta* is incurred, one may hope that the *pārājika* is not committed. It cannot be argued that because the precept exists, one does not commit the *pārājika*, for [the gravity of the act] depends on the object.

Regarding the three types of falsehood: if one lies about oneself while another is correct, a heavy offense is incurred; if one lies about another while being correct regarding oneself, [the offense is different].
Since committing an offense oneself rarely brings about the benefit of self-recruitment, it is also not a fault.
"All below" refers to the meaning of the mind and its objects being inconsistent, divergent, and erroneous.

"Error below" means that while the characteristics of the two objects currently perceived are clearly distinct, when one engages in action, the circumstances may go astray; this is termed the "interpenetration of the various mirrors."
Incorrect. Regarding the error below: if one discusses "error," it refers to a mind that cannot simultaneously apprehend both the preceding and succeeding moments.

As with the previous thought which takes this object and the subsequent thought which takes that object, because the mental perception is delusory and false, it is called "error. Do not [assume] below that the precept against sexual misconduct does not depend on the correspondence between the object and the perception;
rather, as long as it involves a man and a woman via the proper path, the offense is of the highest grade. Although the mind below indicates error, although the object...

The following demonstrates the error [in the previous argument]. If one follows the preceding heading, the meaning of the error should logically come first. Regarding "having no reliance" (*wujì*), it means having nothing upon which to rely within a single object;

thus, the meaning of "indiscriminate" (*màn*) is established. As for the "three destinies," these refer to humans, non-humans, and animals. If one has already committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense with respect to a previous object, but before the mind has shifted to another object, a different object appears and the circumstances differ, one incurs only the *sthūlātyaya* of preparatory effort (*prayoga*). This is because, with respect to the subsequent different object, there was originally no intent to steal.
Regarding that object, no offense can be established; however, if one later becomes aware of it, one must logically return it to him.

If one does not return it, since the state of mind corresponds to the action, how could there be any doubt that a grave offense is incurred? As for "no offense when there is a mistake": this refers to a case where one intends to harm Zhang but not Wang;
while the objective field is clearly present, the mental focus is distinct. Furthermore, at the moment one uses the lethal instrument to harm Zhang, [the intended victim] is... [he]... Wang.
If a king’s man suddenly hands me a wheel-blade sword, even though my life is cut short, because it was not intentional, there is no offense if it was an error.
Furthermore, according to the lower explanation, an error constitutes an offense. Originally, one intended to harm Zhang, but Zhang departed and the King arrived;

if one kills the King, thinking he is Zhang, it is an offense as the perception of the person was not mistaken and the conditions for killing were fulfilled. Thus, although it was an error, one commits a grave offense.
In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there is no offense if the intended victim is mistaken for another; therefore, the subsequent treatise (*śāstra*) judges this case differently.
It states that if one intends to kill one's mother but kills another person, or intends to kill another person but kills one's mother, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Furthermore, it says that if one intends to kill an Arhat but kills an ordinary person, or intends to kill one's mother but kills one's father, and so forth, all such cases constitute a *sthūlātyaya*.
The answer is as follows: The meaning of "lower intention" (*xiayi*) is that one has mistakenly taken "error" (*wu*) for "mistake" (*cuo*), and thus their views appear contradictory.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "These various names for the Vinayas are insufficient to determine whether an act constitutes an offense or its non-observance; one must examine the actual facts and principles before distinguishing between 'error' and 'mistake.

Furthermore, the *Zhisu* (Commentary on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) distinguishes offenses differently because the naming conventions vary. Thus, the present school now adopts the facts and principles of those Vinayas.

This clearly demonstrates that errors and transgressions are mutually manifest. A transgression (*vyatikrama*) occurs because both objects appear simultaneously and one speaks erroneously toward the other, potentially deceiving them for the sake of gain;
a violation (*āpatti*) is spoken of in terms of a deluded mind, hence it is said there is no offense.
