After eating at a later invitation, one must not eat again, hence the rule was established. Regarding "having eaten enough" (*pūrabhukta*): while eating is permitted for those who are ill, if one greedily eats without ceasing, it invites public reproach;
therefore, the rule was established. Because these circumstances differ, two precepts are opened up. As for the outsider nun (*tīrthika-bhikṣuṇī*), it was due to Baddhananda... [text ends].

There were two śrāmaṇeras at Śrāvastī: one who had left the monastic life and one who had joined a group of non-Buddhist outsiders. At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs brought food to a layperson;

for those who had entered the ranks of non-Buddhists, it was permitted to give to a layperson. For young bhikṣuṇīs, it was permitted [to give] to girls aged eighteen who had completed two years of training in the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts and the six rules, and who, having reached twenty, were eligible for full ordination. Furthermore, for those who had been married at ten years of age, it was permitted to give to those who were two [years]... [the text continues].

When the age-precept (*vassa*) reaches twelve years, the calculation of the embryo and intercalary months is permitted for those receiving the full ordination along with the Saṃgha, yet it is restricted to twenty years for others.

Regarding the rainy-season robe (*varṣā-śāṭī*), nuns are permitted four ways to conceal the body while bathing: namely, at a place where the waterbank curves back, under the shade of a tree, where the water itself covers them, or where they are shielded by a cloth.
Furthermore, because nuns were enticed by courtesans and monks had doubts regarding female servants, [the Buddha] prohibited [certain actions]. *Kha* (the syllable *kha*).

The Mother [the Buddha] requested that these be explained, for they all arise from different conditions. There are three [additional categories], namely the three types of light and heavy offenses added to the previous three kinds;

those who commit them equally incur a *pāyattika*. Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, because the disturbance caused by dragging someone out after the monks have already settled their rooms during the summer retreat is slight, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;

however, for a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is the reverse, as the disturbance is grave, thus it is a *pāyattika*. Furthermore, when the two assemblies [of monks and nuns] revile one another... [the offense is determined accordingly].
If one reviles the Great Saṃgha and the original assembly together, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if one reviles only the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*.

When a *bhikṣuṇī* conceals a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is likewise a *pāyattika*. If she conceals an offense from the first category (the *pārājikas*), she incurs a grave *pārājika*; whereas a *bhikṣu* would incur only a *pāyattika*.
If this is the case, the gravity of the offenses differs, not only in the case of the previous thirteen precepts, but when these three precepts are added, they complete the total of sixteen.

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*): in the separate chapter on the *Śīla-vibhaṅga*, a distinct section is established. It states that while the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* contains ninety-one *pācittiya* offenses, it lacks this "precept against not accepting admonition.

Instead, it establishes a "precept against disrespecting those who preach the Dharma" and a "precept against frivolous speech during the *poṣadha*"—the latter being similar to this "precept against causing provocation.
Furthermore, it possesses its own "precept against not responding to inquiries," and there are nine [such rules] in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.

The eleven *pārājika* offenses, the ninety-two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, and the ninety *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses have mutual similarities and differences, as extensively cited in the commentaries (*śāstra*).
These correspond to the twenty-two precepts concerning "digging and destroying" and so forth, found within the second section on "Instructing Others" in the aforementioned lower reference.

However, the current [text] reverses this, explaining that "other" (anya) refers to the sense of spontaneity (*anābhoga*). Regarding the rule concerning the two types of spreading out [robes] in an open space:

if one spreads out monastic property in an open space and leaves the door, one incurs an offense immediately; why then would it be considered spontaneous only later? Therefore, it is said to be "entirely not [spontaneous].
If one spreads them out in a screened place, there may be cases where it is spontaneous and cases where it is not; since it is neither entirely so nor entirely not so, it is called "half. If...
If one has spread out [a seat] and does not put it away, but instead forms the intention to leave permanently and crosses the boundary, one falls into an offense (*pāyattika*);

therefore, there is no "automatic" (*anuvartana*) transgression. Alternatively, if one leaves temporarily with the intent to return—based on the Vinaya which states that staying outside the boundary for two nights and failing to go oneself, send a messenger, or entrust it to a guardian by dawn on the third night constitutes an offense of falling—one commits an offense of falling. According to this principle, at the time of first crossing the boundary, one is a *śrāmaṇera*; by the second night...
At that time, once the ordination is completed, because one does not return to the boundary (*sīmā*), if an offense is committed when dawn appears, it is established spontaneously.
This is based on Master Guangtong’s initial commentary, which groups the ninety precepts under nine categories of characteristics.

According to the present reliance on these characteristics, this principle is not without merit; therefore, I shall now cite and expand upon it. Thus, "intentional play" and "offering a smile" constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense involving repeated glances.
If the offense of *duṣkṛta* applies to both light and heavy cases, why is it that placing another’s robe or bowl inside one’s own storage—down to even doing so in jest—is a *pāyattika*?
The fault lies in the intention: for one who has left the household life, speech must accord with reality and be free from falsehood.

Now, to act contrary to the mind and turn one's back on one's thoughts constitutes a fault regarding the intention; therefore, this is an offense of *pāyattika*. Since joking is not a deliberate deception, it is merely classified as a *duṣkṛta*.
The person who was hidden thought it was lost; because the meaning of "distress" (*nirvedha*) is the same, both commit the offense of *pāyattika*.

Question: Below, if it is said that a lie is not an object of distress, and thus a joke is minor, then consider the case of disparagement and divisive speech (*paiśunya*), where the object of distress is grave.
Should one then incur a *pāyattika* for disparaging two groups of people simultaneously? Answer: Although it is distressing, it is... [text ends]
Although it is a single act, the impairment of the object (ālambana) is not without degrees of depth; for instance, when one destroys two things of the same class (sabhāga-hetu), conflict arises.
Because of this conflict, the meaning of the Saṃgha becomes discordant. Due to this discordance, the common observance of the Uposatha (poṣadha) is obstructed.

Therefore, the destruction of two things of the same class is grave, whereas that of different classes—such as destroying the lower assembly—is light. "Destruction" refers to divisive speech (paiśunya). As the Vinaya says: "One who believes the words of others regarding both sides, and [speaks] to friends..."

This refers to "destruction. The gradations are as follows: for slandering one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, one incurs a *thullaccaya*; for slandering one who has committed a *pācittiya*, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*, and so forth. The increase or decrease [in gravity] is such that if one slanders someone who has committed a *pārājika*, the affliction of the mind increases and the punishment is heavy;
therefore, the lower categories are the reverse and thus light. Furthermore, in the case of verbal abuse (*akkosa*), there is no formal punishment, as it is dealt with individually.

The reason they are not distinguished is that they are both established based on the limit of mental affliction (*kleśa*). If one were to say that there is a difference in degree between the increase and decrease of harm and affliction—such as when it is said that slander increases [affliction] while reviling decreases it—then since reviling that person constitutes a *pārājika* offense which increases affliction, whereas reviling those of lower categories constitutes a minor offense which decreases affliction, there should likewise be a difference in degree. Why is this not the case?
There are two [types of offenses]: wholesome factors and unwholesome factors. Regarding the fourfold division of unwholesome factors, one who reviles says, "You are a transgressor."

Regarding those who revile superior human dharmas and so forth, saying, "You are a forest-dweller," or even "You are a practitioner of dhyāna," and so on—each case is judged according to the specific category and incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.

Since there are no superior human dharmas within the category of slandering [the Sangha], this is why the degrees of the offenses are distinguished by their gravity based on the *pārājika*, *saṃghādisesa*, and other sections.
If, in the case of disparaging others, lightness and heaviness are already differentiated based on good and evil, resulting in a gradation of severity, why is it not the same here?
Furthermore, within the category of unwholesome dharmas, are the stages and gradations distinguished according to the gravity of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses?

First, there is the "lower" [category], which refers to the increase or decrease in the harm and affliction resulting from the gravity of the slander against others; furthermore, it involves the varying degrees of punishment one may incur depending on the severity of that slander.
Moreover, among the constituent conditions, one commits an offense even by slandering in the presence of a single bhikṣu.

Since this is so, there is a reduction in the gravity of the offense committed. Regarding *kṣepa* (slandering/reviling), because it possesses only the first of the three deficiencies and lacks the latter two meanings, the offense is established solely from the perspective of causing distress to the recipient.
Question: What deficiency does *kṣepa* lack regarding the third [meaning]? Answer: Among the conditions for the offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*), it is not stated that one must address a person directly.
According to the Vinaya, the six modes of speech are divided into three grades; "face-to-face reviling" (*mukha-kṣepa*) refers to speaking while facing the person directly.
To speak of "insulting by analogy" (*upamā-vāda*) means to provoke by drawing comparisons; to speak of "insulting by contrast" (*pratyanīka-vāda*) means to say, "I am not [right], you are.

Therefore, these do not constitute slanderous speech (*paiśunya-vāda*), for such speech must be directed toward another person; if it is directed at the very person being slandered, it does not constitute [slander].

The "two assemblies" refer to the monks and nuns. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) simplifies this by excluding the [lower] three assemblies because their slander and vexation are minor in nature and do not hinder spiritual cultivation;
furthermore, while the offense they commit is light, the sin of slandering them is grave. As follows, the subsequent text steps upon the preceding to raise a formal objection:
since the causal conditions for the offense state only that "one person is a bhikṣu," according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one may revile the four assemblies below.
All are auspicious. Regarding the disparagement of a nun by one of higher status or a monk, because there is the principle of the superior instructing the inferior, it is considered light.

However, if a nun disparages a monk, because the inferior has lost the way of revering the superior, it is considered grave. The statement that "a nun reviles [others]" refers to the assembly as a whole, while the phrase "above" (in the previous context) refers to reviling an individual.

The meaning here is that since it is rare for a nun to revile a monastic assembly, it can be said that [reviling] the assembly incurs an auspicious offense (*kṣudrāpatti*), whereas [reviling] a nun [by a monk] is grave.
"Is it permissible to conclude that the meaning of 'the assembly' (*saṃgha*) also includes [the individual] below? This is one question.

Furthermore, if it is said that because the *bhikṣuṇī* rarely reviles the *saṃgha*, a *duṣkṛta* offense may be concluded [for her], then should a *bhikṣuṇī* who slanders the *saṃgha* also incur the same *duṣkṛta* offense?

This is another question. The answer is not in the proper order. The response to the second question is: "Because an individual repeatedly causes vexation [to others]. The intended meaning is as follows: if one considers...

The case of the nun Yīxī (義稀) slandering the Saṃgha is cited as an example of censure; because the offense is committed against a collective, it is classified as a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). This is because slandering an individual may entail formal disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍakarma*), whereas the intent behind slandering the Saṃgha is fundamentally different.

Furthermore, the object of the slander—the Saṃgha—is most venerable. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that this is so that those practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) may dwell in peace while cultivating the Path;

therefore, there is no distinction between the Saṃgha and individuals, and in all such cases, a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession) is incurred. Since there is no principle of formal punishment involved here, [the offense is not further categorized].
Therefore, one may apply the principle of rarity to distinguish between the gravity of offenses for monks and nuns. Regarding the initial question concerning the senior monks:

it is rare for senior monks who know the Dharma to dare to revile the assembly of nuns; this meaning is likewise rare. It is also rare for nuns to revile senior monks, given the latter’s great majesty and virtue.
Thus, when comparing the two sides, both are auspicious; the precept under discussion refers to the precept against false speech.
This is the intermediate and broad explanation of the text.
It asks: "Since [the offense of] lying knowingly in the midst of a great assembly is a *pāyattika*, why are the other offenses—abusive speech and slander—not also included here?

The answer is: because these two [offenses] are committed as *pāyattikas* by all seven classes of followers alike, they are specifically mentioned in relation to the "great assembly. Slander is the opposite of this.
It is not necessary to wear [the robe].

Question: Why is it that the rule regarding sleeping in the same room as a woman—where both nuns and laywomen are subject to the same prohibition—and the rules regarding sitting with women of lower status are separated?
This is as in the twenty-sixth rule, which prohibits sitting with a *bhikṣuṇī*, and the forty-fifth rule, which prohibits sitting with a woman.

Furthermore, regarding the precepts on traveling with those of the same path and riding in boats, for what reason are they divided? Answer: Below, these are distinguished because they differ in their mutual opposites;
thus, they must be separated. For example, when a monk sits during the day with three women, there is a distinction between being instructed and not being instructed;

whereas for a nun with two men, there is none. If we consider the matter of staying overnight: for a monk, there is no instruction regarding staying overnight with [one] woman, but for a nun, there is no instruction regarding staying overnight with [two] men.
The male counterpart is not exempt from this, as it is a case of prior association. First, regarding the "difficulties":

when traveling on a path with many hardships and fears, relying on a monk as a companion is one exception (the first *kai*). Second, when the journey is extremely long and there is a heavy risk of public censure, even if many monks are present, a single nun commits an offense;
she must obtain many companions before it is called non-offensive—this is the second exception (*kai*). This is the opposite of the case involving laywomen.

For this reason, they are separated. As for the two women who shared a lodging in the previous section, they were combined because their purpose was identical—namely, to jointly prevent the reproach of being unseemly.

Regarding the gravity of the offense incurred by inviting reproach, this refers to the prohibition established within the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) concerning the fault of sharing a boat with a *bhikṣuṇī*.
As for why sharing a boat with a laywoman is not prohibited, the *Jieshu* answers that there must be a boatman acting as a third party.
"Since it concerns humans, there is no need for a formal regulation.

Answer: The following is the ancient interpretation. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "In the past, it was said that this applies to men but not to women, because the principle of the offense incurred by staying overnight does not allow for an exemption of three nights.
The *Gālun* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), however, was erroneously cited by ancients to prove their own position; if one relies upon that..."

The main text of the treatise itself states: "There are indeed bhikṣus who, having stayed overnight for more than two nights with a person who has not yet received full ordination, incur two pāyattika offenses.
The answer is: "Having stayed overnight for two nights with a śrāmaṇera, one stays overnight on the third night with a woman" (the above is the main text).
Therefore, it is known that the ancient masters have erroneously cited [this passage]. My current interpretation correctly accords with the intent of the treatise. This question also...
The *Vinayakārikā* establishes two offenses (*pārājika*) based on this.
The *Devapuruṣavinaya* states: "If a male deva, asura, gandharva, yakṣa, preta, or male animal stays for more than two or three nights [with a woman], it constitutes an offense.
Since it does not mention women, why is it said that there is also [an offense] when one stays with a woman?
Question: Can one incur two offenses by staying for more than three nights? Furthermore, this would result in four divisions, which contradicts the *Gāthā-śāstra*. Answer:

Regarding the distinction from the preceding precept—referring to the precept concerning staying with a woman—the previous case concerned a female, such as a celestial maiden or an asura maiden; now, in contrast to the above, the distinctions are divided.
Therefore, it mentions "men" and does not mention "women. If one were to cite examples from below to challenge the logic, it would not be consistent. If...
Regarding the statement that staying overnight with one who is not fully ordained (*asamvṛta*) constitutes an offense only with respect to a male and not a female:
for instance, when reciting the precepts together with one who has not received full ordination, one also mentions "sons of devas" and "sons of asuras," yet females are not mentioned therein.

Why, then, would it be said that reciting together with a female also constitutes an offense? How is this known? It is explained at length in the aforementioned section on staying overnight with one who is not fully ordained.

Regarding "those who have not received the precepts," this excludes bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; it refers to others who have not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*). This was explained above in the section on "staying overnight.
Since the same applies to those below [the bhikṣus], the recitation of the text states that for those who are not fully ordained, the same rule holds.

By excluding the two assemblies [of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs] from the intermediate category, it is verified that those included therein extend to the other five assemblies. Because the five assemblies below include both men and women, they are collectively subsumed under this category.

If these two rules coincide, is it not the case that reciting together with a woman must also be treated as an offense? Now, although they are called "celestial males" and "celestial females," they must likewise be subject to the general rule of offense.
Since the general application of the offense is permitted, what fault would there be in concluding that both *pāyattika* offenses are incurred?
Initially, in the Vinaya, because the group of six monks stayed overnight with a householder, the rule was established: "With one who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
"Staying overnight together [with an army] is a *pāyattika* offense. Later, this was relaxed; because Rāhula was driven away, it was further relaxed so that staying for two nights was permitted.

Subsequently, it was stated that staying for more than two nights—up to three nights—is a *pāyattika*. Why did the later relaxation subsume the earlier original prohibition so that they were combined into a single precept?

For what reason was the initial prohibition against observing an army later modified such that, due to specific circumstances, staying for two or three nights within an army was permitted, rather than the later rule subsuming the former?
Why was the preceding section further divided into two precepts? The answer is: because what follows can encompass what precedes it;
since the subsequent [precept] governs the preceding one, and because contemplation is not of the nature of what has already passed, the latter does not include the former.

The two *duṣkṛta* offenses are both of the highest grade; compared to the two preceding categories, they are termed "light. However, because the karma is grave, it causes one to fall into [saṃsāra] for one kalpa.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense: in the Vinaya, when Śāriputra was sent to recount the faults of Devadatta, he immediately felt fear and caution. The Buddha said:

"Except for those cases involving a formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*), the *pāyattika* and those described in detail as 'crude and evil offenses' (*sthūlātyaya*)—namely, the four *pārājikas* and the *saṃghāvaśeṣas*—" [are excluded].
Why is it that *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is not called *sthūlātyaya*? The answer is: because below [this category], *sthūlātyaya* is divided into three grades;

furthermore, because it encompasses both the primary (*maula*) and the derivative (*anuvyañjana*) offenses. As the *Dàochào* states: "Alternatively, those following after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are grave offenses as they are subsumed under the section on precepts (*śīla-skandha*);
whereas those situated below the *prāyaścittika* are minor offenses as they are subsumed under the section on deportment (*īryāpatha*). Now, if...

To say that the *sthūlātyaya* offense is of the highest grade because it belongs to the category of precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is incorrect; for in the *Vibhāṣā*, when explaining the *sthūlātyaya*, it is stated that this refers to offenses other than those of the middle and lower grades.
To speak of it in this way would merely create confusion regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) and thus it is omitted here.
[If so,] why would a grave slander against one guilty of *pārājika* be [only] a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and why would a slander against one guilty of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* be a *pāyattika*?

Regarding the gravity of offenses, there are distinctions between light and heavy; therefore, the formalization of transgressions is also described according to their corresponding degrees of reduction and suppression.

Thus, while there may be no difference in the depth of the offense, the disciplinary measures are uniform because they equally involve self-destruction, destruction of others, and the undermining of lay faith.
Consequently, the offense is identical to a *pāyattika* (Thullaccaya).
This refers to the occasion when Piṇḍola manifested his supernormal powers for the elder Jyotiṣka.

Thus, the *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography) states that during the First Council convened by Kāśyapa after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Piṇḍola was punished through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations); this very [act] is what is meant by "auspicious.

The underlying meaning is that while he had indeed attained the Path, he committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense by speaking of it to one who had not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*); now, Piṇḍola has truly attained the Path.

Why are supernormal manifestations (ṛddhi-prātihārya) restricted to what is auspicious? If one argues that body and speech are distinct, [we reply] that because bodily expression constitutes a great falsehood as an oral action (vākkarman), it is so.
Answer: Since false speech is fundamentally an oral action, here the body is used as a pretext to manifest signs that express an oral action; thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because the body creates an oral action, giving rise to the non-informative (avijñapti) of speech, a grave offense must be incurred. Although this response concerns bodily expression, [it serves to clarify the nature of the transgression].
The previous statement was not entirely clear regarding the meaning of why Piṇḍola did not incur a *pāyattika* offense; I shall now clarify it.

Piṇḍola took the bowl to manifest his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) for the sake of the occasion of requesting alms from the elder; thus, Kṣemaka’s attainment [of the fruit] was indeed established. Furthermore, it was done to guard against great falsehood.
As for the people of Rājagṛha, they were the Jyotiṣka who resided in Rājagṛha; therefore, that elder entered [the city].
Later, Sāgara again fashioned an almsbowl out of sandalwood, placed it inside a netted bag, and suspended it from a high wooden peg.
He declared, "If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa can obtain it without using a ladder or step-stool, let him take it. Piṇḍola entered into meditative concentration and reached out his hand to take the bowl.
[Sāgara] then rebuked him, saying, "How can you manifest superhuman powers before one who is not yet fully ordained? This is excessive desire and a lack of contentment! Thus he censured him.
Question: Since bodily and vocal actions should also incur the offense of *pārājika*, why is it that one is punished only for a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*)? Answer: As stated in the text. Question:

Furthermore, among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), although they have not yet realized or cultivated the attainment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are those whose karma results in the attainment of such powers;

one should know that because of this potential for confusion, the principle [of punishment] must also be lightened. Answer: The meaning is clear. This question is entirely identical to the explanation found in the *Dàochǎo* (Great Commentary) regarding the characteristics [of offenses].

The meaning of the text is clear. The *Adhimāna-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu, having personally claimed in his mind that he had attained the Path, subsequently applied himself with diligent effort and realized a superior fruit (*adhimāna-phala*).

He then gave rise to doubt and informed the Buddha, saying: 'Does one who acts out of overweening pride (*adhimānika*) not commit an offense? Why is this included within the precept against great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*)? "
Regarding the absence [of certain factors] within this precept: the answer is that they are absent at the time of the underlying causal origination (*nidāna*), and therefore are not included.

Nevertheless, it is stated in the *Kai-t'ung* (Opening the Path) that "there is no offense" in cases such as those involving overweening pride (*adhimāna*), where many distinct categories are differentiated.

This refers to the phenomenon of mutual differentiation and growth occurring upon the branches and trunk; one may observe these by seeking them among the various types of branches and joints mentioned in the Vinaya. [This is] a provisional designation for life.

These are the false and illusory five aggregates that constitute a delusory body; their continuous succession and maintenance are forcibly designated as "life. Since life is a single entity, its impairment or violation is likewise a single act.

Furthermore, regarding lower animals, their nature constitutes a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offense), while plants and trees constitute a *pratikṣepa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense). From the perspective of the path of karma (*karmapatha*), prohibited offenses are light while natural offenses are heavy;

however, when considering the intention behind the restraint, prohibited offenses are heavy while natural offenses are light. This is as explained in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding the prohibition against destroying [plants].
There are three benefits to taking life [as a rule]: first, it prevents the harming of sentient beings; second, it stops slander; and third, it greatly protects the Buddha-dharma.

If the Buddha did not establish this precept, then in all lands, bhikṣus would be subjected to various forms of labor and service, becoming distracted and abandoning their cultivation of the right practice.
Because the Buddha established this precept, kings restrain their minds, and bhikṣus cultivate the Way, develop wisdom, and sever [defilements].

Is it not the case that the benefit of practicing for the removal of delusions constitutes a "great protection"? Since there is no such principle regarding the killing of animals, the underlying intention for the prohibition is considered light.
As for the remaining three—namely, lying, divisive speech, and harsh speech—they require the formal enactment of a rule by the Saṃgha;

that is, they constitute an offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) if committed before the announcement (*jñapti*), and an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension) if committed after the rule has been enacted following the announcement. Thus, the characteristics of these offenses involve a contradiction among the three factors of object, mental state, and speech.
Because they are mutually contradictory—for instance, when one has seen a certain object with the eye, yet upon being questioned about it, one instead says that one heard it;

or when using metaphors and the like to revile another by claiming that something is not actually this object, yet one’s mental conception is likewise not so, yet one instead claims it is—such categories cause harm and affliction.
Deceit causes others to give rise to false trust; verbal abuse causes them to suffer shame; and divisive speech...

This causes them to lose their harmony; it constitutes a profound offense that damages the objective conditions and disturbs the minds of others. Frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) is the opposite of this, and thus it is restricted by the monastic regulations.

Regarding "all," this refers to the four types of offenses such as those incurred despite being admonished. Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, it states: "If one performs [the act] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, it is a *pāyattika*.
From this, we know that if one does not perform [the act] once the motion is concluded, there is no offense.

The precept against diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha into one’s own possession has three aspects: first, that which has already been promised to the Saṃgha (meaning a gift intended for the Saṃgha in general that has not yet been divided into specific portions);
second, that which is being made for the sake of the Saṃgha but has not yet been promised to them (meaning items such as beds, mats, utensils, or other articles provided by laypeople for the Saṃgha;

diverting these constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense); and third, that which has already been given to the Saṃgha—having been promised to the Saṃgha and already relinquished to them (meaning a gift definitely bestowed upon the Saṃgha).

Regarding the offense of "transferring [property] to another" (*pṛthag-āśraya-parivartana*) as a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), the intent of the current inquiry is as follows: In the section on the precept concerning the "transference of *saṃgha*-property," these three types are enumerated to explain the meaning of *saṃgha*-property.
Furthermore, in the subsequent text of that same precept, it is stated that if one consents to the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* transferring property to the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

Now, in the current precept concerning the "spreading out of *saṃgha*-property," these same three types are again enumerated. I do not yet understand with respect to what the formal commission of the offense (*āpatti*) is established.

What further distinction is there regarding the category of "monks"? To permit [the use of] monks' property is the first type of monastic object (*saṃghika-vastu*). The phrase "laid down below" generally indicates both types. Only the phrase "below" provides a dual explanation;
according to the principle, it specifically takes up the phrase "already relinquished to the monks," which explains the text concerning "reclining equipment" (*śayanāsana*) mentioned above.

There should have been an explanation for the "mutual use" [of the two types], but the text should properly include the first clause, "already permitted to the monks. It is likely that this sentence was omitted from the manuscript. Great!
In the *Śāstra* (Commentary), there is also a self-annotation explaining the "concluding auspiciousness" (*kṣema*), which states: "Both refer to what is not yet determined;

if it is determined and given separately, one may consider the offense according to the preceding rule. As for the reason why both are listed individually within the preceding and succeeding precepts:

because they are both monastic property, they are treated collectively in the general sequence; however, when discussing the specific offenses incurred, it is necessary to distinguish their similarities and differences by correlating them with the respective precepts.

"Causing annoyance" refers to the precept against forcibly arranging a seat with the intent to vex another. The answer below states that the preceding precept concerns a secular residence, which is why it is termed a "place.

Regarding the absence of "force" among close friends: within the allowance for forceful arrangement, it is explained that if one has a close acquaintance who says, "Just arrange it yourself," and one addresses the host with these words, then by this inference, arranging a seat for a close friend does not constitute forceful arrangement.

Since it is called a "lay dwelling," it is said to be a place where monks do not reside; therefore, it makes no distinction between a pure environment for those who uphold the precepts and an impure environment for those who break them—provided one forcibly spreads [a rug or mat] there, one commits an offense.

Regarding the covering, the enumeration of conditions states that an offense occurs only when one does not remain within sight or hearing; from this, we know that the sense of "watching over" (or supervising) is implied.

Regarding the point that there is no sense of "self-concealment," the answer is as follows: The Vinaya states that one does not commit an offense if, as previously instructed, one stays at a distance;

however, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*) states that when constructing a dwelling, there are three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and each grade has its own limit for roofing.

If a middling or inferior dwelling is roofed using the method prescribed for a superior one, it constitutes an offense because of the excessive weight. Furthermore, it says: "This dwelling is among the thirteen [cases of]..."
This refers to the case where a large hall costing three hundred thousand coins collapsed as soon as it was completed. This is also listed here because of its urgency.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there is yet another meaning: "Alternatively, this may be explained from the perspective of the *nidāna* (causal origin); because [the Buddha] had it constructed, he subsequently established the precept."
First, regarding the sixth of the eight [rules], the method of requesting the Dharma every half-month: this is because it is a request made to the Saṃgha.

Second, as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, who first observed the eight weighty precepts before she was moved to receive the full ordination; the *Jianlun* (Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā) states: "The reason women are not permitted to go forth is for the sake of honoring the Dharma.
Only when they can act in accordance with this [reverence] is their admission to the order opened. If one were to request this from the Buddha himself..."

This constitutes the loss of the meaning of honoring the Sangha. Regarding the reversal of the two preceding losses: because one invites the Sangha, the two losses are reversed and become two virtues.

Furthermore, regarding the request for the Buddha, the Vinaya states: "At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and said to the World-Honored One:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit the bhikṣus to provide instruction and admonition to the bhikṣuṇīs.'"

Regarding the passage in the *Dharmaparyāya* where the Buddha tells Ānanda, "From this day forward, I authorize you to appoint elder *bhikṣus* in turn to provide instruction and admonition," why is there such a text of repeated request?
The answer is as stated in the text. As for the point that it does not apply to later ages: while the Buddha was present, there were those who could be taught;
after his parinirvāṇa, there are none. Within the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there are generally three faults: first, the fault of narrowness, which is not universally applicable.

In three continents, two [types of persons] may slightly exceed [the limit], while the Buddha alone is restricted by the three short [periods]. This does not apply for ten thousand generations; rather, when a bhikṣu acts as the instructor, it conversely results in three benefits.
This question arises because the Vinaya states: "If one goes to give the instruction on the eight *anavaśeṣas* when the Saṃgha has not appointed him, or on a day other than the day of instruction..."
If one preaches the Dharma to those who are not dispatched by the Saṃgha, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing); however, if one preaches to those who have been dispatched, it is a *pāyattika*.

Why is it said that although the respect shown differs, the offense is a *pāyattika*? The established texts and ancient masters maintain that because the essential nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) of the act does not increase or decrease, the transgression is slight and there is no room for confusion in the classification;

therefore, it is merely a *duṣkṛta*. As for the phrase "preaching below," this refers to preaching in general, which encompasses extensive discourse and allows for the possibility of transforming others through false teachings.
For that reason, one must be specifically selected and dispatched; going without being so appointed constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If it is not a day for formal instruction (*ovāda*), but one goes on that day to preach the Dharma or pay respects, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense according to both the principle and the rule.

This is because the Vinaya speaks only of the distinction between being appointed or not as the basis for the gravity of the offense, and does not mention whether the day is appropriate as a basis for such gravity; therefore, we know that logically they are the same in being a *duṣkṛta*. Second, regarding the mutual clarification of names:

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "One who instructs [is subject to an offense]. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* itself explains: "One who instructs" refers to the eight things that must not be transgressed. Furthermore, the extensive commentary below states:

"One who does not appoint someone to preach the Dharma [is subject to an offense]. Therefore, we know that the meanings of "instructing" (*śāsana*) and "preaching the Dharma" (*dharma-deśanā*) are one and the same;
they merely clarify each other in different contexts. If one investigates in this manner, one will understand that the intent of the Vinaya texts is not inconsistent.

To preach the Dharma when one is not authorized constitutes an offense. Regarding the eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), two offenses are incurred: first, going when not appointed; second, going on a day other than the prescribed date. Below this is the objection:

"If that is so, the Vinaya states that if one goes when not appointed or on a day other than the day for instruction to preach the eight rules that must not be transgressed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
To which [of the two] does this refer? Below this is the explanation. Below this is the further objection regarding the Vinaya.

Since it is stated that one does not go [to instruct] without being appointed, or goes on a day other than the designated day of instruction, why is it that only the latter case—going on an improper day—is defined as a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), while the former case—going without being appointed—is not so defined?
This is explained in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which states: "If a monk instructs bhikṣuṇīs without being appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*.
Thus, we know that the offense was already established previously; the subsequent detailed explanation merely specifies that going on an improper day constitutes the offense.

Question: What is meant by "the day is not [a valid] *saṃghī*"? Regarding the three days prior to the day of the recitation of the precepts (i.e., the fifteenth day) mentioned in the Sūtra, and the two days following it (i.e., the two days before the *poṣadha*), if one departs on these days, it is called "the day is not [a valid] *saṃghī*.
As for the subsequent instruction regarding the evening of the day (*sāyaṃ-sīla*), it should also constitute a *pācittiya* offense;
for the Vinaya states that if one who has been appointed by a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) within the Saṃgha to provide instruction fails to do so until sunset, it is a *pācittiya*.
This implicitly shows that what is not a transgression is auspicious. Now, if we follow the aforementioned instruction, whether it is a day of transgression or not, neither is auspicious;

therefore, on both days of transgression and non-transgression, would it not be a *thullaccaya* at dusk? "The fault is minor because of my slight [transgression]" means that since there is no offense for the nun who has departed, my own fault is also minor.
Regarding the term *thullaccaya*, it is used because *thullaccaya* is a single category that does not include distinctions of light or heavy.

Regarding the distinction between "departing at the wrong time" (*vikāla*) and "not departing at the wrong time," one must differentiate their names in order to encompass the characteristics of the offenses.
If, when it is not the proper time, both departing and not departing result in a *duṣkṛta* (light offense), this is because the term *duṣkṛta* encompasses both light and heavy degrees;
thus, one should understand that departing at a non-proper time results in a heavy *duṣkṛta*, whereas not departing at a non-proper time results in a light *duṣkṛta*. Although...

He said: "Regarding the names 'light' and 'heavy' being auspicious, since there is already a gradation between them, even if the difference from the previous [category] is slight, it does not hinder the similarity of their relative weight.
Question: Regarding the Vinaya rule that states, 'An eater may eat from dawn until midday; for each swallow, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense,' once this food has been consumed..."
If one teaches others to obtain extra robes, undergarments, oil for lamps, or oil for anointing the feet, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Why is food heavy while these other items are light?
The answer is that the meaning can be understood through reflection. This explains that when a nun receives [food] from the monks, she commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Whether it be a small amount or like a cloud, because the meaning of receiving oil-cloth is rare, the offense is settled as a *duṣkṛta*. Why? Because receiving food that contains oil is also minor;
however, according to principle, the meaning of receiving [excess] should be counted as a formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

Now, the Vinaya settles this only as a *duṣkṛta* because the substance is destroyed—since it is cooked food that can be eaten, the original substance no longer exists—and because the affliction is deep, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Yet, regarding the donor...

This explanation below states that when a hall, a dwelling, clothing, or other items are offered for the use of the Sangha rather than being assigned to specific individuals, their substance still belongs to the donor and does not undergo destruction. This is the only exception;
the following discussion regarding the two conditions is based solely on the single circumstance mentioned in the ancient *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* concerning the time of making robes.

[Question: Is it so? [Answer: When making robes after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, there is no need for a *kāṭhina* robe for one month; when there is cloth available, [the period extends] up to five months.

Even making a single "horse-tooth" stitch constitutes this. A boat on the road travels back and forth for half a *yojana*. At a great assembly, food is sufficient for four people, yet having one person in excess is a hardship;
even for a hundred people, having one in excess is a hardship. This is because during times of abundance, one must observe moderation due to the scarcity [of resources].

Regarding the opening [of the precept]: that which is beneficial to one's own person, the Vinaya clarifies as occasions for opening [the rule]. Among these, the category of "monastic order" (*saṃgha-krama*) and the like bring benefit to both oneself and others.

Furthermore, in cases such as illness and other circumstances, if one can only benefit oneself and there is no harm—specifically, no sense of giving that causes distress to the host—it is permissible.

This is because, during times of abundance, those who are superior and simple-minded might harbor excessive greed; fearing they would select only the finest offerings and depart, one might thereby cause distress to others and disturb the mind of the previously invited host. Therefore...

Because it spoils the food and utensils prepared for others, the phrase "śramaṇas here" refers to those other than these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, namely those who have gone forth among outsiders and those who have gone forth from non-Buddhist paths;
this specifically indicates the precept against eating in a separate group (*gaṇabhojana*). The phrase "now below" specifically indicates the precept against successive meals (*paramparabhojana*).
The phrase "Buddha’s disciples" refers to lay followers who have placed their faith in the Buddha; the phrase "while for... refers to [the present case].

There are two reasons for giving robes during the period of transition: first, to provide for monks whose physical needs must be met while they wait, as it would be difficult to obtain them later when required;
second, to benefit the donor, so that they may receive both the abundant rewards of food and clothing as a karmic return.

According to the rules below regarding visiting other households before or after meals, these [transitional periods] are likewise permitted during times of illness and during the time of making robes.

Regarding the passage on the time for giving robes, from the point of not accepting the robe down to the arrival of the one who brings the robe, this is the Vinaya’s explanation of the text concerning the "time for giving robes.
Since it states that this period is excluded, we can verify from other times that [the allowance] also extends beyond these specific times. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"The former interpretation held that the provisional method of 'giving during the [prescribed] time' was permitted; however, such a practice does not exist today. This 'giving of robes' extends to both the prescribed time and non-prescribed time. This is because... [the following section provides the counter-argument].
Since it is inherently permitted during the [specified] time, it is said, "Do not ask," and so forth.

If, in the case below, [the practice] were inherently permitted during the time [of the occasion] without depending on conditions such as illness or the distribution of robes, why would the *Śīla-mūla* (Fundamental Precepts) only cite the times of illness and the distribution of robes, rather than citing the *Kārttika* period?

As for the textual passage regarding the time below, it refers to what is stated in the detailed explanation (*Vinaya-vibhaṅga*) of the *Pravāraṇā*: "Regarding the distribution of robes, [it is] self..."
Since the *kāṭhina* robe has been formally discarded (*utsarita*), there is a one-month period for robes and a five-month period for robes.

Thus, if it is stated below that because the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the "Precept Text") lacks [the relevant passage], one suspects that the suspension [of the rules] does not apply, then one might also propose that the formal relinquishment (*pratyosarana*) and the invitation (*jñapti*) are likewise absent;

however, while there is no such text [for these], there is a text within the *Vibhaṅga* (the "Broad Explanation"). Should these also not be suspended through relinquishment and invitation? One must compare these two cases against one another.
This may be understood through a general inquiry. The answer below states that since the food and utensils have already been prepared, not going would render them a mere waste;

furthermore, there is no principle of prolonging the meal indefinitely, hence it is said that "the object is spoiled. Regarding clothing, even if one does not go to receive it, there is no sense in which it is immediately spoiled; thus, the loss does not extend to it.

For example, if two households each invite monks to observe the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), and one prepares grain in advance while the other does not, both violate the precept against breaking one's word;
however, since the food has not yet been prepared, it cannot be destroyed, and this case may be understood by analogy with the rules regarding robes.

If one violates a single day’s invitation, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), which is said in reference to cooked food. One must understand that this applies whether the food has already been prepared or not.

Furthermore, regarding the three recitations, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu, in the early morning, should perform the rite for offering food, saying: 'Today I have obtained food; I offer it to [Name];
I do not consider it as my own; I shall eat it. Thus he should say this three times. According to the fundamental Vinaya, one must speak the truth in the presence of a single person.
Because the Buddha has relinquished [them], the text says: "Elder, I should go there; now I give these to you. The meaning of the current question is this:

among the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) practiced during the *śīla* (precepts) section, why is only this second one explained with three recitations, while the remaining five are each explained with only one?
It is because the fourth recollection concerns the mindful retention of the three robes (*tricīvara*) and the practice of not accepting them as pure gifts (*apariśuddha-dāna*).

The superior [position] suggests that one may form the mental resolve (*manasikāra*) to guard against [the food] being "invited away" (*pariṇata*), but could one not likewise form the resolve to guard against it being "not formally declared pure" (*apariśuddha*)? Answer:

Because the lower robe belongs exclusively to oneself and is thus designated as "specifically attached," it cannot be used by forming a mere mental resolve; rather, it must be formally declared pure (*pariśuddha*). Food, however, does not belong exclusively to oneself;
furthermore, since it remains in the house of the donor, if one does not go there oneself, it can be given to others. Therefore, it is said that "the flavor is common."

Whether it be "low" or "restricted," since the taste of food is common to all, one may form a mental resolve to turn away from it. For instance, as in the fifth resolve, one may also form a resolve regarding eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Does this not also serve to prevent eating in a separate group once the resolve is completed? As for those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha, the single precept against eating in a separate group was specifically established to restrain those who are difficult to tame;
by forming a separate group and begging for alms from house to house, they create the very cause for a schism in the Saṃgha.

If one were now to permit the practice of forming a mental resolve (*saṃjñā*) to prevent schism, this would open the door to breaking the Saṃgha. Furthermore, it is because the Buddha previously permitted the formation of a mental resolve to relinquish [the offense] under the preceding precepts;

moreover, once the relinquishment is complete, one does not go back personally—this principle applies universally and differs from the case of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) which forms a resolve at dawn and remains non-separate until later, at which point it becomes separate, thereby blocking the principle. Furthermore, food cannot be shared, as its flavor is different.
This is the reason why the prevention [of further eating] involves opening and closing [the door]. The above was in response to the *Śāriputra-vinaya* (*Zhi lü*), which raised this question.
According to the *Mūla-vinaya*, however, it is not necessary to supplement [the meal]; one immediately commits the offense of the *pūrva-bhakta* (eating after the proper time).

*Pūṣanīya* (or *puṣanī*) is translated here as "proper food," referring to the five types of staple foods: parched flour, boiled rice, dry rice, fish, and meat. "Inviting in advance" (*niè qǐng*) means inviting before [the meal is ready], or otherwise, that which was not previously... [provided].

Regarding the statement that one incurs no offense for eating at the third house by intentionally reversing the order: this does not constitute a *pāyattika* (defeat) because the formal rule has not yet been established;
rather, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). It is only when one reaches the second house and eats while reversing the sequence that the full offense is incurred.

This is analogous to the case of the *śīlavatī* (virtuous woman) cited in the *Samantapāsādikā* regarding the theft of land, where the offense is established in relation to a single owner who was initially disregarded.

Regarding the statement that "when one takes up [the food], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; when two signs are indicated, it is grave," the commentary in the text says, "all refer to pointing out [the bowl].

The explanation states that this refers to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Zhendi’s Commentary). Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there is no offense" in all cases: according to the *Mūla-vinaya*, this is correct because [the offenses] are few;
however, if they were correct and numerous, there would not be a lack of the offense of *pūrva-bhakta* (eating after the proper time).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*) states:
"If a bhikṣu or a layperson acting as a donor (*dānapati*) separately invites four or more [monks] to eat together in one place, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, that same treatise states: "In all cases of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*), it is entirely food provided by a donor. What follows is an inferential explanation of this point.
It is said that while laypeople may possess the sense of accumulating food and drink, those who have left the household life are the opposite; therefore, it says "it is not so.
Thus, below, the Great Master cites the Vinaya as evidence, stating, "He has compassion for the white-robed [laypeople]," which proves that the laity serve as donors.
Furthermore, below, this explains that the two types of śramaṇas—those within and those without [the community]—do not constitute donors, and thus one commits a *thullaccaya* offense. Therefore...
Later, he again cites the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, stating that there is no offense because a bhikṣu cannot constitute a donor.
This point is also found in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Pó-lùn), which says: "If all of the *saṃghika* food is consumed, there is no fault of eating separately from the assembly;
however, if one eats *saṃghika* food in an improper manner, the food is impure and one incurs the sin of stealing from the Saṃgha. Therefore, it is necessary to rely on a layperson as the donor."

This is said because, when one commits the offense of *pṛthag-bhikṣu-saṃgha* (separate assembly), it is distinguished from [the case where] one commits the offense of theft regarding monastic food; thus, this is for the purpose of such distinction.

The second interpretation groups the two preceding treatises into two explanations: the "broad" and the "strict. Regarding the strict, it follows the first explanation of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which takes both monastics and laypeople as donors (*dānapati*).
Therefore, the citation of the *Vinaya* below as proof applies to the case where a *bhikṣu* serves as the donor; it should be so.
The initial explanation in the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Shangduo lun) is clear regarding what is urgent. This is because, generally speaking, laypeople (*avadātavasana*) provide much alms-food.
Regarding the conditions, in the Vinaya, the Buddha rebuked Devadatta, saying: "By means of countless skillful means, I have benefited and shown compassion toward the households of laypeople;
why, you foolish man, do you beg for food from five families? Nevertheless, the following passage distinguishes those who are excluded, as follows:

If the Dharma and the proper time coincide, one commits an offense; if the Dharma and the proper time do not coincide, one does not commit an offense. This is evidenced by the text concerning the distribution of rooms and bedding in the *Aniyata-khandhaka* (the section on the rules for the rainy season retreat).

"Teachers" refers collectively to Dharma-teachers and Vinaya-teachers. One who is unable to [uphold the precepts] is not among the superior ranks, yet they may still receive [the requisites] from the Saṃgha.

Next is the "Invitation by Seniority" (*anupūrvika*), which is not like the [other types]. It says: "Regarding 'invitation by seniority,' whether one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*), whether engaged in seated meditation, reciting sutras, or assisting in communal affairs, as long as one has left the household life for the sake of liberation, one may enter the order of seniority. This excludes only those with corrupt precepts (*duḥśīla*).

Even if one was previously invited separately, if there is now no discrimination [against them], how could they not be included in the order of seniority? Thus, the *Shishi yaowen leiju tiaofu chao* (The Collected Explanations on the Essentials of the Vinaya) cites this passage.

First, it clarifies that "individual invitation" (*bipie*) refers precisely to the sequence of the *saṃgha*. Furthermore, below, whenever the term "Chan master" is used, it distinguishes them from "Sūtra masters" and "Vinaya masters";
therefore, they are not termed the "sequence of the *saṃgha*. In the *Śraddhā-pratiṣṭhāna-sūtra*, when inviting people according to the Dharma of Arhats, one does not mention their names;
yet this is still called an "individual invitation," for which the Buddha rebuked them.

In the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, there are four propositions regarding this; here we refer to the second proposition. The phrase "For what reason? (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) is the master’s own rhetorical inquiry.
Thus, the Master says: "For what reason? Because one accepts the food at one time. Among the four propositions, only the third proposition does not constitute an offense (namely:

receiving invitations at different times, departing separately, accepting separately, and eating separately). Below [the section on] "separately," there are likewise four propositions, and again it is the third...
The three phrases regarding non-offenses are as set forth in the *Shichao* (Commentary on the Vinaya); the wording is abbreviated.

Each section removes the latter part to show the initial phrase for a separate invitation (*biéqǐng*), and each removes the latter part to show the subsequent text for a separate request (*biégǐ*). This is because the *Śāstra* mentions two kinds of separate assemblies;

thus it says: "There are two kinds of eating in a separate assembly: first, invitations; second, requests. As for the "mixed assembly" (*zázhòng*), this refers to those who participate through the monastic order (*sēngcì*) and includes both monastics and laypeople.

Furthermore, because they are noble (*ārya*), and because masters of dhyāna and discipline alike would be subject to the same [accusation]; because their heterodox views differ, as in the case of Devadatta forming a faction and begging separately;

and because, being inferior, their intentions are limited, whereas [the noble ones] have no restrictions and nothing is prohibited, thus they do not commit an offense—whereas the opposite constitutes an offense.

Therefore, the *Shishi yaoyong chao* states: "The single category of 'monastic turn' (*saṃghakrama*) is restricted solely to those who do not assemble; the offense is incurred through begging separately."
Whether one is gathered or not gathered, both are bound [by the offense]. That which is "not proper" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (translated here as "improper"), namely:

branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and finely ground flour-based foods; *saṃghāṭī* cakes, large and small barley, wheat, rice, beans, and made-up cakes; ghee, oil, and *modaka* (joy-pills); all types of made-up cakes;
and, with the exception of meat, all other foods that do not constitute a separate assembly, such as those where one is satisfied at various locations. These are not [permissible].

"Purity" refers to food that has been left over overnight, touched by impurities, and so forth. "Non-ritual" (*akalpa*) refers to illegal rituals (*adharmakarma*), such as acting as a matchmaker for the Sangha;
