Furthermore, even if birth and the completion of the *varṣā* retreat during the spring season were equal, the timing of receiving [the precepts] would still differ between monastics and laity.
Thus, among the eight statements, only the final one receives two names. [The detailed explanation follows below.]
This is clarified in the nineteenth fascicle. Alternatively, if one forgets and does not remember [the age], it means the years have not been fulfilled.
These three cases all concern the response given to those who receive the full ordination with faith; thus, the three preceptors and seven members of the *saṃgha* incur no offense.

However, even if one has actually reached the required age, because they responded that they had not fulfilled it, they do not obtain the precepts. This applies unless they simply respond that they do not know, or respond with doubt, rather than responding that they have not fulfilled it.

The principle is that the limit is reached upon the formal act of ordination; however, it is not auspicious for the Saṃgha to fail to inquire thoroughly. This refers to what was previously stated: "it is improper not to ask in detail.

Regarding the case where one who knows they have fulfilled the requirements answers that they have not: according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two interpretations. First, if it was due to error or forgetfulness, one obtains the precepts.
Second, if the person does not intend to receive them but the teacher forces them to do so, they say they have not fulfilled them; such a person [does not obtain the precepts].
The precepts cannot be obtained. Furthermore, the word "also" (*yòu*) is used because it refers back to what was previously cited; that [text] says:
"At that time, King Bimbisāra established a five-year intercalary cycle, and while the heterodox śramaṇas and others all followed it, the bhikṣus alone refused to do so.

The subjects and citizens censured them, until the Buddha said: 'I permit three-quarters [of the month] plus one small portion for the uposatha. This concerns both [the lay and monastic communities]."
In this month, one month is considered large and one month small;

in the large months, it is always the fifteenth day, making two quarters, while in the small months, the first half consists of one quarter, totaling three quarters, and the second half ends on the fourteenth day, thus lacking one day.
Over the course of a year, six such days are deducted—namely, from the six large and six small months—and thus thirty days are accumulated over five years.

Thirty days constitute one month; therefore, after five years, an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) is reached. Although the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states it is six years, this is based on a calculation of five years, where the accumulated [days] are extracted and assigned to the sixth year.
Thus ends the fifth fascicle of the *Fuyaoji* (Supplementary Notes) to the *Shifenlü shi pin yi chao* (Explanatory Draft on the Meaning of the Vinaya of the Four-Part Dharmaguptaka School).
*Fenbu lü shi pin yi chao fu yao ji*, Scroll Six.
Narrated by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan. Regarding "not seeing":

this refers to perverted explanations of the four matters—such as declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma, or claiming there is no offense where there is an offense—and so forth. The Saṃgha asks: why?

When asked whether he has seen [the offense], he replies that he has not seen it; the Sangha then suspends him for "not seeing" (*adarśana-utkṣepa*) and subjects him to the disciplinary measure of "not seeing.

If he does not repent, he is subject to the disciplinary measure of "not repenting" (*apratikarmāraha-utkṣepa*). Since offenses have no fixed nature but arise according to conditions, they ought logically to be eliminated through repentance, and one should originally remain pure.
Yet, now, having broken the precepts and committed these four types of offenses, he refuses to repent and instead falsely offers prevarications, saying, "I do not repent."

Therefore, it is necessary to raise and set aside these two points: why are these two also considered wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), yet instead of being termed "expelled" (*pravāsanīya*), only the śrāmaṇera who claims that sensual desire does not obstruct the path is specifically called "expelled"?
Furthermore, since the claim that desire does not obstruct [the path] is mentioned within the enumeration of the three formal accusations (*tṛtīya-utkṣepaṇīya-karman*).

To avoid confusion with the teachings, since it is stated in the sutras that "sexual desire is itself the Way," one might now disregard their own spiritual stage and recklessly rely upon this as a pretext;
because such confusion exists, they must be expelled so that the heterodox and the orthodox may be distinguished. Had they not seen [this teaching], there would be no such confusion;

furthermore, there would be no basis for the Sangha to perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) of admonition, nor would there be the sentiment of the Sangha being troubled by those who refuse to accept such admonition.

Furthermore, because one does not see one’s own faults, fails to repent those faults, and lacks the sense of following [the precepts] or transforming others through sympathetic engagement, one merely cites the Dharma to cast them out.
Conversely, those who act otherwise would blur the distinctions of the teaching. Moreover, there is the method of admonition;

when the fault of the disposition is grave, and one further desires to transform others by declaring that there is no obstruction—because these three conditions are met—one must perform the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

The *Yàlǜ* (Yaśas-vinaya) states that because the Buddha ordered a formal motion with three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to offer counsel, and [the offender] did not relinquish [his position], he was expelled (*pravāsanīya*).

The full text of the *Gāxià* (Vinaya of the Lower Section) says: "If a monk, during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), expels another monk, may they dwell together? The answer is: for three months one may dwell together.
This is extracted from the third fascicle. Furthermore, the second fascicle is cited below; its full text says: "Expelling a *śrāmaṇera*..."
One should abandon what should be abandoned; one should respond by abandoning what should be abandoned. If a śrāmaṇera confesses before the Saṃgha during the poṣadha, he should be accepted.
This rule refers to the origin story in the Vinaya concerning the two śrāmaṇeras, Upananda and his companion, who engaged in unchaste conduct together.
The second article constitutes the boundary for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension), but it does not mean that the gravity of the offense lies in the act of sexual intercourse itself.

If one has already committed the act of sexual intercourse, one should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*) and cannot subsequently receive ordination; however, because this [novice] has not yet committed it, he may later receive ordination.

Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Since this śrāmaṇera has not yet received full ordination, declaring his desire [to commit the act] is not an obstacle; it does not violate the three admonitions of the Saṃgha."

Because a mind of wrong view is established, it is difficult for one to subsequently succeed in the matter of receiving the precepts; therefore, the "heavy" dharma (*guru-dharma*) was established to create the name of "expulsion" (*pravāsanīya*) as a means of instilling fear so that they might enter the Path.
If one has already committed an offense, why would it be necessary to first admonish them and only later expel them to instill fear for entering the Path?

This is because expulsion (*pravrājana*) is carried out immediately upon the completion of the offense. The *Ji-zu* (Commentary on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) and other texts all state that committing sexual misconduct constitutes impurity (*aśuci*), which is not the meaning of "heavy."

If one were to refute this by citing the following passage: "Furthermore, if it is said that those who are subject to *pravāsanīya* (banishment) mostly speak of it as being grave, why is the second method of *pravāsanīya* among the seven *karmas* lighter than the three subsequent *utkṣepaṇīya* (suspension) procedures? By this analogy, one knows that one cannot unilaterally regard [the former] as grave.

Regarding the statement "below": this refers to the case where, as the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is about to conclude, one fails to lend an ear for even a single session; such an act incurs all the minor offenses (*dukkaṭas*) collectively to constitute one formal offense (*pācittiya*).
Regarding the passage "Nuns below," this follows the precedent of the above to pose a question concerning the relevant section:

from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, every day constitutes the period for the formal boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) of that respective station. This is a fixed division; it is not the case that the preceding and succeeding periods together form a single limit. This is the answer.

In the case of lower offenses, such as those concerning sexual misconduct or theft, if one fails to apply the appropriate remedy or fails to comprehend the object due to ignorance, this offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*) applies throughout all four categories of rules.
If, however, one’s intention is merely to refrain from further transgression while engaged in training, one incurs only a light offense for failing to train (*aśikṣita*).
Here, since the ear is not being attended to, it is precisely an offense of ignorance (*pāyattika*); thus the Vinaya-mūla states: "One does not listen with both ears with a single-minded focus."

"Knowing the Dharma [to be otherwise] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This one question should properly be placed before the precept on "listening attentively," as it belongs within the section on "defaming the Vinaya.

[The reason for] asking here is that one fears losing the opportunity for cultivation. If we proceed downward to cite the conditions for the offense, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) lists five conditions: first, having previously initiated four types of disputes; second, another...
If one privately evaluates the three actions [of others] with the intent to cause strife, or goes to listen to them, or hears their words and acts upon them, then what need is there to mention this?

The root of the precepts says: "To speak thus is contrary to what? This refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*), for by transmitting words from one side to the other, one causes separation and estrangement.
The preceding precept is precisely the precept against divisive speech.

Regarding the rule that "only one who is senior by ten *varṣas* may address a junior as 'Venerable' (*bhadanta*), while one junior by nine *varṣas* must address a senior as 'Venerable Sir' (*āyuṣmat*)," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks:
"If a junior who is senior by one *varṣa* addresses a senior who is junior by one *varṣa*, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; why then was such a regulation established? The answer is as follows:

When three or five companions enter a village together, they must address one another as "Venerable" at the village boundary and again upon reaching the side of the village; thus it is called "the edge. Furthermore, when a senior addresses a junior as "Venerable," he does not act with unrestrained freedom.
Therefore, how could the great be subordinate to the small? How could the small be independent? This is also a warning against the extreme of wandering and distraction.

The "original boundary" refers to the boundary of the original monastery; this concerns the time of first exiting the original boundary. Within the boundary, one does not distinguish between large and small, and mutual notification (*śuddhi*) is permitted.
There are two reasons why notification within the boundary is required: first, it is to avoid obstructing the affairs of the Saṃgha, for fear that...

When performing a *karmavācanā*, there may be other circumstances requiring one to go together with others; if it is unknown where they have gone, it causes distress to the Saṃgha, and furthermore, it prevents one from entering the homes of laypeople at will.
Thus, the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If, for such a reason, I must go to a certain place, I inform the Venerable Ones so that they may know.
When they respond, "It is permitted," this is called the *jñapti-dharma*.

Regarding "taking [the robe] equal to the Buddha’s robe" and so forth: if the nun’s offense is light, it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉); if heavy, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (提). When both commit the offense together, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (提) for both.

As for "ugly features manifesting externally," the *Jieshu* (戒疏) states "bodily defilement exposed externally" (*shenran wailu*); there is an alternative version that reads "obstructing" (*zhang*), which contradicts the *Jieshu*.
The remaining three [offenses] add the phrase "Buddha’s robe" at the end.
Regarding "measuring the lower": this refers to how people vary in height while their garments vary in size; thus, one's clothing must be measured according to the body.

Since the human body is eight feet tall, that of the Buddha is double that. To now arbitrarily model the Buddha’s proportions [after humans] is like a small child wearing an adult’s robes—wherein lies the cultivation of wholesome qualities through dignified deportment and adherence to the rules?
If the lower garment is stepped upon by the upper one, it is a violation of the Dharma-robes; if not...
Question: Since the alms bowl is now also a dharma-vessel, why is its quantity fixed? Answer:

It is fixed because even for those of inferior capacity, whether their food intake is large or small, it can accommodate the three grades of quantity—little, moderate, or much—and thus it is limited. Question:

If you say that clothing is a dharma-robe but its quantity is not fixed, why then was the Buddha’s robe prescribed with a fixed measure? Answer: The previous statement that clothing is not fixed was made in contrast to [the bowl].

The bodies of disciples have no fixed limit, whereas the Buddha is one; therefore, he may be said to be fixed. This is stated as a response to the preceding point, hence the word "furthermore" (*yòu*).
Regarding cutting [robes], because they are used after being cut, there is the possibility of exceeding the prescribed number through repeated making; thus, cutting is permitted.

Regarding the bowl, however, it is the opposite of this, and therefore cutting is not permitted. If it is argued that while robes may be cut and thus exceed the limit, the bowl cannot be cut and yet also exceeds the limit, [the response follows].

If it were made to the same size as the Buddha’s, why is it now entirely missing? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The various Buddhas-dharmas maintain two types of fields of merit for beings:
those of the devas and those of humans. Because celestial stone is fine and capable of being maintained, bhikṣus cannot obtain it.
Human stone is coarse and unfit for polishing; because their merit and virtue are shallow and thin, they do not induce celestial bowls, and their physical strength and power are inferior."
It is not that it cannot be carried; rather, out of compassion for the bhikṣus, he did not permit its possession.

This is not the same as the case of the Buddha, who possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa; Ānanda’s strength was such that he could turn a boulder forty *li* in circumference and carry it for the Buddha without regarding it as heavy.
*Tiṣaṇī* (提舍尼) is translated here as "confessing to another"; this refers to the rule in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* stating that one "should confess one's transgression to another bhikṣu," and so forth.

"Internal relatives" (*nija-kula*) refers to the first two pairs of offenses committed against nuns. "External relatives" (*bāhya-kula*) refers to the latter two pairs of offenses committed against laypeople. "Private and secluded" (*raho-praticchanna*) refers to the [first]...
First, taking food from a nun who is not a relative within a village is an offense;

furthermore, eating a second meal in the midst of the assembly when it has been specifically assigned by the nun constitutes a transgression. "Black clothing" refers to one of the three types of permissible colors;
that which is called black is like various fruit juices mixed together in an iron vessel to form a paste, or like the mud from a pond or well.
Dyeing is not the primary color of the north; "private and crooked" means belonging to oneself and being unjust, while "crooked" refers to a lack of uprightness.

"Gathering *ārāma*" refers to gathering at a village or a forest hermitage (*aranyaka*). Exhausting oneself brings forth reproach. In the Vinaya, when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a householder couple who had both attained the vision of the Truths (*dṛṣṭisatyā*);
they had no sense of attachment or regret, even offering their own flesh as an offering. Since such instances of providing food and clothing were numerous...

The prohibition was established because householders criticized and disparaged [the practice]. Regarding the fourth precept explained below, the absence of a separate offense is explained as the reason why no specific name for the offense was established.

Regarding those who violate the monastic regulations: because the Buddha, within the Vinaya, commanded the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to prohibit such actions, it was only after the prohibition was subsequently lifted that they were permitted again.
Since, due to the Saṃgha’s existing regulation, one may not receive [the precepts], to now violate that regulation constitutes an offense.

Because they are applied according to the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha in the sections below, it is said that while the "Saṃgha regulations" (*saṃghakṛta*) are mentioned as a general term, they are all actually established by the Buddha.
From this point downward, since there are no longer formal procedures of the Saṃgha, they receive their designation solely from the fundamental regulations established by the Buddha.

Regarding "If a *bhikṣuṇī*... [this] explains the second [point]. Regarding "If he sees... [this] introduces the fourth [point]. As for the distinction between name and essence (*nāma* and *svabhāva*):

the distinction in name lies in the difference between cessation (*saṃvara*) and performance (*pravṛtti*); furthermore, the former—taking the physical act of ceasing from eating as the essence of the observance—and the latter—taking the verbal and physical act of eating only after seeing faults and rebuking [the donor] as the essence of the observance—are distinct.
Another interpretation of the *Śīla-viniścaya-ṭīkā* states: "Seeing a *bhikṣuṇī*" refers to...

To reprimand according to the Dharma without transgressing the verbal injunctions constitutes *zhi-chi* (restraint by cessation). To reprimand without ceasing [the act], such that there is no fault in eating after [the meal] and the body and speech perform the action, constitutes *zuo-chi* (restraint by performance).
In the term "eating" (*shi*), the upper character belongs to the act of eating and chewing, while the lower character belongs to the eating implements;

the substance of the offense is one, as it involves the integration of body and speech to constitute a single transgression. There is no contradiction in the two names being distinct, for they are merely different designations based on the causal activity.
The names differ, but the substance of the offense is one.

Conversely, regarding the aforementioned "eating what has been brought to the throat" and its like, these constitute *āpatti* (transgressions) through *kriyā* (action); conversely, the aforementioned "stopping and maintaining" (*sthiti-dhāraṇa*) refers to non-speaking, which should be known as stopping transgressions through *avākya* (non-speaking).

Conversely, that which is called "maintaining through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) refers to the remainder: not taking food from a nun within a village, and taking [food] from a family under disciplinary restrictions (*śikṣādattaka*).
"Eating" refers to maintaining the precepts; conversely, "acting against" refers to those of middling or inferior faculties who act contrary to their own level.
"Superior progress" refers to practitioners of tranquility (*śamatha*), for they dwell in an araṇya and possess superior virtue.

If one now sits peacefully and causes them disadvantage, how can this be the mind intent on progressing toward the Path? "Seeing the Truths" refers to those who perceive the principle of the Four Noble Truths and realize the Unconditioned.
Because it is a partial elimination of the outflows (*āsrava*), it is the first fruit (*phala*). This continues up to the brief mention of the two [stages] for the *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Since they are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), the four fruits of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are excluded. Regarding "family" (*kula*), the *Mahāsāṃghika* says it refers to the families of the four castes. Answer: As stated below, the *Mahāsāṃghika* uses a motion with announcement (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*);

the *Dharmaguptaka* uses a motion with announcement twenty times; the *Mahīśāsaka* uses a motion with announcement twice; and the *Sarvāstivāda* uses a motion with announcement to resolve [the boundary]. The *Dharmaguptaka* uses a motion with announcement four times.
Both the formalities for binding [the precepts] and those for releasing them employ the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

These are found within the various *catur-utkṣepa-dharma* (four methods of suspension) of the Vinaya, specifically within the section on miscellaneous deportment (*viniyaka*) at the end of the various chapters and among the clusters of dharmas (*dharma-puñja*).

Whether acting as a cause for others or serving as a result in itself, how could one possibly enumerate all such instances? Thus, the *Jieshuo* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The dharma-cluster of deportment consists of forty-two thousand [rules]."

Whether they number one thousand, eighty thousand types, or extend throughout the entire dharma-realm—even if one were to briefly summarize them by means of their respective dharma-gates, they would still be included therein.
Now, because several dozen individuals are particularly prone to committing these offenses, I have again compiled and recorded them. Regarding the term *śikṣā*, there are two Sanskrit pronunciations:
the first is *śikṣā-karmanī*, which is the same as the *Vinaya*; this is a corruption or confusion of the original Sanskrit sound. The latter is *śikṣā-kara*.
The *dhāraṇī* [term] here refers to "training" (*śikṣā*). One should transpose the phrasing to accord with the local idiom, meaning "one should train.
Regarding this precept below: since it is said to be difficult to maintain and easy to violate, one must constantly remain vigilant and cautious, keeping the mind focused on training.
This is why no offense of *duṣkṛta* (or *dukkaṭa*) is established; rather, it merely indicates that one "should train. As for *sthūlātyaya*...
*Duṣkṛta* (突吉羅): *Duṣ* means "evil" (*pāpa*), and *kṛta* means "to do. According to the phonology of *śabda-vidyā*, the correct pronunciation is *duṣ-kṛta*.

Since it is called "evil-doing," it encompasses both bodily and vocal karma. In relation to the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) as the remedy (*pratipakṣa*), and in relation to evil karma as that which is to be prevented (*pratiṣedhya*), it is said to be "hidden" (*gupta*) by virtue of its capacity as the remedy. The four mentioned above are *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *pāyattika*.
Tiśya has already established that according to the Buddha’s regulations, all must advance in their studies; if one does not pursue learning, there is no way to understand the essential meaning.
Why, then, is only the fifth [stage] given the name "study"? Regarding "subtlety," the *Daciao* (Great Commentary) cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as evidence, stating:
"The divine eye sees a bhikṣu committing an offense like a torrential rain falling. Is this not precisely because the focus is concentrated within the mind? Therefore, the Hu monks [called it] *mu*.

This is for the sake of guarding the precepts. To be able to maintain what is ultimately difficult to maintain demonstrates the merit of training and study. Furthermore, if there is not even a deficiency in the subtle, how could one permit transgressions in the coarse?
Moreover, the coarse constitutes the beginning and the subtle constitutes the end; because there is no failure at the end, the practice of study is perfected.

Thus, the name "training" (*śikṣā*) is established by taking the ultimate limit of maintaining and guarding as its basis; it does not mean that the preceding sections are entirely devoid of the meaning of training.

If, below, the mind is unobstructed, it becomes functional as soon as one thinks of it; yet because the preceding and succeeding moments arise alternately and the acts of ceasing and acting arise in conjunction, in the case of wholesome states there is dual maintenance, while in the case of unwholesome states there is dual transgression.
Thus, with respect to the mental faculty, both maintenance and transgression are simultaneous. In the *Miscellaneous Rules on Staffs and Alms-bag Pouches*, it says:
"At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was weak and old, unable to walk without a net-bag to carry his bowl or without a staff. And so forth.
He addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I allow you to grant that elderly bhikṣu a staff and a pouch through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
Now, following the teaching, the name 'observance by cessation' (*zhi-chi*) refers to ceasing what is unrighteous; its opposite constitutes the two types of transgressions.

Regarding the remaining ninety-nine precepts, if one relies on the teaching to cease what is unrighteous according to the specific application of the matter, it is called 'observance by cessation'; if one violates the teaching and pursues faults, it is called 'commission' (*zuo*')."

If one commits these infractions, how could there be any instruction for others to say, "Do not wear your robes unevenly for my sake"? If the offense is grave, one must perform a confession before another (*pratideśanā*);

if the offense is light, one performs a mental confession (*cittotpāda*). Furthermore, for heavy offenses, the mental reproof is heavy; for light offenses, the mental reproof is light; one should always deliberate and examine the matter according to the circumstances.
Regarding "walking with a swaying body" (*tūxiá jí yáo shēn xíng rù bāiyī shè*): the Vinaya states this refers to walking while swaying the body to the left and right.

Regarding "defecating or urinating upon living grass," both Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs incur a *pāyattika* offense. Since there is no "lower" [category] (i.e., no minor offense), and since there is no instruction to have someone else do it for oneself, within the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) there is no sense of an offense being incurred spontaneously (*an-ābhoga*).
This can be understood by cross-referencing these points against the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. As for the "single substance" (*yītǐ*):

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The essence is the essence of mind, which is originally undefiled; because it is obscured by delusion and inversion, the notions of 'false' and 'correct' arise.

Now, realizing that the fundamental principle of dharmas is in reality without these three [distinctions], one distinguishes them according to their phenomenal functions in order to guide and transform others through a single direction. Thus, when reflecting upon the aspect of principle, it constitutes the meaning of 'Awakening' (*bodhi*);

when the essence transcends names and words, it constitutes the meaning of 'Dharma'; and when the ultimate truth is unhindered and harmonious, it constitutes the meaning of 'Sangha'. It is not [otherwise].
Because one does not know the Dharma, it must be placed at the beginning; it is not because the Buddha was unaware of it that it is taught later.
Furthermore, it is said that "that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma"; therefore, in terms of the single essence of the Dharma, it should logically come first.

As for the distinct characteristics, these are also called "transformed characteristics," such as when Śākyamuni first attained enlightenment and was uniquely honored as the Buddha alone, thus being the head. As for afflictions and delusions, they must rely upon the Dharma for their removal.

Therefore, the teaching by means of sound (*śabdadharmadeśanā*) is expounded next, as it serves to cleanse the afflictions of the mind; thus, the Dharma occupies the second position. If one were to preach only [the Dharma] to those without the capacity [to receive it], there would be no benefit;

therefore, the assembly of Kauṇḍinya who attained sainthood constitutes the Saṃgha at the end. Now, below, one should first raise the objection: "If one relies on the single essence (*ekatva*), the Dharma should logically come first;
if one relies on distinct characteristics (*bhinnalakṣaṇa*), the Buddha must occupy the foremost place. Why, then, are the various trainees (*śaikṣa*) listed [in this manner]?"
Regarding the sequence in which the precepts first clarify respect for the Saṅgha, followed by the Dharma, and finally the Buddha—this is explained below in the commentary.

This means that because the present exposition distinguishes [the Three Jewels] based on the *saṃbhoga* (institutional) Three Jewels, the Saṅgha is mentioned first, followed by the Dharma, and then the Buddha. Why is this? It is because the Way relies upon persons to be propagated;

such is the natural order of the world. Thus, when Kāśyapa-mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, they manifested the outward appearance of the Saṅgha. To describe the Five Vehicles as the causes of goodness clarifies [this principle].
The three miserable realms are the manifest fruits of evil; the ritual for the present dharma is intended to be vast and sublime, not something opened up for ordinary or small-minded people.
Therefore, the painted images displayed on the cool terrace represent the ritual of the Buddha as he appeared when he taught them. Thus, the list of precepts presented here follows this very ritual.

Regarding the first section below, if one were to rely solely on the rules concerning the wearing of robes, there would be only two precepts; however, we must now comprehensively include what follows, which reverses the previous order.

Regarding "teaching the Dharma while wearing robes improperly," the forty-nine precepts below must be supplemented by adding the two characters "teaching the Dharma" (shuōfǎ) after "neatly arranged" (qízhěng) to complete the fifty-one articles.

Question: The interrogative phrasing here also originates from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Duōlùn*). That treatise explains the meaning of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (*Shísòng*), for that Vinaya states:
The bhikṣus were wearing their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes (undergarments) in various ways—some very high, some very low, and others uneven. When the Buddha saw this, he thought:

Regarding the "five factors," this refers to the settlement of disputes of medium intensity; for disputes of low intensity, there are only three factors.

There must be no concealment. Regarding the *dharma* (the teaching), when it manifests before one, the Saṃgha must perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and conduct a detailed evaluation according to the prescribed rules.

As for the *vinaya* (discipline), which is the fifth [requisite], when it manifests before one, one must employ the *karma*; those with virtue shall participate in the evaluation, while those without virtue shall be censured and expelled.

Regarding the four types of *saṃgha-pratyakṣa* (presence of the Saṃgha) and the three methods for establishing the boundary markers (*sīmā-sthūṇā*) and chanting the *karmavācanā*:

1. **The presence of persons**: Both parties gather together and each expounds their respective teachings and principles. 2. **The presence of the Dharma**: One adjudicates by means of the Tripitaka teachings. 3. **The presence of the Vinaya**:

The purport of the teaching is clear, and doubts and obscurities are naturally dispelled. Since these do not depend on the four [members of the Saṃgha], the formalities of the Saṃgha are excluded; thus, the two boundaries are established naturally.
Because it is attained through general application and does not require the gathering of all [members], the *dhātu* (realm/assembly) is excluded; this also refers to the cessation of minor disputes.

As for those capable of severing [disputes]—namely, the *samyak-prahāṇa* (right abandonments)—this applies generally to the members of the Saṃgha; thus, we do not here distinguish between two separate types of Saṃgha members, but apply the general term "Saṃgha" to those present.
Furthermore, since the individuals involved in the dispute also include both the Saṃgha and individuals, why is it that [the term] is applied exclusively to "individuals present"?

Question: What is the difference in meaning between the former [the "presence of the Saṃgha"] and these? Answer: Among the latter five, the "presence of the Saṃgha" refers to the fact that the ability to adjudicate and the administration of the Dharma are accomplished by the Saṃgha as a whole rather than by an individual; thus, the designation "Saṃgha" is retained here.

In the case of the "presence of persons," although there may be both the Saṃgha and individuals among those for whom the rite is performed, because these two categories do not themselves administer the Dharma, it is restricted to being called the "presence of persons. Within the three types of presence, this refers to the "presence of the Dharma."
In the preceding [section], there are also two distinct categories: the one who performs the severance and the one for whom it is performed.

Why, then, is only the person for whom it is performed established as a "person," while the Sangha that performs the severance is not mentioned? It is because from three or four people upwards, provided they do not themselves preside over the *karmavācanā*, they are all termed "persons.
If one were to establish the name "Sangha" here, it would be confused with the "Sangha of the fivefold *karmavācanā*" among the five types of Sanghas. For this reason, it is not established.

"Why do you not further establish that the person who can effect the severance being present constitutes four factors? [Answer: "Because among the three [factors], the person includes both the one who effects the severance and the person for whom it is to be severed.
This refers to the latter half of the forty-third [chapter], the Cankī-khandhaka, in the Vinaya. Why? [The text] below points to the Vinaya.
Because this is from the preceding section of the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (Methods for Settling Disputes), it says "the two persons above. That text states:
"Two bhikṣus [settling] for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, or for the Saṃgha; even the Saṃgha [settling] for the Saṃgha—this is settling a dispute in accordance with the Dharma.

Since this method of settling disputes applies universally to both the agent (*karaka*) and the object (*karma*), as well as to individuals and the Saṃgha, why is it specifically mentioned here in the context of the formal act (*kamma*)?

Question: Does the act of formal accusation apply to laypeople, to other monks, or to the monk who is being accused? Answer: It is not permissible for a single individual to wield the Dharma to punish another;
such a person is at fault. Nor may four individuals arbitrarily administer punishment, because they do not constitute a formal assembly (*saṃgha*).

Furthermore, it is incorrect for a *saṃgha* to perform the rite of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) [against one of its own members], as this is intended to extinguish disputes (*adhikaraṇasamatha*) rather than to carry out an act of banishment or disciplinary treatment. Therefore, it is appropriate to accept their own confession (*pratyāpatti*), as stated in the Vinaya.
Why does it say that confessing the names and categories of offenses is its "lower" explanation?

This is because it is identical to the *vinaya* among the five [methods] and identical to the *vinaya* among the three; thus, it is not non-existent. "Non-existent" (*wu*) here carries the meaning of "extinguished," for *vinaya* is named as "extinguishing.
Therefore, it alone is capable of [resolving disputes]; this refers to the fact that while there are three grades of verbal disputes, the five methods are able to [settle them].
Because the middle and upper grades among those [three grades] are extinguished, if it concerns a minor grade of verbal dispute (*vāda-vivāda*), it is settled using three methods.

If it is a minor grade, it is then assigned to the other six methods, such as *smṛti* (recollection) and so forth, which can universally extinguish disputes regarding accusations (*anuvāda-vivāda*) and matters concerning offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*).

Just as with the three grades within disputes over offenses, the minor grade is extinguished by the manifestation of five methods along with the medicine of recollection; furthermore, it is extinguished by the manifestation of five methods along with the method of "not being insane" (*amūḍha*).

To resolve a middling offense through *bhaiṣajya* (medicinal treatment), five methods are employed in conjunction with the formal act of confession (*āpattisthāna*). To resolve a superior offense through *bhaiṣajya*, these same four methods [used for resolving disputes arising from accusations] are used together.
Furthermore, regarding disputes arising from offenses: a middling offense is resolved through the formal act of confession (*pratijñākāraka*) when five methods are present;

a superior offense is resolved through the "covering over as with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) when five methods are present. Regarding disputes arising from matters, seven methods are generally employed for resolution, and the five methods are also included therein.

Regarding the statement that within the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of legal disputes), the middle and upper grades are extinguished by means of the five methods (*pañca-dharma*) being present and the majority vote (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*), these five methods are thus broad in application.
Furthermore, because they are applied concurrently with the six *vinayas*, the three methods [of the lower grade] do not apply;

they apply only to the extinction of the lower grade among the two types of disputes (*dvaya-vivāda*). Consequently, in comparison to the remaining middle and upper grades, they do not apply at all. This is the separate chapter.

In the *Vinayaviniścaya* (the section on the methods for extinguishing disputes) and the *Śīlaskandha-śāstra*, it is clarified that because all seven [categories] below are termed *vinaya*, the general term cannot fail to encompass the specific names above.

However, if one discusses the categories below, such as "presence" (*sammukhavinaya*), they cannot encompass "recollection" (*smṛtivinaya*) and so forth; thus, the seven distinct names do not mutually include one another.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of the essential natures, they do not exceed the five or three dharma-bodies. Furthermore, among the [four] types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), the five dharmas and the three lower disputes are able to extinguish the five dharmas;
since their essential natures are not distinct, their application is universal. This is because they are equally able to extinguish the four disputes and also apply to the remaining six *vinayas*.
As for the examples cited below, the explanation of this universality from here on down refers to "one's own statement" (*svavacana*).

The remaining six [cases] are "comprehensive" (*sāmānya*) in the same way as "recollection" (*smṛti*); that is, one says of oneself, "Even in my dreams I do not speak falsely," or "My illness has been cured.

One should know that each of these has its own specific verbal description; thus, "self-assertion" (*svavacana*) can encompass the other six and is therefore called "comprehensive. Now, what is meant by "restricted" (*viśeṣa*)?
It refers to cases such as those six types of self-assertion mentioned above taken individually, for example, when one says, "I am truly... and so forth.

Because one confesses by acknowledging the commission of a certain offense, it is as explained below: to show that there is no grasping at faults, but rather returning them to oneself and speaking of them oneself.

As for the subsequent resolution of contradictions, it is as previously stated regarding the gravity [of the offense]; subsequently, one causes the contradiction to be resolved by stating that the offense committed was light.

All of these are not the principle of grasping at faults and returning them to oneself. Therefore, the following concludes the separate chapter; this is also found within the *Vinaya* section on the extinction of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*).

To broaden this point for later students to examine: all [the seven types of] medicine are discussed in terms of being "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*), because the act of extinction cannot be accomplished if the three factors—person and so forth—are not present before one. Thus, each must possess a presently manifest dharma.

As stated in the Vinaya text itself within the section on the extinction of the Dharma, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) also provides a detailed analysis of the characteristics of the three and five methods within the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face settlement).
It states briefly in the section on the "medicine of one's own confession" (*svavāda-bhaiṣajya*) that there are likewise three methods and five methods of confession;

these can be understood as being the same as those in the aforementioned *pratyakṣa*. As for the others, such as *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection), they do not possess the three methods of recollection.

Regarding the five methods of recollection—namely, *smṛti-vinaya* (recollection), *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of one not insane), *yadbhūyaś-chanda* (the majority decision), *tṛṇa-prastāraka* (covering over as with grass), and the fifth category—none of these five names appear here.
This can be understood by observing that where they are identical, they share the same *karmabhūmi* (boundary for formal acts).

As for "the extinction of the Dharma," "extinction" refers to the *vinaya*. Where they differ, one must apply whichever method or *vinaya* is appropriate according to the specific circumstances of the dispute.

Although they are thus excluded, they do not fall outside the two categories of *dharma* and *vinaya*. These five types of persons are all those who initiate disputes; that is, among these five, they are "persons who initiate.
Only the single case of "decision by the majority" (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*) applies to both the person who can resolve and the person who is resolved;

the remaining [methods] belong solely to the category of the person who is resolved. Regarding the ten qualities: first, being fully endowed with the precepts (*śīla-saṃpanna*); second, being much... [text truncated].
1. Having heard the two sections of the Vinaya three times and recited them twice, one is extremely proficient; 2. if one can extensively explain their meaning; 3.

if one is skillful in speech and possesses clear eloquence, capable of engaging in question and answer to bring joy to others; 4. if one can extinguish disputes when they arise; 5. if one is without attachment;
6. if one is without anger; 7. if one is without fear; 8. if one is without delusion—one who possesses these ten virtues should be appointed to serve together with [the candidate].

Those who sever [the precepts] and are not fully endowed [with them] do not fall under this category; those who act as monks interchangeably with one another—this describes the person to whom the confession belongs at that time, whereas [in other cases] it belongs to the Saṃgha;
that person and this Saṃgha are likewise equal. These four are taken collectively: attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, which together constitute the four.
The Vinaya states: "One who is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion is the most noble and supreme among all people."
The first is like milk producing curd, curd producing butter, and butter producing clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which is supreme and peerless;
this is the mark of a person of balanced integrity. Since such a person possesses these virtues, they will certainly not falsely recommend others for office.

Regarding "confession by one's own word" (*svavavāda*), this refers to those among the latter two types [of disputes] that are subject to repentance; since the confession is made truthfully, it can be purified through repentance. Regarding "extinction through mutual agreement" (*ubhayābhimata*):

when two parties each state the names and categories of their offenses and seek repentance, the offense is extinguished once this is done, and the dispute is extinguished through reconciliation. Regarding "non-extinction of the offense":

this refers to cases where, after the fundamental offense has been adjudicated and dealt with, one subsequently repents according to the specific category (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.); although the dispute may be settled, the offense itself is not extinguished.

First, the [formal act] is extinguished, yet the offense has not been extinguished; the remaining four—namely, *pratijñā* (confession), *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is no longer deluded), and *yadbhūyaḥ-saṃmata* (the majority decision)—are then brought into effect.

Regarding the six types of places for the removal of offenses, once the place for the removal of the offense has been finalized—that is, once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) regarding the place for the removal of the offense has been concluded—one subsequently deprives [the offender] of the thirty-five matters.
If the person submits to their original offense, it should be dealt with according to the Dharma by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

Regarding those who can be absolved of an offense through repentance: one must bow the head in submission and thereafter no longer conceal the transgression; according to the specific category of the offense, one should perform the ritual of confession (*pratideśanā*).

As for those whose offenses are "inexpiable" (*anāpatti*), this refers to cases where one initially admits, "I have committed such-and-such an offense," but then immediately says, "I do not regret it; I committed a grave offense merely as a joke.

The Saṃgha should grant them the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) of lifelong inexpiability. Other than these, there are no further categories mentioned above that need to be discussed regarding absolution.
In that Vinaya, there is only the *karman* of non-remorse (*a-pratikarman*), and no *karman* of release (*vimokṣa-karman*). For this reason, it is not discussed here.

The single phrase "release" should be combined with the preceding phrase "in other cases where there is no [remorse]"; only then will the meaning be coherent. The answer below distinguishes that the assembly of wise people to perform the *karman* belongs to the category of the Dharma-precepts.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The previous application of the *karman* involves joint deliberation by those with virtue and the demotion of those without virtue."

Furthermore, what teaching should be applied to eradicate this ailment? This medicine is like treating a specific disease: first one selects a skilled physician, and next one administers the medicinal herbs and stones.
If there is a physician but no medicine, the illness will not be healed; likewise, if there is wisdom but a lack of teaching, such disputes cannot be eradicated.
Therefore, these are gathered together to form a single treatment; it does not hinder the fact that the essence of the Dharma-medicine is inherently diverse. It does not diminish [the truth].
Regarding the three categories: first, the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), which is a single method for proving the Dharma and recording that there has been no offense;
second, the *tatsvabhāva-naiḥsargika* (settlement by acknowledging the nature of the act), which is a single method with no other remedy;

and third, the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one not insane), which refers to the place where an offense is established through common consensus. According to the commentator following the title, it should say "the *Cao* (Excerpts)," or perhaps this was originally in the primary commentary (*shu*).

Master Yi then said: "The commentators of the *Śāstra*—as seen in the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), which cites the opening passage of the *Shu yi* (Meaning of the Commentary)—are indeed the 'commentators.

Now, since it has been stated that the substance of the Dharma and the medicine are distinct, why do you provide a general explanation without determining the actual entities of these two, the Dharma and the medicine?"
First, the establishment [of the position]; second, the extension of the objection; third, the explanation of that objection. As for the intent of the objection:

if it is argued that because [the *bhaiṣajya*] is not ultimate, it is not included [in the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha*], then while this may apply to the *dharma*, the *bhaiṣajya* occurs later and properly belongs to the ultimate stage;

why then is its essence not included? Here, the explanation states: if one raises the objection as above, then according to what you yourself have said regarding the *vinaya*, the cessation of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) can be explained.

Because speech is ultimately extinguished, one may say that the substance of the medicine possesses the sense of finality. However, according to the majority of the *Svavāda-mukha* (the Gate of Self-Statement), if speech has not yet been extinguished, it is said:
"Suppose there is a bhikṣu who commits a *pārājika* offense; he first says he did not commit it, but later says he did.
If the Saṃgha grants this person the *yathābhūta-paryeṣaṇa-vinaya* (the Vinaya of searching for the truth as it is), this is called illegal (*adharma*). Why? Because this person..."

Because it is for the purpose of settling through *nihsargika* (formal act of banishment), this text serves as proof that although the matter has been concluded by one's own admission, since the legal procedure (*dharma*) is not based on a dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), how could it be a "settling"?
This too is not ultimate; therefore, its essential nature cannot be definitively established.

To seek out a dispute means that when a bhikṣu has committed an offense, three authorities or five virtuous ones bring him before the Saṃgha to investigate and seek out his prior transgression; because of this investigation and evaluation of the offense, the dispute subsequently arises.
Because these disputes vary in magnitude, they are divided into three grades; accordingly, the application of the medicinal remedies is also not fixed.

When the five factors are present, the "remedy of recollection" (*smṛti-bhaiṣajya*) extinguishes minor disputes. When the five factors are present, the "remedy of non-delusion" (*amoha-bhaiṣajya*) extinguishes middling disputes.

When the five factors are present, the "remedy of the locus of the offense" (*āpatti-sthāna-bhaiṣajya*) extinguishes major disputes. Regarding "disputes concerning speech" (*vāda-vivāda*), this refers to evaluating the right and wrong of the characteristics of the Dharma.

One must know that when the heterodox and the orthodox each cling to their own views, disputes arise; these also have three grades. Lower-grade verbal disputes are extinguished through the presence of three factors.

Middle-grade disputes are extinguished through the application of five factors. Higher-grade disputes are extinguished through the application of five factors as well as the "words of many" (*bahujana-vāda*).
As for disputes involving transgressions, the fault remains within the heart and the characteristics of the offense are difficult to discern; thus, various discussions become confused.

From this proliferation, disputes arise; these also have three grades. For the lower grade, the application of remedies is not fixed, and the offense is extinguished through the *prātimokṣa* (self-avowal) when three factors are present.
For the middle grade, it is extinguished through the *prātimokṣa* when five factors are present.

For the upper grade, it is extinguished through the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) when five factors are present. Since there is deliberation, discussion, adherence to views, and shifting positions, further remedies are employed.
There is no fixed standard; by inferring from this, one cannot definitively determine its essence.

As for the remaining four—namely, the three types of remedial dharmas (*dharmabhaiṣajya*) concerning offenses other than those involving memory or non-delusion—their essence is external to the aforementioned.

This is because the three preceding codes of discipline (*vinaya*) actually derive their remedial dharmas from the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures). Thus, [the remedies] such as being "in the presence of the assembly" (*sammukhībhāva*) do not constitute an actual essence, as is the case according to the Vinaya.
It is asked: "What are the *dharmas* maintained by the presence of which disputes are settled? What is the *vinaya* maintained by the presence of which disputes are settled?
Therefore, one should know that this is a general reference to both *dharma* and *vinaya*. At the time of actual application, one must skillfully understand how to select the *dharma* for use;
thus, it cannot be definitively specified. As for those who increase or decrease [the number], [it is because they have not understood this].

Among the five methods, those that can effect severance constitute the *saṃgha*; thus, adding three methods constitutes the "increased" category. Among these, those that can effect severance through both general and specific means constitute the "decreased" category.

As for the subsequent items—first, second, and third—these are for addressing individuals; one personally confesses the offense before them. Fourth, this is for addressing the assembly. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"Regarding 'self-accusation' (*svavāda*) as a means of discipline, the offense arises from oneself and must therefore be confessed by oneself, being presented face-to-face before the assembly."
Regarding the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for reconciliation: when one confesses before the Sangha and receives the rite of atonement (*pratideśanā*), one should perform the formal announcement.

When seeking the formal announcement, if the dispute over the offense has not yet been settled, the conflict may still arise because the Sangha has not yet reached harmony. There are three types [of disputes]: first, those that are manifest; second, those that are concealed;
and third, those settled by whispering. As in the midst of the assembly, there are preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), elders (*sthavira*), and wise persons who uphold the Dharma.

Regarding those who uphold the Vinaya-mātṛkā, they should all act openly in accordance with the Dharma; conversely, acting otherwise constitutes the two lower types of conduct. As for the five differences:
first, there are five aspects of open conduct, while the remaining two each have four. Now, as for the first five:

(1) when there are many persons who do not act according to the Dharma among one's preceptors and teachers, one should act openly in accordance with the Dharma; (2) when there are many persons who do not act according to the Dharma... [text continues]

1. Furthermore, the elders, wise ones, upholders of the Dharma, and upholders of the Vinaya should manifest [their conduct], yet they do not know whether this dispute is mostly in accordance with the Dharma or mostly contrary to the Dharma;

nevertheless, the elders and others who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya should manifest [the correct course]. 2. They do not know whether the discourse on the Dharma is mostly in accordance with the Dharma or mostly contrary to the Dharma; nevertheless, those elders and others who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya should manifest [the correct course]. 3. This dispute... [is mostly in accordance with the Dharma or mostly contrary to the Dharma]; nevertheless, the elders and others who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya should manifest [the correct course]. 4. They do not know whether the discourse on the Dharma is mostly in accordance with the Dharma or mostly contrary to the Dharma; nevertheless, those elders and others who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya should manifest [the correct course]. 5. This dispute... [is mostly in accordance with the Dharma or mostly contrary to the Dharma]; nevertheless, the elders and others who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya should manifest [the correct course].
When those who speak according to the Dharma are numerous, one should immediately manifest two types of concealment (*paticchādana*). There are four [cases]:

first, when those who act according to the Dharma are numerous, while the elders (*sthavira*) and others act contrary to the Dharma, one should perform concealment; second, when those who act according to the Dharma are numerous, while the elders and others act contrary to the Dharma, one should perform concealment;

third, regarding cases where the points are unknown, proceed as in the preceding examples; fourth, regarding the practice of whispering (*karṇajāpa*), there are likewise four [cases], which may be understood accordingly.
In the above [text], simply change "concealment" (*paticchādana*) to "whispering" (*jappā*) and read it; the difference can thus be seen.

Regarding the appointment of a person to distribute *śalākā* (voting sticks) by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*), the Vinaya states that one must possess five qualities: being free from favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion, and knowing when to proceed and when not to proceed.
Furthermore, two kinds of *śalākā* are made: one broken and one whole. Once they have been made, one should perform the formal motion.

One who speaks thus according to the Dharma should be seized; one who speaks thus contrary to the Dharma should be seized. Having distributed the *śalākā* (voting sticks), they should be counted in a separate place.

If those who speak according to the Dharma are numerous, one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). If those who speak thus [according to the Dharma] are numerous, the matter of dispute may be settled.
If those who speak according to the Dharma are few, one should create a disturbance and depart; because the dispute has not yet been settled, it is known that although the procedure was performed...
Since the superior methods are not yet ultimate, one cannot definitively establish the substance of the medicine.
If one looks toward the two groups each presenting their own confession of faults, this dharma allows for the matter to arise again later; thus it is not ultimate. As the Vinaya says:

"What is 'covering with grass' (*tṛṇapraticchādana*)? It is when one does not state the name of the offense or its category, but instead performs a confession and atonement. This is [the method] by which a dispute is settled."
The phrase "to initiate it again hereafter" is the final line that serves as a general conclusion.
As for the *vinaya*, among the seven types of *vinaya*, the *sammukhavinaya* (presence) and *pratijñāvinaya* (admission) apply to both the *saṃgha* and the individual;

the five methods beginning with *smṛtivinaya* (recollection) apply exclusively to the *saṃgha* and do not apply to the individual. Why is this? For example, the *smṛtivinaya* is employed in cases of offenses involving non-delusion (*amūḍha*).

Through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the *bahujana-vāda* (majority vote), the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*), the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *tṛṇa-praticchādana* (covering with grass), and the *jñapti-mātra* for repentance, it is known that this applies specifically to the Saṃgha.
As for Arhats, such as Śāṇavāsa, they are taken as examples; since those who have realized the stage of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning) must never commit intentional offenses, the *Karmasūtra* states:
"Those in the stage of the four fruits may only commit accidental offenses, whereas those in the stage of the third fruit may also commit intentional offenses. *A* (the letter A).

Because this person has exhausted the afflictions of both the views and the meditative cultivation of the desire realm, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Having abandoned nine [categories of afflictions], one is indeed a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Although there may be transgressions, they ultimately do not constitute a violation of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). If even the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) does not possess such a violation of the fundamental nature, how much less so the third fruit?

The *Yejieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The recipient of the 'Come hither' (*ehibhikṣu*) ordination is superior; because they lack the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), there is no possibility of a concealed transgression. This is correct. Nevertheless, at the beginning—

The fruit [of the Stream-enterer] merely severs the eighty-eight delusions regarding principle; the two fruits of cultivation have not yet severed them at all. Only when one reaches the second fruit [the Once-returner] does one sever six grades of the desires of cultivation.

Therefore, the treatise takes the Anāgāmin as the example, because they sever all nine grades of the afflictions of cultivation. As for the three groups [of those who do not appear], because it is improper for them to hear the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), they can only perform it from a distance;
thus it is said they "do not appear. "Internal rot" means that the substance of the precepts is internally corrupted, like an object [rotting from within].

Regarding this putrefaction: it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for the monk; it is not a *sthūlātyaya*. If he does not perform the formal act of "not taking to heart" (*an-asmaraṇa-karman*), then by means of that proof of "not taking to heart," the Saṃgha also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he does not perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, then by means of that formal act of "not performing," he is expelled directly.
Although the expulsion is accomplished as a disciplinary measure, because he cannot expect the Saṃgha to apply the formal procedure, he incurs an offense of violating the teaching.

To respond with "auspiciousness" is like having medicine for a disease but being unable to use it; this refers to when people are present yet one must perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), or when there are virtuous persons who should deliberate together, yet one fails to do so.
Among these eight [cases], the first four involve the deprivation of one's followers (*parivāra*), while the latter four involve the deprivation of one's intelligence (*prajñā*).
One who acts as an agent (*karmakāraka*) must possess both eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and great wisdom, and must not refuse to receive their commission.
Only those who have received the formal invitation are fit to be dispatched; since it is said that they shall meet in succession, this refers to the principle of the monastic order (*saṃghakrama*).
Only those seeking liberation may participate. Now, as there has been a transgression, it is logical that [the offender] be excluded.
Whether the entire assembly is depleted or only a small portion remains until the required number is reached, or even if the whole assembly departs, it is still permissible for him to attend.
Generally, as disputes arise from the subtle to the manifest, the seven medicines for settling them are likewise arranged from small to great.

If a dispute is settled through *saṃmukhavinaya* (decision in the presence of), *smṛtivinaya* (decision based on memory), or *amūḍhavinaya* (decision for one not insane), these belong only to the middle and lower grades of medicine.

For major disputes, one employs *yadbhūyaśo-vinaya* (majority decision) or *tṛṇastāra-vinaya* (covering over as with grass). Furthermore, there are those who speak contrary to the truth, causing offense and distress to the Saṃgha.

Because heavy disputes are difficult to settle, one is granted the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of motion and three proclamations) as a disciplinary measure for the offense; the original offense is taken up and the [remaining] thirty-five matters are forfeited.
Subsequently, another *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is added to resolve this. Thus, the latter three [measures] serve as superior medicines. Answer:

In the case of the "manifest" (*sammukha*), it universally extinguishes all three grades—low, middle, and high. Only the "majority decision" (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*) exclusively extinguishes the high grade of verbal dispute (*vāda-artha*); therefore, it is used alone.

Second, the determination through the "removal by medicine" (*bhaiṣajya-vinaya*). If one intends [to say]: "If one uses the three types of determination—recollection (*smṛti*) and so forth—it may be possible to seek out whether a dispute is clear or turbid;
however, if one definitively asserts it to be a dispute, how can its being 'wrong' or 'right' be understood? Rather, it would only give rise to further dispute.

In this case, the characters for "clear" and "turbid" should be replaced with "wrong" and "right" respectively, to clarify that there is no dispute. The phrase "not a dispute" below means that the basis of the dispute is not a matter of an offense (*āpatti*).

Furthermore, since there are varying degrees of gravity regarding offenses committed through non-contention, it is clear that one need not personally confess [the offense]; rather, it is evident that only the latter two types of *vinaya*—*tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering over as with grass) and *pratijñākāraka* (acting according to confession)—are employed, while the other five are not.
Answer: A single bhikṣu and the Saṃgha constitute the "persons capable of deciding" (the *vinītakas*), while the bhikṣu [in question] is the "person to be decided" (*vinītya*).

Both belong to the category of persons present before the assembly. Regarding the phrase "this Dharma and Vinaya are present," the formal scriptural text contains no such expression as "good words" or "excellent instruction.

It merely states, "according to the Dharma," etc., with the words of the Great Teacher [the Buddha] serving as the general heading. Furthermore, this indicates that the person capable of deciding must be free from faults and not subject to cessation.
It is called such because the characteristics of the Dharma are coarse and rugged. As the Buddha taught, "The teachings that encompass both the Dharma and the Vinaya are what the Buddha has spoken.

The Vinaya states that if a matter of dispute is not resolved according to the ten methods—that is, the ten virtues, which range from upholding the precepts and extensive learning to being free from delusion—then it cannot be extinguished. Regarding the phrase "as cited above, there are others below," this refers to...

Regarding those who adjudicate legal matters but do not recite the *Prātimokṣa*, do not know the *Vinaya*, and instead of grasping the correct meaning, utter illegal speech—the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) to expel them. The *jñapti* is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That bhikṣu so-and-so does not recite the *Prātimokṣa* and does not know the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Vinaya*; he thus abandons the correct meaning and utters illegal speech. If it is the time for the Saṃgha..."
"May the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha now sends forth this bhikṣu. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this includes anger, fear, and delusion;
one must know what is permissible and what is not. *Śalā* refers to voting sticks (or tallies). If one intends to cast the voting sticks immediately, one should first form the thought:
"In this assembly, there are such persons as these who should be sent out"—that is, those who follow what is not the Dharma—and one should then secretly dispatch them.

[The Buddha] went among the Saṃgha and summoned those who were qualified according to the Dharma to take up voting sticks (*śalākā*) so that this matter might be extinguished together; [it was said that] "the merit would be great and equal. The answer is:
among these, the one type known as *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) applies universally to extinguish all three grades [of offenses], yet it requires five factors.

As for the other remedies: *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) extinguishes minor offenses; *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) extinguishes middling offenses; and *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement by investigating the nature of the offense) extinguishes major offenses. Therefore, four medicinal remedies are required. Why is this so? This is a rhetorical inquiry.
"Seeking" (*mṛgayati*) is the explanation. That which arises from persons is twofold: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the person who brings it forward.

Because one investigates the offense based on the formal accusation, the dispute subsequently arises; thus, it originates from "seeking. Regarding "not disputing," the following distinguishes the medicine of non-application.
Answer: "Below" refers to a case where a bhikṣu has not actually committed the four pārājikas, the saṃghāvaśeṣas, or the sthūlātyayas, yet other bhikṣus claim he has.

Since he is a person of purity, one should simply grant him the *pratijñā-smṛti* (recollection before the assembly), just as in the case of Trapusa; the Buddha commanded that such a person be granted recollection.
Thus, although the fifth [category] of the Vinaya is improper—even if the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal motion with three proclamations) for granting recollection is performed—it remains invalid.
If the Dharma is not established and one acts contrary to this, it is called the "five cases of acting according to the Dharma. The two types of cessation (nirodha) manifest immediately;

"attaining a non-deluded mind" refers to recovering one's original sanity after a bout of madness has subsided. The "five matters" refer to the aforementioned five cases of acting according to the Dharma.
Regarding the term *qiè nán* (一切難) in the Vinaya text, *qiè* is pronounced as *qiè* (同竊), meaning "to obtain intimately" or "pressing difficulty," which encompasses the commentary on the precepts.

It is also said that this refers to obtaining an external inquiry (*bāhiraka-pucchā*); this inquiry does not appear in the Vinaya texts. Regarding the Master’s [Buddhaghosa’s] intention, it seems there may be cases where a dispute can be settled through a *sāmukkaṃsika*, a *tassapāpiyasika*, or a *tiṇavatthāraka*.
For now, we shall simply employ the one currently available: obtaining settlement through a *saṃmukhā-vinaya*. As for whether this applies to a dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), the answer is no.

This is as explained below in the three sections on seeking a dispute (*mūla-samatha*), where disputes involving one, two, or three persons, or the Saṅgha, may be easily settled through reconciliation at the first instance.

Therefore, there is no need for the *tṛṇa-praticchādana* (covering with grass). Consequently, regarding the subsequent mention of the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of disputes) involving *tṛṇa-praticchādana*, it is pointed out here again that there are also cases of settling a dispute through *saṃmukhavinaya* (decision in the presence of the parties), which is identical in meaning to the settlement of a *anvaya-vivāda* (dispute concerning an offense).

Question: Since this *anvaya-vivāda* is not settled by *tṛṇa-praticchādana*, why is it cited so circuitously? Answer: It is indeed as you have challenged; however, the Great Master [the Buddha] established this based on the underlying principle (*yukti*). Because there is... [text ends].

One should inquire as if searching for a dispute, or it may be extinguished by using the four medicines as described above. Alternatively, if the matter is allowed to spread and cannot be resolved through investigation, one should apply the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇapraticchādana*) method;
thus, the text below states that when a flow reaches the upper grade, it is extinguished by "covering over with grass," which can be applied by analogy to other cases.
Currently, the lower grade is extinguished by three methods and by one's own admission (*svavavāda*), while the five methods [apply] to the lower grade.
If one confesses the extinction of the five dharmas of the medium grade along with the *tṛṇastāra* (covering over as with grass) for the superior grade, it reaches three [stages].

If one does not descend [to confession], but rather employs the five dharmas in the presence [of the assembly] and the *tṛṇastāra* for the superior grade because the self-confession does not cease, then it flows upward to the superior grade.

Since the five dharmas are already present and the *tṛṇastāra* has been performed, once one has descended [to confession], there is no further need [for these procedures]. As for "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes that which is not [the case].

If one commits an offense with a deranged mind, what use is "non-delusion"? Furthermore, since there is no contradiction [in the rule], why would it be necessary to place this within the category of offenses?

These two cases are both determined: the former, characterized by turbidity, refers to those who have definitely committed an offense; the latter, characterized by clarity, refers to those who definitely did not commit an offense.
However, the subsequent conclusion employs the three medicinal remedies. The text is abbreviated here; the *Māyī* (presently extant) is translated as *Mūla-mātṛkā*, which is the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*.
The numbers two, three, and four all refer to those against whom the confession is directed; this includes cases where five or more persons are involved.

In such instances, the presiding monk (the *sāṃghika*) must perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Therefore, the Vinaya states: "One who wishes to confess within the Saṃgha should assume the proper posture, join their palms, and say:

'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess it before the Saṃgha. (This is to be said three times. The one receiving the confession should likewise perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*)."
The procedure is as prescribed in the Vinaya: if two or three people are receiving the confession, one must question those nearby.
If there is someone among that group who possesses wisdom, he should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*), saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now perform the 'grass-covering-the-earth' (*tṛṇastāraka*) confession regarding this dispute. This is the announcement. Having made the announcement, he further says: "O all..."

"Elders, regarding these matters of dispute that I have now committed as offenses—excluding the heavy offenses and the *karmavācanā* for prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople—if the elders grant their consent, I shall perform the 'covering with grass' (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) confession. The second assembly shall also speak thus;

this also contains the underlying meaning of the Great Teacher [the Buddha], which is consistent with what was previously stated regarding the seeking of resolution in disputes: a single approach toward reconciliation suffices to extinguish them."

This is it. Regarding the "four disputes" (*catur-vivāda*) of the Vinaya, when subdivided, they become eighteen. This means that each of the four types of disputes—such as the dispute regarding offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*)—is further divided into three, resulting in nine categories.

When these nine categories are applied across the three preceding types of disputes, they collectively form eighteen disputes; that is, each of the first three types of disputes gives rise to [these subdivisions].

This is a *vastu-araṇā* (dispute concerning a matter). What is it? For example, within a *vāda-araṇā* (dispute concerning speech), if one evaluates the right or wrong of the teachings and principles, or the lightness or gravity of the characteristics of transgressions, this is called a *vāda-araṇā*.

If one evaluates the right or wrong of a *karma* (formal ecclesiastical act), or whether there is confusion or awakening and fails to reach a decision, this is called a *vastu-araṇā* within a *vāda-araṇā*.

If one evaluates the clarity or turbidity of the three roots [of action], or the pervasion or obstruction of the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*), this is called an *anveṣaṇa-araṇā* (dispute concerning investigation). If one evaluates the application of the Dharma to discipline or reprove someone, this is called a *vastu-araṇā*.

To verify the reality of a matter by investigating its substance and essence is called "a dispute concerning the matter within a dispute over offenses" (*āpattiartha-adhikaraṇa*). Among the five groups of offenses, there are instances where the confession and evaluation are confused;

such cases are termed "offenses. Furthermore, when legal procedures (*dharma-karman*) are improperly conducted to determine the gravity of an offense, this is also called "a dispute concerning the matter within a dispute over offenses.

Since these follow the distinctions of the three preceding categories and their three grades, they encompass all seven types of remedies for extinction (*praśamana*); thus, they are termed "universal extinction" (*sarva-praśamana*).
I fear that, according to the *Vinaya*, disputes concerning matters (*vastu-ādhikaraṇa*) are extinguished by all methods of settlement (*sarva-samatha*), each according to the offense committed;

therefore, I shall explain this. If one says "fearing confusion" and so forth—such as when there is a dispute over words (*vāda-ādhikaraṇa*) or even a dispute over matters within a dispute over offenses (*āpatti-ādhikaraṇa*)—then there is no confusion.

Question: Regarding the four types of disputes mentioned previously, with the exception of the single question posed by the Great Master, all others were inquiries made by Ānanda to which the Tathāgata responded accordingly.
Now, why does the Great Master pose a question based on these by referring to the first three types of disputes?
