Ānanda initially asked generally about the application of medicine, and subsequently asked specifically about what was diminished. In the present case regarding the single type of dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), there is only a general question and it lacks a specific one;
why is this? It is because it is said that [the dispute] is completely extinguished without requiring further medicine, as it can be entirely eliminated by one or two [means].
Therefore, a specific question is posed to investigate and bring about understanding. Since this matter of dispute applies universally to all forms of extinction, [it is so treated].
Furthermore, because it is divided according to the preceding disputes, there is no exclusion regarding the sense of whether the matters are exhaustive or non-exhaustive.

Therefore, Ānanda remained silent and did not inquire, and the Tathāgata likewise did not provide an answer; thus it is said that this matter was left unresolved. Regarding the "matter" (*vastu*) as established by the Vinaya text, it states:

"Among the disputes over speech (*vāda-vivāda*), the matter is as follows... up to the disputes over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*); this constitutes the manifestation of the dispute over matters (*vastu-vivāda*)."
In the case of disputes arising from minor matters, the lower grade is settled by means of the three *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of); the middle grade is settled by five methods;

and the upper grade is settled by the method of the majority (*yebhuyyasikā*). Regarding disputes arising from recollection, the lower grade is settled by means of the five methods of *sativinaya* (settlement through recollection);

the middle grade is settled by the five methods of *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane); and the upper grade is settled by the method of *tassapāpiyasikā* (settlement by pronouncing the offense).
The superior grade of disputes arising from admissions is extinguished by the manifestation of the three methods together with the settlement through admission;

the middle and inferior grades of disputes arising from offenses are extinguished by the manifestation of the five methods together with the settlement through admission; the middle grade is extinguished by the manifestation of the five methods;

and the superior grade of disputes arising from matters is extinguished by "covering over as with grass. Thus, one should know that for disputes arising from matters, there is no separate remedy other than that which corresponds to the three grades.

Regarding the phrase "the upper [remedies] are applied," since each is extinguished along with its corresponding [defilement], it is said that "all are extinguished by extinction. Regarding the ten lower [remedies], these refer to matters of constant practice;
even if disputes arise, one need only apply the single remedy present at hand for extinction, without having to employ additional or separate remedies.
To introduce what was previously explained: the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*) are the medicines capable of eradicating [conflict].
Since medicine is not administered in vain, there must be the corresponding illnesses for which it is prescribed; therefore, the four types of dispute (*catvāry adhikaraṇāni*) are clarified here.

According to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the four disputes are first explained as the source from which illness arises, followed by the listing of the seven medicines as the methods for their removal and eradication. This also follows the intent of the author’s composition. Now that this has been stated:
Because there are seven methods for extinguishing disputes, it is logically sound that the "medicine" is placed first and the "disease" last;

this does not detract from the principle. Since the principle below is profound and quiescent, it cannot manifest itself in a formal sequence; it must rely on provisional verbal expressions (*upāya*) to illuminate and reveal it.
To examine what follows, one evaluates the principle as the cause for the arising of disputes. Regarding the section on "disputes," the third part concludes.

Regarding the "roots" (*mūla*): one may employ whichever root—seeing, hearing, or suspicion—to bring forth the confession. The preceding offenses encompass the five and seven categories of transgressions, as well as violations of the precepts, views, and deportment.

The conditions consist of both general and specific factors, none of which may be lacking. The objects of the action include the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), the *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*, and other such objects.
The violation of the teachings refers to non-compliance with the two types of instruction: prohibitions and permissions. As for the performance of the act, it is...
Regarding matters such as sexual misconduct and theft, the *Baoyi dacao* (One Hundred and One Abstracts) states: "This is a general enumeration and not necessarily fixed to that number;
it may also be cited according to the *Śāriputra-vinaya* (*Shisong*). In that [text], there are definitely one hundred and one [cases];

if one performs one motion (*jñapti*) and one formal act (*karmavācanā*), then these are cited broadly as the matters to be judged by means of the motion and the formal act. When categorized by type, there are one hundred and thirty-four rules, as follows:

This passage from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* cites the text of the eighth fascicle. That source introduces it as: "The Vinaya for extinguishing strife and litigation," followed by the explanation: "Now, the original text of the *Śāstra* is not skillfully phrased;
the *Chao* (the present commentary) has made revisions. For instance, where that source says: 'Striking one another and using abusive language is called strife (*yù*)', the current text simply says:
'Two persons contending together is called strife. Furthermore, 'to break the track' (*zhé duàn*) refers to breaking the path; [the text] has been revised to 'to adjudicate' (*píng duàn*)."
The *Yi* (Book of Changes) says regarding the hexagram *Song*: "Heaven and water move in opposite directions; this is the image of *Song*. Kong Yingda explains:

"The Way of Heaven turns westward, while water flows eastward; this is the image of *Song*. Now, [the text] says that when each asserts their own principle, they contradict one another—this is the meaning.

That [commentary] says that when each asserts their own affairs and assists in determining right and wrong, it is called *Song*. Here, we simply say that asserting one's own principle is called *Song*, summarizing the underlying cause.
Regarding the determination of what is right or wrong through verbal dispute, there has not yet been a definitive resolution; one seeks out the dispute by investigating prior offenses.

As for the statement "not yet knowing whether an offense exists," this refers to receiving [the designation] based on the cause. Regarding those said to be "based on the object" (*ālambana*), an offense is committed in relation to an object; however, while it is already an offense, its gravity has not yet been distinguished.

As for "matters" (*vastu*), these arise from objects and matters such as formal procedures (*jñapti-karman*). Therefore, the dispute concerning offenses and matters is established in relation to the object.
If the title were "Disputes over Objects," why would it not say "Disputes over Causes" instead, but rather "Matters of Seeking Faults through Speech"? Why is there a general inquiry [into this]?

The section beginning with "What are the objects? is the explanation. If it were called "Disputes over Objects," since objects are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one would have to know which specific object is intended;
therefore, it does not follow from the object, but establishes the two names based on "matters of offenses. The section beginning with "Speech" explains that it does not say "Disputes over Causes."

As for "by means of" (*yi*), in terms of discourse it universally subsumes both heterodox and orthodox views; in terms of seeking (*mi*), it universally contains both the pure and the turbid, as well as transgressions and non-transgressions—all of which are essential points to be understood through concise summary.
If one speaks of "cause" (*yin*), one must know what kind of cause this is;

therefore, knowing that the two meanings of "discourse" (*yan*) and "seeking" (*mi*) are inferred from this "cause," yet cannot themselves be designated as the "cause," it is said: "it does not rely on the name 'cause.'"
Question: You stated that the term "dispute over names" (nāma-vivāda) generally encompasses all [four types of disputes];

however, since the principle (*artha*) being expressed is likewise encompassed, why not designate it as a "dispute over principles" (*artha-vivāda*)? Answer: This is because each of the four disputes possesses its own distinct principle.

If only one were established, there would be no basis for distinguishing the others. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "distinctly grasped with attachment" (*pṛthag-abhiniveśa*), the character "without" (*wu*) should be understood as applying throughout [the entire passage].
Because there is attachment and emotional clinging toward what is below, the three grades are the superior, middling, and inferior.

This means that while the essence of principle is uniformly harmonious and follows a single standard regardless of manifestation, it is fundamentally without fault or affliction; yet, due to attachment and conceptualization, it is divided into three grades—this is the first meaning.
Furthermore, the principle also penetrates all four [grades]—this is the second meaning. Since these two meanings are clarified, the name "dispute over principle" is not manifested.
Although the term "dispute" (*vāda*) encompasses one sense among the four [types of disputes], it lacks the sense of "adherence to error" (*abhiniveśa*).

Since there must be adherence to error for something to be called a "contention" (*vivāda*), it is permissible to derive its designation from the word "speech" (*vāda*). Regarding the remaining three [types of disputes], one should first raise the objection:
"Since 'speech' applies to all four, why are the latter three not called 'speech-contentions'? This is answered by the text: "They are named according to their respective preceding matters. If...
Furthermore, those who propose alternative definitions fail to distinguish [the categories].

In the subsequent discussion, one should first raise the objection: "If 'seeking' (*vitarka*) is established based on its object (*ālambana*), why is it that only 'concealment' (*mrakṣa*) is named after its cause (*hetu*)?
The intent of the following explanation is this: "If it were established based on the object, then since the objects differ in being clear or turbid, there ought to be two distinct categories."

If the categories were opened up, they would become fragmented and tedious; therefore, we establish only the "search for names" (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*), which comprehensively includes both conformity to purity and opposition to turbidity.
If that is so, then the two disputes regarding transgressions (*adhikaraṇa*) may also be called "causes" (*hetu*);

since turbid transgressions are subsumed under these causes, and since these matters extend to speech—given that the search for speech is already termed a "cause"—then matters may also be termed "causes. Why, then, do you restrict it solely to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*)? Will you...?

Regarding the phrase "the offense is established": if the name were derived from the cause of the offense, it would not differ from the term "seeking" (*vitandā*), and furthermore, the two types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) would become confused.

Furthermore, the sub-commentary (*śū*) should ask: "The dispute of seeking (*vitandā-adhikaraṇa*) cannot be defined by its object (*viṣaya*) because it distinguishes between clarity and turbidity; therefore, the dispute of speech (*bhāṣaṇā-adhikaraṇa*) should [be defined by its object]."

One may follow the perspective of the objects (*viṣaya*) and immediately explain the meaning of the commentary as follows: "Although there is no distinction between clarity and turbidity, there is a distinction between the 'dust' and the 'sands.
Since verbal disputes do not exist, and there is no distinction between the immeasurable 'dust' and 'sands,' it is likewise impossible to designate [the two truths] based on their objects.

The phrase "if below" is a concessive inclusion (*yady api*), while "capturing below" is a refutation (*tathāpi*). The "Two Truths" refer to the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). This means that even if one were to establish the inclusion based on the objects, [it would still not be tenable].

Why is it that this statement does not exhaustively cover all forms of dispute? It is because disputes regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) may be said to involve objects (*viṣaya*), yet how could disputes regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) possibly involve objects?

Therefore, this [definition] does not encompass them all. Furthermore, since the ultimate and the conventional do not necessarily depend upon one another—just as one may dispute the objects of conventional truth without necessarily depending on the ultimate, and since the ultimate is not mutually dependent [on the conventional]—it follows that, with respect to objects, [the distinction between the two truths is not exhaustive].
It is clear that while the conventional can be subsumed, the ultimate cannot; this is explained by the principle that the lower does not depend upon the higher.
Since the former is named after its object because it is dependent upon that object, this is also established through a reciprocal inversion of the terms.

"Right" and "wrong" constitute one pair; "pure" and "turbid" constitute another. Since the search for dispute already contains the distinction between the pure and the turbid, it cannot derive its name from the object [of the dispute].
Furthermore, since the matter of dispute (*vastu-kalaha*) also contains the distinction between right and wrong, how could it derive its name from the object?

The phrase "already performed" means that only what has been performed is called a *karmavastu* (formal act). Since this does not apply to other matters, its meaning is strictly limited; because it is limited...

Therefore, while the object (*viṣaya*) is restricted to one, that which has not yet been performed—though it may be both *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and non-*karmavācanā*—is nonetheless called an "affair" (*vastu*).
Since both are termed "affairs," they are likewise one and the same. Thus, the offense (*āpatti*) and the affair both derive their names from the object;
they are not comparable to the distinction between clarity and turbidity or beginning and end. Consequently, one cannot seek [the offense] apart from the object.

Question: Regarding "accusing of offenses" (*āpattipratijñā*), it is as explained in the text. "Regarding activity" (*karmasamutthāna*) refers to the formal ritual (*karma*), which is the business of the Saṃgha.

Regarding "activity," there is dispute; regarding "instruction and practice," there is seeking [fault]; regarding "discipline and practice," there is the commission of an offense. "Regarding principle" (*yukti*) below indicates the extensive explanation; "now below" (*athedānīm*) concludes the summary.

The treatise states that when verbal expressions reach their conclusion, they are termed "contention" (*vivāda*). Although such contention exists, it is not called "verbal contention" because it does not require the *vinaya* for its resolution.
Why is this so? This interrogates the reason. First, it explains that the two assemblies—the monks and the nuns—are distinct in status;
furthermore, it is rare for nuns to seek a formal debate against the monks. Second, it is because the nuns belong to the lower assembly.

One must not overstep by imitating the rules of the Great Sangha, nor does this fall within the limits of a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). If a dispute arises, why must it be extinguished immediately? Since there is no doctrinal obstruction, one may proceed.
Regarding the three lower [categories], two involve the removal of offenses and the receiving of confession; apart from these, there are none that share the same method.

As for the "immediate" (*sadyas*) category, if one speaks within their own respective assemblies, the opposite of the three aforementioned meanings constitutes the remaining three cases; the same applies to the other three, though the text is abbreviated.
Because one seeks out the offense, it is said: "down to the point where there are differences. In the *Vinaya*, there are four propositions:

a bhikṣu disputes with a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu disputes with a bhikṣuṇī; a bhikṣuṇī disputes with a bhikṣu; and a bhikṣuṇī disputes with a bhikṣuṇī. For this reason, we now examine the matters of offenses.
Regarding the two types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), each has three points of difference. First, regarding the offense itself, there are three [points].
Regarding the differences: "one or two bhikṣus" refers to one or two; "or [one or] three" refers to three. The aforementioned "two assemblies" refers to the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs.
They are not included among the offenses of dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) because they are not the primary assembly for disputes, and thus they are not termed "offenses of dispute.
However, this does not preclude their being subsumed within the category of "offenses of contention" (*vivāda*). Alternatively, the phrase "one or two bhikṣus" below serves as a further explanation.
The second phrase concerns the grounds for a *vāda-vivāda* (verbal dispute). Regarding what constitutes a verbal dispute:

although the offense may have arisen among the community of nuns, the dispute itself occurs among the bhikṣus because their views differ and they voice these differences, thereby forming a dispute; hence it is called a "verbal dispute.

Alternatively, regarding the three points of contention within the lower-tier matters of the bhikṣus, the contrast with the upper-tier matters can be understood by analogy. This is because one fears that this community might, due to a dispute over those [lower] matters, [cause trouble].
As for "breaking" (the Saṃgha), it constitutes the principle of breaking the Saṃgha; logically, this must rely on the aforementioned "majority decision by those present.

It applies to both many and few: four or more is called "many," while three or fewer is called "few. Regarding the "searching for a dispute" (mṛgita-kalaha) and so forth, this conversely clarifies that with three people—if four were present they would constitute a formal assembly and thus could not be censured—it results in a formal censure by the Saṃgha. Third, regarding the "judgment" (vinirṇaya), it follows the words [of the majority]. "Searching" (mṛgita) means...
This constitutes three judgments regarding transgressions.

As for "root" (*mūla*), it carries the meaning of "arising and developing. First, the *Vinaya* states: "By what is one rooted? Greed, hatred, and delusion are roots; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are roots.
This is explained in terms of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings. Second, [the root refers to] the basis.
The *Vinaya* (Jīlü) states: "The Saṃgha is the root; the boundary (*sīmā*) is the root; the person is the root. To explain this further:

regarding the four types of Saṃgha-roots, in terms of number, they consist of four, five, ten, or twenty persons. Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Buddha spoke to Cunda, he taught that there are four types:

first, those who have reached the ultimate (*atyanta-prāpta*; meaning those beyond training who have exhausted all afflictions); second, those who show the path (*mārga-darśaka*; referring to those at the three lower fruits who are able to correctly [teach]...).

1. Teaching the Dharma to others so that they may practice it; 2. Receiving the Path (referring to those from the stage of the candidate for the first fruit [srotāpanna-pratipannaka] downward, who possess the noble path within their bodies); 3. Polluting the Path (referring to those who violate the precepts); 4. Regarding the realms and persons, this is based on the *Prakaraṇapāda* and other treatises:
boundaries (*sīmā*) arise naturally, or disputes arise concerning one, two, or three persons; thus, the "roots" (*mūla*) are explained in terms of both non-sentient objects and sentient matters.
Furthermore, the following citation from the *Śāstra* explains the six types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), categorized according to the object of the dispute itself.
To give rise to views that do not accord with reality, to conceive of and grasp at what is not the truly supreme Dharma as being so, is called "view-grasping" (*parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*).
To hold to an extreme mind is called "extreme view" (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). To grasp at a principle with a deviant mind is called "false view" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
These arise from karma and afflictions; thus they are explained by way of their faculties. Below, the eighteen dharmas are extensively explained: namely, dharma, non-dharma, and so forth.

Regarding the Vinaya offenses—whether they are offenses or non-offenses, light or heavy, with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) or without remainder, gross or not gross, habitual or not habitual, prescribed or not prescribed, and taught or not taught—such matters as these arise from the evaluation of superior qualities and give rise to disputes.
This, then, explains the roots based on the nine right and nine wrong dharmas. The first two are the same as before: namely, greed and non-greed.

The second is the boundary of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-sīmā*). As stated above regarding the "roots," the *Vinaya* says that one seeks out offenses by means of the three types of formal accusations (*tri-ud-dhura*):

namely, for breaking the precepts, for wrong views, and for improper conduct (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, they are not the same; the aforementioned three accusations constitute the matters of the offense (*āpatti-vastu*).
The passage beginning with "greed" explains the first root. According to this, it is from the three wholesome minds of accusation that disputes arise.

Furthermore, whereas the preceding section was based on the matters under evaluation, this section also encompasses the matters of offenses (*āpatti*). This is because when the Saṃgha does not censure a monk, that monk now conversely censures others arbitrarily, thereby giving rise to dispute.
Regarding the remote conditions (*dūrapratyaya*): the formal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) arises directly from the offense, while the peripheral cause arises from the boundary (*sīmā*);

thus, the offense still belongs to the remote condition. As for the "others," this refers to persons; that is, the search for the dispute arises because of a person’s offense, taking the person as its root.
Regarding the six ways offenses arise, the *Vṛddha-śāstra* states: "There may be an offense arising from the body but not from mind or speech;

there may be an offense arising from speech but not from body or mind; there may be an offense arising from both body and speech but not from the mind; there may be an offense arising from both mind and body but not from speech;
there may be an offense arising from speech and mind but not from the body; and there may be an offense arising from the body [but not from mind or speech]."

The arising [of disputes] through speech and mind constitutes the sixth. Since it is stated below that among the transgressions within the Vinaya, only the three roots such as greed (*lobha*) are taught as roots and not the three such as non-greed (*alobha*), this explains [the matter]: the "arising of disputes" refers to evaluating a prior transgression and thereby giving rise to a dispute;
it does not preclude the presence of the three roots such as non-greed as the root of the dispute. The first two [roots] are simply greed and non-greed.

These two refer to persons within the *saṃgha-sīmā*; this is explained in terms of disputes concerning single matters. If combined with the three lower types of disputes regarding matters, they will differ accordingly.

As for the remaining three, since their meanings as the three lower disputes are already distinct, there are no eighteen matters; thus, the three formal accusations (*tri-ud-dhura*) are included within the search (*paryeṣaṇā*).
Regarding the six offenses among the minor matters within the disputes: since there are no three types of formal accusations (*tri-uddeśa*) therein, the six offenses are also not mentioned.

According to those who apply the principle of generalization, because speech is common to all, the three types of formal accusations and the six offenses may also exist within the disputes over speech;
likewise, because there are matters of offense, non-offense, lightness, and gravity within the eighteen matters, these eighteen matters may also exist within the search for offenses (*paryeṣaṇā*).

Within the category of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), there can likewise be eighteen instances of formal accusation (*tri-uddeśa*) and six instances of offense (*āpatti*), because the dispute over matters (*vastu-adhikaraṇa*) permeates all [disputes].
This refers to the fact that within each of the three aforementioned types of disputes, a dispute over matters may arise.

Regarding the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), these are the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; however, whichever of these three natures one engages in gives rise to the four types of disputes.

The principle is easy to understand; therefore, it is said that by following the meaning, the characteristics can be known. To know their full extent, one should refer to the detailed explanations in the *Pravāraṇā* (Extinguishing Disputes) section.

Generally speaking, those from the stage prior to the Path of Seeing up to the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are all called "ordinary beings," and they do not transcend the categories of the outer and inner ordinary beings.

Regarding the broad and concise [classifications], the former refers to the two types of training in the precepts, while the latter refers to the three fruits of the seeker (*śaikṣa*). Below this, because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of both the views and the thoughts within the three realms have been exhausted, there is only...
Regarding the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), there is the transgression of neither-good-nor-evil; this refers to the transgression of both natures.

If it were to encompass the wholesome, even the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) would seem to include transgressions of a wholesome nature, which are merely prohibitions against transgressing the precepts. Alternatively, according to the Vinaya, the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) are said to be "either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

Why, then, is it here stated that they are unwholesome? The answer is that the following section provides a detailed classification based on verbal disputes (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*). This is in view of the initial evaluation.

At that time, the subsequent mind is discordant and afflicted; this is "contention" (*raṇa*). Since contention belongs to the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and because it is precisely the contention of the subsequent mind that is being extinguished here, it is said to be unwholesome.
It is not the case that at the initial moment of extinction the wholesome nature of the analytical investigation is indeterminate;

rather, depending on the three types of contention that arise, there is "contention regarding matters. Consequently, [the nature] may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, and is thus also indeterminate.

Question: Since the three natures (trisvabhāva) are fundamentally distinct, why do you say that "wholesome" includes both wholesome and neutral, while "unwholesome" includes both unwholesome and neutral?

If this were so, the three natures would become conflated. Answer: In various treatises, the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome actions are all explained as having three grades. Actions performed with a fierce and intense mind are classified as superior;

those performed with a casual or indifferent mind are classified as inferior; and the remainder are classified as middling. Within these categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, it is the superior grade that is taken [as the definitive standard].

Regarding the karma that projects the total retribution (*vipāka*) induced by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*): because inferior and middling grades of karma are weak and cannot act as projectors, they can only act as completing karma (*paripūrakakarman*).
What is now termed "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) refers only to the middling and inferior grades;

these are called neutral in relation to their inability to project the total retribution of wholesome or unwholesome states. If this is so, why not call them all "neutral," and why further speak of "wholesome" and "unwholesome"?
Regarding the explanation of "distinct retribution" (*viśeṣa-vipāka*) below, it is so named in contrast to the aforementioned "general retribution" (*sāmānya-vipāka*).

This is because the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) is able to draw forth a general existence, while the completing karma (*paripūrakak-karma*) is able to embellish the particulars. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "One karma projects one birth; many karmas can complete it.

What is here termed "inducing" (*karoti*) refers to wholesome or neutral karma inducing a wholesome distinct retribution, and unwholesome or neutral karma inducing an unwholesome distinct retribution.
"Retribution" (*vipāka*) does not refer to the "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), nor does it refer to the "unspecified" (*avyākṛta*) that is indeterminate and devoid of both good and evil;
therefore, one may now speak of "good," "unspecified," and so forth.

If that is so, then regarding the "dispute over matters" (*vastu-vivāda*): when one seeks an offense based on words, it is called a dispute over matters (*vastu-vivāda*); however, it is merely like [the following].

Regarding the formal acts (*karmas*) such as the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations) for the reception [of precepts] and so forth: if there are those who do not comply with the seniority descending from the three [higher ordinations], this is termed a "contention.

As for the methods of treatment for such persons, they include censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), and so on. As for the "accusation of an offense" (*codanā*): one must raise the offense of the person in question;

the accuser must be able to present evidence before the Sangha to correctly establish the offense. Only when the accused has submitted should they be summoned to enter the assembly and stand before [the Sangha].

Once a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) has been performed, if one does not confess according to the facts but instead bows their head in feigned submission, then acts such as the "not seeing" (*appaṭikamma*) or "not acknowledging" (*adesanāgāminī*) offenses, as well as the method of expelling a "bad horse," all involve searching for matters within the proceedings.

Now, regarding the evaluation of using [such acts] to incite disputes, this involves searching for matters within the proceedings, such as harboring malicious intent; this applies to both the agent and the object, just as when a governing monk intends to bring ill repute upon another.

Those who falsely attribute [an offense] to another, those who desire to perform confession but do not apply the proper method, and those whose minds are not purified of malice toward the person being disciplined—such as by concealing or hiding the offense rather than confessing—are considered "offenses" (āpatti) in terms of their transgressions; yet, in terms of the formal ritual (karmavācanā), they are designated as "matters" (vastu).
Therefore, within the category of offenses, these matters are treated as a separate chapter, namely, the *Śīrṣa-vyākhyā* (The Commentary on the Head).

Alternatively, the *Vinaya* states: "If monks engage in verbal disputes based on eighteen matters, such that they listen to one another and are in disagreement regarding right and wrong, this constitutes 'verbal dispute.
It is like parents speaking with their children, children speaking with their parents, or even others engaging in mutual verbal disputes;
this is what is meant by 'speech. If monks engage in verbal disputes with other monks based on these eighteen matters, it is likewise."
This non-harmony is speech; it is both dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) and one of the eighteen matters of dispute.

There are cases where there is speech but no dispute, such as when children speak with their parents—this is dispute that is speech, namely one of the eighteen matters of dispute. There are cases that are not speech:
excluding disputes of speech, the remaining three types of dispute are as described in the *Vinaya*’s methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), where "single dispute" refers to just one.
"Person against person" (*puggalā puggalaṃ*) and so forth: this establishes a syntactic structure based on the singular sense of one person following another.
Alternatively, as stated in the *Upāli-vinaya*, "there is speech that constitutes verbal dispute" (*vādo vādādhikaraṇaṃ*); this is established in contrast to the preceding [category].

That is to say, when two individuals each singly cite eighteen matters and contend with one another in discord, this is a verbal dispute (*vādādhikaraṇa*). Since there is no companion and the force is solitary, it is further a "solitary dispute."

Alternatively, following the preceding section, "non-contention through speech" (*avivāda-vāk*) refers to instances where one person speaks alone—such as when addressing parents or others—without each party vying with the other;
thus it is called "non-contention through speech" rather than "single contention.
This explains the preceding term "contention through speech," which refers merely to words exchanged in mutual dialogue and response; therefore, it is not [contention].
Regarding "dispute" (*adhikaraṇa*): some [commentaries] state below and above that "dispute by speech" (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) refers precisely to speech;

this too is intended as such. That is to say, eighteen matters of disharmony are termed "dispute by speech," which is simply speech. All such cases belong to the category of simple "dispute by speech.

This is not the same as the three types of disputes involving the search for an offense (*mārga-apatti-adhikaraṇa*). While previously there was one person without a companion, now these two people together have [the dispute].

It is called "heavy" (*guru*) because it is accompanied [by other factors]. Alternatively, the following cases are also the same as the preceding; they are established as in the first instance, namely, by means of the eighteen matters of the first phrase to manifest this.
The remaining phrases may be understood by analogy with the above; one simply adds "accompanied" to constitute "heavy," which differs from the preceding.

The three types of disputes, such as "seeking" (*mṛgayā*), etc., should likewise follow the above by having categories of single and heavy [cases]; the method for understanding them should be taken from within the discussion of disputes.
The drum has a sound that, though long suppressed, does not vibrate; with but a single lift of the mallet to awaken it, those who follow may together explore the secret treasury.
May all wear the seal of the precepts upon them, so that these teachings may be transmitted to the future without being reduced to ashes.
